The popular advice is straightforward: install more solar, add a battery, fit a heat pump and charge the electric vehicle when the sun is shining. That advice misses the most expensive part of **renewable energy integration** in a high-end home. The challenge isn't just generating clean electricity. It's coordinating generation, storage, heating, charging, architecture and the local network connection, often within a listed building, a conservation area or a tightly constrained South West London plot.

The national picture is encouraging. Official government statistics record that renewables generated **50.4% of total UK electricity in 2024** , up from **46.5% in 2023** , with renewable output at about **144 TWh**. Wind supplied **29.2%** , solar supplied **5.2%** , and low-carbon sources reached **65% of generation** in that year. This was the first full year in which renewables supplied more than half of UK electricity. [_The UK Government's DUKES 2025 statistics_](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68dbe477ef1c2f72bc1e4c4d/DUKES_2025_Chapters_1-7.pdf) show how far grid integration has progressed.

That achievement doesn't guarantee an easy connection for a house in Wimbledon Village, Richmond or Surrey. A property can have an excellent roof for photovoltaic panels and still face export restrictions, limited local capacity or a need to manage simultaneous loads. In affluent homes with pools, basement amenities and full electrification, **local flexibility and coordinated design increasingly matter more than adding generation alone**.
  

## Why National Renewable Records Do Not Guarantee Easy Home Integration
  

A national renewable record describes the electricity system as a whole. It doesn't tell you whether a particular street can accept additional export from rooftop solar, whether a local transformer can accommodate a heat pump and EV charger, or whether a listed roof can accept visible panels. Those questions sit much closer to the property.

The UK's renewable mix is also variable. Wind and solar output changes with weather, daylight and season, while household demand often peaks at different times. That mismatch is manageable at system level only when storage, demand response, network operation and generation work together. The [_UK Government's Clean Flexibility Roadmap update_](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50fce4a4890e65cce64d07/clean-flexibility-roadmap-2026-update.pdf) records **2.3 GW of new flexibility capacity energised in 2025 alone** , and describes flexibility procurement as a distinct system-operations discipline.
  

For a homeowner, flexibility means the ability to change when electricity is imported, exported or consumed. A battery might absorb surplus solar. An EV might charge later. A heat pump might preheat hot water before a period of higher demand. These controls can help, but they don't remove the need to understand the local connection.

### The local constraint is often hidden
  

Transmission constraints already affect renewable deployment across Great Britain. [_Cambridge academic analysis_](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/d7d5cd74-275f-410f-a2fb-123e52872638) identifies the north/south divide as a fundamental bottleneck, with Scottish wind facing greater curtailment risk when power cannot move efficiently towards southern load centres. A separate Cambridge paper found that under zonal constraints, variable renewable energy curtailment reached **10,426 GWh** , compared with **8,771 GWh** under a copper-plate assumption, a difference of **19%**. [_The EPRG paper explains the effect of network constraints_](https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/eprg-wp2524.pdf).

The lesson applies at a different scale to homes. A property isn't an isolated energy island. Its equipment interacts with a distribution network that has physical limits, operating rules and connection procedures. A larger solar array can therefore create more export management work rather than a smoother project.
  

> **Practical rule:** Treat the grid connection as a design input, not an administrative form to complete after the architectural scheme is fixed.
### Why architects need to be involved early
  

The architectural consequences are substantial. Solar panels need a visually acceptable location, inverters need a dry and accessible position, batteries need suitable ventilation and fire strategy, and heat pumps need plant space, acoustic consideration and sensible routes for services. In a basement extension, these requirements compete with cinema equipment, gym ventilation, pool plant, wine storage and joinery.

Early coordination lets the design team reserve space before every cupboard and riser has been claimed. It also gives the M&E consultant a realistic building model rather than an equipment list attached to an unchangeable plan. For a listed property, the same process helps separate what can be concealed, what can be reversed and what may need conservation officer discussion.
  

National renewable records are a reason to plan confidently, not a reason to assume that every home can connect without friction.
  

## Understanding How Home Energy Systems Work Together
  

A high-end home behaves less like a collection of appliances and more like a small, managed energy system. Solar PV produces electricity when daylight and weather allow. A heat pump converts electricity into heat, an EV charger can create a substantial flexible load, and a battery shifts electricity between generation and demand. The value comes from how these components are controlled together.

A property with a swimming pool may have pool circulation, filtration, heating and dehumidification. A basement cinema adds ventilation, projection, audio and conditioning. A gym can require fresh-air systems and cooling, while a wine room needs stable environmental conditions. None of these loads is incompatible with renewable energy, but simultaneous operation can create a sharp demand peak.
  

![A diagram illustrating a home renewable energy system integration hub connecting solar panels, battery, grid, heat pump, and EV.](https://cdnimg.co/115ce871-5d39-4334-a7fe-0d49d566c436/664c8419-e23d-46b3-af8a-af0c2d124a72/renewable-energy-integration-energy-hub.jpg)
  

The central question is not, “How large should each product be?” It is, “What should happen when several demands occur at once?”
  

### Solar PV needs a destination

The central question is not, “How large should each product be?” It is, “What should happen when several demands occur at once?”
  

### Solar PV needs a destination
  

Solar electricity has several possible destinations. It can serve immediate household demand, charge a battery, heat water through an appropriate control strategy, charge an EV or be exported to the grid. Without a hierarchy, the system may export at an inconvenient time, leave the battery empty before evening demand or charge the vehicle when imported electricity is expensive.
  

**Load shifting** means moving a flexible activity to a more suitable period. EV charging is usually the clearest example. If the vehicle doesn't need to leave immediately, charging can respond to solar production, tariff periods or a wider household control strategy. Hot-water heating can sometimes provide a form of thermal storage, allowing the home to use electricity at one time and retain useful heat for later.

### Heat pumps need a building strategy
  

A heat pump performs best when the building's heat loss, emitters, controls and hot-water requirements have been considered together. In a draughty or poorly insulated property, specifying a larger unit can increase plant size, running cost and spatial pressure without resolving comfort or efficiency problems.
  

The building fabric remains part of the energy system. Windows, insulation, airtightness, shading and ventilation affect the heat pump's workload. For refurbishment projects, material choices and detailing should be coordinated with the services strategy. Guidance on [_sustainable insulation materials for residential projects_](https://www.harperlatterarchitects.co.uk/post/sustainable-insulation-materials) can help inform that conversation, particularly where wall build-ups and internal character need careful treatment.
  

### Batteries are control assets, not ornaments

### Batteries are control assets, not ornaments
  

A battery shouldn't be sized solely to maximise storage on paper. Its useful role may be reducing evening imports, absorbing constrained solar export, supporting selected loads or responding to tariff periods. Those objectives can conflict. A battery held in reserve for backup won't behave like one optimised for daily cycling, and a battery in an unconstrained location may offer financial value without solving a local network problem.
  

For high-end homes, the control platform deserves as much attention as the battery chemistry. It should coordinate PV, the heat pump, EV charging, hot water and selected discretionary loads, while allowing the homeowner to override schedules. Good controls reduce the likelihood of every system starting at once, which is often more valuable than installing the largest available components.

> The most expensive system is often the one that has been specified correctly in isolation but incorrectly as part of the house.
## Assessing Your Property for Renewable Energy Integration
  

The assessment should begin with the building, not a product brochure. A sensible sequence prevents the common mistake of selecting a heat pump, battery or PV array before understanding where it can go, how it can be routed and whether the network can accept the proposed operation.
  

![A property assessment infographic for renewable energy integration showing site appraisal, structural survey, and energy audit sections.](https://cdnimg.co/115ce871-5d39-4334-a7fe-0d49d566c436/def73b55-004a-4417-9f7c-bfb69428f67a/renewable-energy-integration-property-assessment.jpg)
  

### Start with the site and envelope

### Start with the site and envelope
  

Record roof orientation, pitch, shading, overlooking conditions and likely visual impact. In South West London, mature trees, neighbouring rooflines and conservation policies can matter as much as compass direction. A roof that appears suitable from the garden may be unsuitable once dormers, chimneys, parapets and protected views are mapped.
  

Check the existing roof before placing a structural load on it. The survey should consider condition, build-up, access, fire separation and future maintenance. Installing panels on a roof that needs replacement soon can create avoidable removal and reinstatement costs.
  

### Map plant and service routes

### Map plant and service routes
  

Draw the complete route from generation to control equipment and distribution board. Identify positions for the inverter, battery, heat-pump cylinder, buffer components, ventilation plant and any required isolators. Basements need particular care. A technically convenient plant room may be too remote from the electrical intake, difficult to ventilate or exposed to flood risk.
  

Reserve access for replacement and servicing. High-end interiors often conceal equipment beautifully at completion but leave no practical route for a future engineer. A removable panel or properly sized riser is a small architectural decision with long-term value.
  

### Test the energy and connection assumptions

### Test the energy and connection assumptions
  

An energy audit should distinguish annual consumption from peak demand and identify which loads are flexible. A family's routine, pool schedule, EV use and occupancy pattern may matter more than an annual total. Ask the M&E consultant to model half-hourly operation where possible, because average consumption hides the moments that stress the system.
  

The DNO conversation should happen before equipment is committed. Ask about import and export capacity, application requirements, likely reinforcement, export limitation and whether flexibility could reduce the required connection scope. The [_Clean Flexibility Roadmap update_](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50fce4a4890e65cce64d07/clean-flexibility-roadmap-2026-update.pdf) describes a practical pattern of identifying local constraints, placing or contracting flexibility nearby and verifying dispatchability against half-hourly balancing needs.

A useful appraisal pack contains:
  

  * **Measured baseline:** Gather bills, meter data, plant schedules and occupancy patterns.
  * **Architectural constraints:** Record listed status, conservation context, roof visibility, protected fabric and basement limitations.
  * **Services model:** Map heat, hot water, ventilation, charging, storage and control locations.
  * **Network response:** Keep the DNO correspondence, application assumptions and export conditions with the design information.


  

## Integration Approaches for Listed Buildings Versus New Builds

## Integration Approaches for Listed Buildings Versus New Builds
  

Listed buildings and new builds can both achieve effective renewable energy integration, but they start from opposite positions. A new build allows the architect to set orientation, roof geometry, plant space, risers, insulation and electrical infrastructure before construction. A listed building asks the team to fit modern performance into an existing composition without damaging significance or creating an intrusive visual result.

In Wimbledon, Richmond and nearby conservation areas, the planning case may depend on what can be seen from public viewpoints, how reversibly an intervention can be installed and whether historic fabric remains intact. Roof-mounted PV may be efficient but unacceptable on a prominent front slope. A discreet rear roof arrangement, a carefully designed outbuilding or a ground-mounted solution may be more appropriate, although each has its own planning, shading and environmental implications.
  

![A comparison infographic showing the challenges and opportunities of renewable energy integration for listed buildings versus new builds.](https://cdnimg.co/115ce871-5d39-4334-a7fe-0d49d566c436/f1a5a6b1-3ab7-4b95-9c76-393d8b38707a/renewable-energy-integration-building-comparison.jpg)
  

### Listed buildings require selective intervention

### Listed buildings require selective intervention
  

A conservation-led strategy doesn't mean refusing modern services. It means choosing where intervention creates the least harm. Heat-pump equipment may need a concealed garden position, acoustic screening or a route through later fabric rather than historic rooms. Internal insulation can improve performance but may affect cornices, shutters, skirtings and room proportions. Services should follow existing voids or secondary spaces wherever possible.
  

Battery placement is another design issue. A basement extension provides useful plant capacity, but the battery still needs a suitable environment, access, separation and a coherent relationship with the electrical intake. Hiding equipment behind bespoke joinery without considering heat, maintenance or fire requirements is not integration. It's concealment, and concealment can make servicing harder.

For homeowners considering air-source systems, the technical and architectural implications are set out in [_this guide to air-source heat-pump installation_](https://www.harperlatterarchitects.co.uk/post/air-source-heat-pump-installation). The correct solution depends on the building, the heat emitters, the available external position and the planning context.
  

### New builds offer freedom, but only if it is used
  

A new build can orient roof planes for PV, set aside a dedicated energy centre and design ceiling zones for distribution. It can also accommodate larger thermal stores, plant access and future cable routes without cutting through finished spaces. These advantages disappear if the services strategy arrives after the floor plans and elevations have been fixed.

New-build design still involves trade-offs. More plant space can reduce storage or increase the footprint. A flat roof may simplify panel placement but complicate maintenance and drainage. A highly glazed façade can improve daylight while increasing cooling demand. The best approach is not to maximise technology. It is to coordinate envelope, equipment, controls and planning from the outset.
  

  

The comparison is therefore not old building versus modern equipment. It is **adaptive integration versus late-stage insertion**. Listed buildings need a more surgical response. New builds need discipline before architectural decisions become expensive to change.
  

## Financial Realities Including Grants and Return on Investment

## Financial Realities Including Grants and Return on Investment
  

A persuasive payback calculation can still lead to the wrong design decision. In an affluent South West London home, the budget extends well beyond panels, cylinders, batteries and heat pumps. Design coordination, structural work, planning submissions, acoustic treatment, fire strategy, electrical alterations, access and commissioning can determine whether the installation performs as intended and whether it remains practical to maintain.
  

Grant support and VAT treatment need checking against the current project and the client's eligibility. Treat neither as a permanent assumption in an early feasibility model. Separate equipment costs from integration costs, then test the system against different occupancy patterns, energy tariffs and levels of export.
  

A more useful cost review groups expenditure by the work the property requires:

A more useful cost review groups expenditure by the work the property requires:
  

  * **Solar PV:** roof access, structural checks, planning, inverter location, cable routes and export controls.
  * **Battery storage:** battery capacity, electrical alterations, fire strategy, controls, ventilation and plant access.
  * **Heat pump:** heat-loss calculations, emitters, cylinders, acoustic treatment, distribution and electrical capacity.
  * **EV charging:** cable routes, parking arrangements, load management and consumer unit capacity.
  * **Integrated controls:** metering, software, commissioning, tariff settings and interfaces between systems.

Project quotations remain necessary, but the cost drivers should be identified before the design is fixed. A basement extension with a long cable route, restricted plant access and a protected façade requires a different allowance from a straightforward roof installation in a new build. The quotation should also distinguish enabling works from the equipment itself. Otherwise, a low headline figure can conceal the work required to make the system legal, quiet and serviceable.
  

### Curtailment changes the value calculation

### Curtailment changes the value calculation
  

Curtailment is a system reality, not only a utility-scale issue. Great Britain curtailed **over 10 TWh of renewable electricity in 2025** , with curtailment payments totalling **£363m** , according to [_Montel's 2025 GB and Ireland curtailment report_](https://montel.energy/resources/reports/2025-gb-and-ireland-curtailment-report). The report states that **98% of curtailed volume** and **94% of curtailment costs** came from turning down wind turbines in Scotland.

A home has different financial exposure, but the design lesson still applies. Export assumptions can be optimistic when the property cannot use generation as it becomes available. Batteries, hot-water controls and flexible EV charging can raise self-consumption, yet each introduces capital cost, maintenance and control requirements. In a constrained local network, more generation on the roof does not automatically produce a smoother connection or better performance. The DNO connection terms, export limit and control strategy must be reflected in the financial model.
  

### Use total cost of ownership
  

Assess every option against four questions:

### Use total cost of ownership
  

Assess every option against four questions:
  

  * **What does it replace?** A heat pump may form part of a fabric and heating upgrade rather than a standalone purchase.
  * **What must be altered?** Include distribution boards, floor build-ups, roof work, plant rooms, ventilation, access and planning.
  * **What can it control?** Load shifting may justify additional integration work where export is restricted.
  * **What happens if assumptions change?** Test lower export, altered occupancy, future EV use and maintenance access.

The strongest return is not always the fastest payback. In a sensitive renovation, the appropriate solution may preserve historic fabric, reduce future disruption and keep the house adaptable. [_Solar thermal systems_](https://www.harperlatterarchitects.co.uk/post/solar-thermal-systems) also deserve comparison where hot-water demand, roof geometry and plant strategy make them suitable, rather than assuming photovoltaic generation is the only route.
  

## Implementation Sequence from Design to Commissioning
  

Renewable energy integration succeeds when responsibilities are clear before work starts. The architect coordinates spatial and planning decisions, the M&E consultant models performance, specialists confirm equipment requirements, and the DNO assesses the connection. Problems arise when each party designs its own portion without a shared set of drawings, load assumptions and control principles.
  

### 1. Freeze the design logic before the product list

### 1. Freeze the design logic before the product list
  

Begin with the building envelope, occupancy pattern and energy objectives. Agree which loads are essential, which can shift, where generation and storage will sit, and how the control system will prioritise competing demands. Only then should the team confirm equipment selections.
  

The design freeze should include roof layouts, plant-room plans, service routes, acoustic measures, electrical schematics and a schedule of interfaces. It should also record assumptions about export limitation and future equipment. A late change from one heat-pump arrangement to another can affect cylinder space, floor loading, pipe routes, ventilation and elevations.
  

### 2. Coordinate permissions and the grid application

### 2. Coordinate permissions and the grid application
  

Planning, listed building consent and DNO processes can influence one another. A visually acceptable PV position may alter the electrical route. A DNO export condition may change battery control requirements. A conservation officer may support a reversible intervention but reject visible equipment on a principal elevation.
  

Submit coordinated information rather than separate drawings that contradict each other. Keep a decision register showing who approved each change and whether it affects planning, structure, fire safety, acoustics or commissioning.
  

![A project implementation timeline showing four steps from initial design to final commission and handover.](https://cdnimg.co/115ce871-5d39-4334-a7fe-0d49d566c436/7d2e3e6b-1cec-437f-a2bd-91771aab44d1/renewable-energy-integration-implementation-timeline.jpg)
  

### 3. Install in a controlled sequence

### 3. Install in a controlled sequence
  

First protect routes, openings and plant areas. Install containment and primary services before finishes close up, then fit major equipment with enough clearance for inspection and replacement. The architect should check that the installed arrangement matches the approved visual and spatial intent, not merely that each component switches on.
  

The project team should verify:

The project team should verify:
  

  * **Electrical interfaces:** Confirm protection, metering, isolation and load-management arrangements.
  * **Mechanical performance:** Test heat-pump operation, flow temperatures, hot-water recovery and controls.
  * **Acoustic behaviour:** Check external and internal noise under realistic operating conditions.
  * **Water and drainage:** Verify condensate, discharge, frost protection and plant-room resilience.
  * **Control sequences:** Test what happens when solar production changes, the battery is full, the EV is connected and the heat pump calls for heat together.


  

### 4. Commission, train and document
  

Commissioning isn't a handover ceremony. It should prove that the system responds correctly under representative conditions and that the homeowner understands the controls. Provide warranties, manuals, electrical certificates, planning records, product information, maintenance schedules and an as-built services model.

The owner should know which settings can be changed safely, which alerts need professional attention and how export limits affect operation. Retain the documentation for future alterations and property sale. An advanced installation without usable records becomes a liability when the original installer or project team is no longer available.
  

## Living with Integrated Renewable Systems in Your Home
  

The first year is usually a period of calibration. A family may discover that the EV needs charging late in the evening, the pool plant runs during a high-demand period, or the heat pump's original schedule doesn't suit weekday occupancy. Those findings aren't necessarily faults. They show how the designed system meets real life.

A practical approach is to review the monitoring data regularly without chasing every daily fluctuation. Look for repeated patterns, such as a battery reaching full capacity too early, hot water being produced when nobody uses it, or simultaneous charging and importing. Adjust one control at a time so the effect is clear.
  

In a basement-heavy home, the owner might initially prioritise uninterrupted cinema, gym and pool comfort. After several months, the controls could shift flexible hot-water production and EV charging towards periods of stronger solar output, while retaining manual override for entertaining. The architecture remains unchanged, but the operating strategy becomes more closely matched to the household.

Maintenance calls are appropriate for persistent faults, unusual noise, water leaks, repeated alarms or performance that differs materially from the commissioned settings. Seasonal variation is normal. What matters is whether the system remains understandable, accessible and aligned with the connection conditions.

# Executive Summary ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Long-term deep emission reductions, including the reduction of emissions to net zero, is best achieved through institutions and governance that nurture new mitigation policies, while at the same time reconsidering existing policies that support continued Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions (robust evidence, high agreement). To do so effectively, the scope of climate governance should include both direct efforts to target GHG emissions and indirect opportunities to tackle GHG emissions that result from efforts directed towards other policy objectives. {13.2, 13.5, 13.6, 13.7, 13.9}

Institutions and governance underpin mitigation by providing the legal basis for action. This includes setting up implementing organisations and the frameworks through which diverse actors interact (medium evidence, high agreement). Institutions can create mitigation and sectoral policy instruments; policy packages for low-carbon system transition; and economy-wide measures for systemic restructuring. {13.2, 13.7, 13.9}

Policies have had a discernible impact on mitigation for specific countries, sectors, and technologies (robust evidence, high agreement), avoiding emissions of several GtCO2-eq yr–1 (medium evidence, medium agreement)  . Both market-based and regulatory policies have distinct, but complementary roles. The share of global GHG emissions subject to mitigation policy has increased rapidly in recent years, but big gaps remain in policy coverage, and the stringency of many policies falls short of what is needed to achieve strong mitigation outcomes (robust evidence, high agreement ). {13.6, Cross-Chapter Box 10 in Chapter 14}

Climate laws enable mitigation action by signalling the direction of travel, setting targets, mainstreaming mitigation into sector policies, enhancing regulatory certainty, creating law-backed agencies, creating focal points for social mobilisation, and attracting international finance (medium evidence,  high agreement ). By 2020, ‘direct’ climate laws primarily focused on GHG reductions were present in 56 countries covering 53% of global emissions, while more than 690 laws, including ‘indirect’ laws, may also have an effect on mitigation. Among direct laws, ‘framework’ laws set an overarching legal basis for mitigation either by pursuing a target and implementation approach, or by seeking to mainstream climate objectives through sectoral plans and integrative institutions. {13.2}

Institutions can enable improved governance by coordinating across sectors, scales and actors, building consensus for action, and setting strategies (medium evidence, high agreement). Institutions are more stable and effective when they are congruous with national context, leading to mitigation-focused institutions in some countries and the pursuit of multiple objectives in others. Sub-national institutions play a complementary role to national institutions by developing locally-relevant visions and plans, addressing policy gaps or limits in national institutions, building local administrative structures and convening actors for place-based decarbonisation. {13.2}

Sub-national actors are important for mitigation because municipalities and regional governments have jurisdiction over climate-relevant sectors such as land-use, waste and urban policy; are able to experiment with climate solutions; and can forge partnerships with the private sector and internationally to leverage enhanced climate action (robust evidence, high agreement). More than 10,500 cities and nearly 250 regions representing more than 2 billion people have pledged largely voluntary action to reduce emissions. Indirect gains include innovation, establishing norms and developing capacity. However, sub-national actors often lack national support, funding, and capacity to mobilise finance and human resources, and create new institutional competences. {13.5}

Climate governance is constrained and enabled by domestic structural factors, but it is still possible for actors to make substantial changes (medium evidence, high agreement). Key structural factors are domestic material endowments (such as fossil fuels and land-based resources); domestic political systems; and prevalent ideas, values and belief systems. Developing countries face additional material constraints in climate governance due to development challenges and scarce economic or natural resources. a broad group of actors influence how climate governance develop over time, including a range of civic organisations, encompassing both pro-and anti-climate action groups . {13.3, 13.4}

Mitigation strategies, instruments and policies that fit with dominant ideas, values and belief systems within a country or within a sector are more easily adopted and implemented (medium evidence, medium agreement)  . Ideas, values and beliefs may change over time. Policies that bring perceived direct benefits, such as subsidies, usually receive greater support. The awareness of co-benefits for the public increases support of climate policies (robust evidence,  high agreement ). {13.2, 13.3, 13.4}

Climate litigation is growing and can affect the outcome and ambition of climate governance (medium evidence, high agreement).  Since 2015, at least 37 systemic cases have been initiated against states that challenge the overall effort of a state to mitigate or adapt to climate change. If successful, such cases can lead to an increase in a country’s overall ambition to tackle climate change. Climate litigation has also successfully challenged governments’ authorisations of high-emitting projects setting precedents in favour of climate action. Climate litigation against private sector and financial institutions is also on the rise. {13.4}

The media shapes the public discourse about climate mitigation. This can usefully build public support to accelerate mitigation action, but may also be used to impede decarbonisation (medium evidence, high agreement). Global media coverage (across a study of 59 countries) has been growing, from about 47,000 stories in 2016–2017 to about 87,000 in 2020–2021. Generally, the media representation of climate science has increased and become more accurate over time. On occasion, the propagation of scientifically misleading information by organised counter-movements has fuelled polarisation, with negative implications for climate policy. {13.4}

Explicit attention to equity and justice is salient to both social acceptance and fair and effective policymaking for mitigation (robust evidence, high agreement)  . Distributional implications of alternative climate policy choices can be usefully evaluated at city, local and national scales as an input to policymaking. Institutions and governance frameworks that enable consideration of justice and just transitions are likely to build broader support for climate policymaking . {13.2, 13.6, 13.8, 13.9}

Carbon pricing is effective in promoting implementation of low-cost emissions reductions (robust evidence, high agreement)  . While the coverage of emissions trading and carbon taxes has risen to over 20% of global CO2 emissions, both coverage and price are lower than is needed for deep reductions. The design of market mechanisms should be effective as well as efficient, balance distributional goals and find social acceptance. Practical experience has driven progress in market mechanism design, especially of emissions trading schemes (robust evidence,  high agreement ). Carbon pricing is limited in its effect on adoption of higher-cost mitigation options, and where decisions are often not sensitive to price incentives such as in energy efficiency, urban planning, and infrastructure (robust evidence, medium agreement )
. Subsidies have been used to improve energy efficiency, encourage the uptake of renewable energy and other sector-specific emissions saving options (robust evidence,  high agreement ). {13.6}

Regulatory instruments play an important role in achieving specific mitigation outcomes in sectoral applications (robust evidence, high agreement)  . Regulation is effective in particular applications and often enjoys greater political support, but tends to be more economically costly, than pricing instruments (robust evidence, medium agreement ). Flexible forms of regulation (for example, performance standards) have achieved aggregate goals for renewable energy generation, vehicle efficiency and fuel standards, and energy efficiency in buildings and industry (robust evidence,  high agreement ). Infrastructure investment decisions are significant for mitigation because they lock-in high- or low- emissions trajectories over long periods. Information and voluntary programmes can contribute to overall mitigation outcomes (medium evidence,  high agreement ). Designing for overlap and interactions among mitigation policies enhances their effectiveness (robust evidence,  high agreement )
. Designing for overlap and interactions among mitigation policies enhances their effectiveness (robust evidence,  high agreement ). {13.6}

Removing fossil fuel subsidies would reduce emissions, improve public revenue and macroeconomic performance, and yield other environmental and sustainable development benefits;  subsidy removal may have adverse distributional impacts especially on the most economically vulnerable groups which, in some cases can be mitigated by measures such as redistributing revenue saved, all of which depend on national circumstances ( high confidence); fossil fuel subsidy removal is projected by various studies (using alternative methodologies) to reduce global CO2 emissions by 1–4%, and GHG emissions by up to 10% by 2030, varying across regions (medium confidence). {6.3, 13.6}

National mitigation policies interact internationally with effects that both support and hinder mitigation action (medium evidence, high agreement)  . Reductions in demand for fossil fuels tend to negatively affect fossil fuel exporting countries (medium evidence,  high agreement ). Creation of markets for emission reduction credits tends to benefit countries able to supply credits. Policies to support technology development and diffusion tend to have positive spillover effects (medium evidence,  high agreement ). There is no consistent evidence of significant emissions leakage or competitiveness effects between countries, including for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries covered by emission trading systems (medium evidence, medium agreement ). {13.6}

Policy packages are better able to support socio-technical transitions and shifts in development pathways toward low-carbon futures than are individual policies (robust evidence, high agreement). For best effect, they need to be harnessed to a clear vision for change and designed with attention to local governance context. Comprehensiveness in coverage, coherence to ensure complementarity, and consistency of policies with the overarching vision and its objectives are important design criteria. Integration across objectives occurs when a policy package is informed by a clear problem framing and identification of the full range relevant policy sub-systems. {13.7}

The co-benefits and trade-offs of integrating adaptation and mitigation are most usefully identified and assessed prior to policy making rather than being accidentally discovered (robust evidence, high agreement). This requires strengthening relevant national institutions to reduce silos and overlaps, increasing knowledge exchange at the country and regional levels, and supporting engagement with bilateral and multilateral funding partners. Local governments are well placed to develop policies that generate social and environmental co-benefits but to do so require legal backing and adequate capacity and resources. {13.8}

Climate change mitigation is accelerated when attention is given to integrated policy and economy-wide approaches, and when enabling conditions (governance, institutions, behaviour, innovation, policy, and finance), are present (robust evidence, medium agreement). Accelerating climate mitigation includes simultaneously weakening high carbon systems and encouraging low-carbon systems; ensuring interaction between adjacent systems (e.g. energy and agriculture); overcoming resistance to policies (e.g., from incumbents in high carbon emitting industries), including by providing transitional support to the vulnerable and negatively affected by distributional impacts; inducing changes in consumer practices and routines; providing transition support; and addressing coordination challenges in policy and governance. {13.7, 13.9}

Economy-wide packages, including economic stimulus packages, can contribute to shifting sustainable development pathways and achieving net zero outcomes while meeting short term economic goals (medium evidence, high agreement). The 2008–2009 Global Recession showed that policies for sustained economic recovery go beyond short-term fiscal stimulus to include long-term commitments of public spending on the low-carbon economy; pricing reform; addressing affordability; and minimising distributional impacts. COVID-19 spurred stimulus packages and multi-objective recovery policies that may have the potential to meet short-term economic goals while enabling longer-term sustainability goals. {13.9}
#  13.1Introduction ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

This chapter assesses national and sub-national policies and institutions. Given the scale and scope of the climate challenge, an immediate challenge for this assessment is defining its scope. Because a very wide range of institutions and policies at multiple scales carry implications for climate change, the approach followed here is to embrace a broad approach. Consequently, institutions and policies discussed include dedicated climate laws and organisations ([Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)) and direct mitigation policies such as carbon taxes ([Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6)), but also those, such as sectoral ministries and their policies (Sections 13.6 and 13.7) and sub-national entities such as regional bodies, cities, and their policies ([Section 13.5](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.5)), the implications of which are salient to mitigation outcomes

.5](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.5)), the implications of which are salient to mitigation outcomes. This approach recognises that there are important linkages with international climate governance (Chapter 14), notably the role of internationally mandated Nationally Determined Contributions’ in stimulating domestic policy development ([Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)), transnational networks in spurring sub-national action ([Section 13.5](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.5)), and international effects of domestic policies ([Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6)).

This encompassing approach to climate governance is also built on a recognition that climate policymaking is routinely formulated in the context of multiple policy objectives such as energy security, energy access, urban development, and mitigation-adaptation linkages. This informs policymaking based on an understanding that to fully maximise direct and indirect climate mitigation potential, maximising co-benefits and minimising trade-offs should be explicitly sought rather than accidentally discovered and policies designed accordingly. This understanding also informs the design of institutions ([Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)) and policies (Sections 13.6 and 13.7) as well as the linkage between mitigation and adaptation ([Section 13.8](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.8)).
The chapter also engages with several new developments and an expansion of the literature since AR5.

A growing literature assesses how national policymaking on climate mitigation is dependent on national politics around, and building consensus on, climate action. This, in turn, is shaped by both nationally specific structural features ([Section 13.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.3)) and the role of different actors in the policymaking process ([Section 13.4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.4)). Important new avenues through which climate policy making is shaped, such as climate litigation ([Section 13.4.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.4.2)), and channels for public opinion formation, such as the media ([Section 13.4.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.4.3)) are also assessed. The chapter weaves discussions of the role of justice, understood through a discussion of procedural justice ([Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)), distributional justice ([Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13

.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)), distributional justice ([Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6)) and vulnerability ([Section 13.8](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.8)), and its role in creating public support for climate action ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)).

A significant new theme is the focus on the dynamic elements of policy making, that is, how policy can be designed to accelerate mitigation. This includes through technological transitions, socio-technical transitions, shifts in development pathways and economy-wide measures. This literature emphasises the importance of examining not just individual policies, but packages of policies ([Section 13.7](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.7)) and how these are enabled by the alignment of policy, institutions, finance, behaviour and innovation ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)). Also new is attention to the opportunities for economy-wide system change presented by consideration of post-COVID recovery packages, and wider efforts at sustainable economic restructuring ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9))

.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)). Consistent with the discussion in Chapter 4, these larger approaches offer opportunities to undertake systemic restructuring and shift development pathways.

Finally, the chapter addresses core themes from earlier assessment reports, but seeks to do so in an enhanced manner. The discussion of climate institutions assesses a growing literature on climate law, as well as both purpose-built climate organisations and the layering of climate responsibilities on existing organisations at national and sub-national scales ([Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)). The discussion of policies focuses on an ex post  assessment of policies, as well as the interaction among them, and learnings on how they can be combined in packages (Sections 13.6 and 13.7). It also lays out a framework for their assessment that encompasses environmental effectiveness, economic effectiveness, distributional outcomes, co-benefits, institutional requirements, as well as a new criterion of transformational potential ([Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6)).

The aim of this chapter is to assess the full range of the multi-stranded and diverse literature on climate institutions and policy, reflecting the richness of real-world climate governance.
#  13.2National and Sub-national Institutions and Governance ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section
Institutions and governance arrangements can help address ‘policy gaps’ and ‘implementation gaps’ (Cross-Chapter Box 4 in Chapter 4) that hinder climate mitigation. While the need for institutions and governance is universal, individual country approaches vary, based on national approaches and circumstances, as discussed in this section.

Since AR5, the understanding of climate governance has become more encompassing and complex, involving multiple actors, decision-making arenas, levels of decision-making and a variety of political goals. Climate governance sometime directly targets GHG emissions; at other times mitigation results from measures that primarily aim to solve other issues, for instance relating to food production, forest management, energy markets, air pollution, transport systems or technology development, but with mitigation or adaptation effects ([Karlsson et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Karlsson--2020)).

Consistent with usage in this assessment, institutions are rules, norms and conventions that guide, constrain or enable behaviours and practices, including the organisations through which they operate, while governance is the structure, processes and actions that public and private actors use to address societal goals (See Glossary for complete definitions). Multiple terms are used in the literature to discuss climate governance, often varying across countries. Climate laws, or legislation, is passed by legislatures, and often sets the overarching governance context, but the term is also used to refer to legislation that is salient to climate outcomes even if not centrally focused on climate change. National strategies, often referred to as plans, most often operate through executive action by government, set guidance for action and often are not legally binding, although strategies may also be enshrined in law

. Both laws and strategies may elaborate targets, or goals, for emissions outcomes, although these are not necessary components of laws and strategies. While laws typically operate at the national level (states may also make laws in federal nations), strategies, plans and targets may also operate at the sub-national level.

This section begins with a discussion of national laws for climate action ([Section 13.2.1](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2.1)), followed by a discussion of national strategies ([Section 13.2.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2.2)). The third section examines institutions (Section13.2.3), including organisations that are established to govern climate actions, and the final section explores sub-national institutions and their challenges in influencing climate mitigation ([Section 13.2.4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2.4)).
##  13.2.1Climate Laws ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

National laws that govern climate action often set the legal basis for climate action ([Averchenkova et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2021)). This legal basis can serve several functions: establish a platform for transparent target setting and implementation ([Bennett 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bennett--2018)); provide a signal to actors by indicating intent to harness state authority behind climate action ([Scotford and Minas 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scotford--2019)); promise enhanced regulatory certainty ([Scotford et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scotford--2017)); create law-backed agencies for coordination, compliance and accountability ([Scotford and Minas 2019](https://www.ipcc

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scotford--2017)); create law-backed agencies for coordination, compliance and accountability ([Scotford and Minas 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scotford--2019)); provide a basis for mainstreaming mitigation into sector action, and create focal points for social mobilisation (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Dubash et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2013)). For lower/middle income countries, in particular, the existence of a law may also attract international finance by serving as a signal of credibility ([Fisher et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2017)). The realisation of these potential governance gains depends on local context, legal design, successful implementation, and complementary action at different scales.

There are both narrow and broad definitions of what counts as ‘climate laws’. The literature distinguishes direct climate laws that explicitly considers climate change causes or impacts – for example through mention of greenhouse gas reductions in its objectives or title ([Dubash et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2013)) – from indirect laws that have ‘the capacity to affect mitigation or adaptation’ through the subjects they regulate, for example, through promotion of co-benefits, or creation of reporting protocols ([Scotford and Minas 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scotford--2019)). Closely related is a ‘sectoral approach’ based on the layering of climate considerations into existing laws in the absence of an overarching framework law ([Rumble 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rumble--2019)). Many countries also adopt executive climate strategies (discussed in [Section 13.2](https://www

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rumble--2019)). Many countries also adopt executive climate strategies (discussed in [Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)), which may either coexist with or substitute for climate laws, and that may also be related to a country’s NDC process under the Paris Agreement.

The prevalence of both direct and indirect climate laws has increased considerably since 2007, although definitional differences across studies complicate a clear assessment of their relative importance (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Iacobuta et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Iacobuta--2018); [Nachmany and Setzer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nachmany--2018)). Direct climate laws – with greenhouse gas limitation as a direct objective – had been passed in 56 countries (of 194 studied) covering 53% of emissions in 2020, with most of that rise happening between 2010 and 2015 (Figure 13.1)

.1). Both direct and indirect laws – those that have an effect on mitigation even if this is not the primary outcome – is most closely captured by the ‘Climate Change Laws of the World’ database, which illustrates the same trend of growing prevalence, documenting 694 mitigation-related laws by 2020 versus 558 in 2015 and 342 in 2010 ([Nachmany and Setzer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nachmany--2018); [LSE Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#LSE%20Grantham%20Research%20Institute%20on%20Climate%20Change%20and%20the%20Environment--2021)). Some direct climate laws may serve as ‘framework’ laws ([Averchenkova et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2017); [Rumble 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rumble--2019)) that set an overarching legal context within which other legislation and policies operate. Framework laws are intended to provide a coherent legal basis for action, to integrate past legislation in related areas, set clear directions for future policy, and create necessary processes and institutions (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Townshend et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Townshend--2013); [Averchenkova et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2017); [Fankhauser et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2018); [Rumble 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rumble--2019); [Averchenkova et al

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2018); [Rumble 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rumble--2019); [Averchenkova et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2021)). There are a variety of approaches to framework laws. Reviews of climate legislation, many of which draw particularly from the long-standing UK Climate Change Act, suggest the need for statutory targets with a long-term direction, shorter term instruments such as carbon budgets to induce action toward targets, a clear assignment of duties and responsibilities including identification of policies and responsibility for their implementation, annual reporting to Parliament; an independent body to support evidence-based decision-making and rules to govern information collection and provision ([Barton and Campion 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barton--2018); [Fankhauser et al. 2018](https://www

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barton--2018); [Fankhauser et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2018); [Abraham-Dukuma et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Abraham-Dukuma--2020); [Averchenkova et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2021)).

However, country examples also suggest other, different approaches to framework laws. Korea’s Framework Act on Low Carbon, Green Growth seeks to shift business and society toward green growth through a process of strategy setting and action plans ([Jang et al. 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jang--2010)). Kenya’s framework Climate Change Act creates an institutional structure to mainstream climate considerations into sectoral decisions, one of several examples across Africa of efforts to create framework legislation to promote mainstreaming ([Rumble 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rumble--2019)). Mexico’s General Law on Climate Change includes sectoral emission targets, along with the creation of coordinating institutions across ministries and sub-national authorities ([Averchenkova and Guzman Luna 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2018))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2018)). Consequently, different countries have placed emphasis on different aspects of framework laws, although the most widely prevalent approach is that exemplified by the UK.

Climate laws spread through multiple mechanisms, including the impetus provided by international negotiation events, diffusion by example across countries, and domestic factors such as business cycles (medium evidence, medium agreement ). Major landmark events under the UNFCCC have been associated with increases in national legislation ([Iacobuta et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Iacobuta--2018)), with a stronger effect in countries where international commitments are binding ([Fankhauser et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2016)). Diffusion through example of legislation from other countries has been documented ([Fankhauser et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2016); [Fleig et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fleig--2017); [Torney 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torney--2017); [Inderberg 2019](https://www

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fleig--2017); [Torney 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torney--2017); [Inderberg 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Inderberg--2019); [Torney 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torney--2019)). For example, the UK Climate Change Act was an important influence in pursuing similar acts in Finland and Ireland ([Torney 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torney--2019)) and was also considered in the formulation of Mexico’s General Law on Climate Change ([Averchenkova and Guzman Luna 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2018)). The presence of a framework law is positively associated with creation of additional supportive legislation ([Fankhauser et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2015))

. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2015)). Domestic contextual factors can also affect the likelihood of legislation such as a weak business cycle that can impact the political willingness to pass legislation ([Fankhauser et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2015)). In some cases, civil society groups play a role as advocates for legislation, as occurred in the UK ([Lockwood 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lockwood--2013); [Lorenzoni and Benson 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lorenzoni--2014); [Carter and Childs 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carter--2018); [Devaney et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Devaney--2020)) and in Germany in the build up to passage of their respective Climate Change Act ([Flachsland and Levi 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Devaney--2020)) and in Germany in the build up to passage of their respective Climate Change Act ([Flachsland and Levi 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Flachsland--2021)).

The performance of framework laws suggests a mixed picture. While the structure of the UK Act successfully sets a direction of travel and has resulted in a credible independent body, it performs less well in fostering integration across sectoral areas and providing an enforcement mechanism ([Averchenkova et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2021)). a review of seven European climate change acts concludes that overall targets may not be entirely aligned with planning, reporting and evaluation mechanisms, and that sanction mechanisms are lacking across the board ([Nash and Steurer 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nash--2019)), which limit the scope for legislation to perform its integrative task. These observations suggest the need for careful attention to the design of framework laws.

There is extremely limited evidence on the aggregate effects of climate laws on climate outcomes, although there is a broader literature assessing climate policies ([Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6) in this chapter and Cross-Chapter Box 10 in Chapter 14). a single assessment of direct and indirect climate laws as well as relevant executive action across a global database finds a measurable and positive effect: global annual emissions have reduced by about 5.9 CO2 compared to an estimation of what they otherwise would have been ([Eskander and Fankhauser 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eskander--2020)). Climate laws require further research, including on the quantification of impact, framework versus sectoral approaches, and the various mechanisms through which laws act – target setting, creating institutional structures, mainstreaming and ensuring compliance.

##  13.2.2National Strategies and Nationally Determined Contributions ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
National climate strategies, which are often formulated through executive action, contribute to climate governance in several ways. Strategies enable discussion of low-emissions pathways while accounting for uncertainty, national circumstances and socio-economic objectives ([Falduto and Rocha 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Falduto--2020)).

They frequently set out long term emission goals and possible trajectories over time, with analysis of technological and economic factors ([Levin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levin--2018); [WRI 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#WRI--2020)). This can include quantitative modelling of low-emissions transitions and their economic effects to inform policymakers and stakeholders of potential outcomes ([Waisman et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Waisman--2019); [Weitzel et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Weitzel--2019)). Scenario analysis can be used to explore how to make strategies more robust in the face of uncertainty ([Sato and Altamirano 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sato--2019)). Strategies and their regular revision can support long-term structural change by stimulating deliberation and learning ([Voß et al

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sato--2019)). Strategies and their regular revision can support long-term structural change by stimulating deliberation and learning ([Voß et al. 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Vo%C3%9F--2009)), and to make the link between mitigation and adaptation objectives and actions ([Watkiss and Klein 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Watkiss--2019); [Hans et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hans--2020)). As part of the Paris Agreement process, several countries have prepared and submitted long-term low-emissions development strategies ([Levin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levin--2018)), while others have different forms of national climate change strategies independently of the UNFCCC process. Strategies set over time by the European Union are discussed in Box 13.1.

Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) prepared under the Paris Agreement may be informed by national strategies ([Rocha and Falduto 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rocha--2019)). But the process of preparing NDCs can itself raise political awareness, encourage institutional innovation and coordination, and engage stakeholders ([Röser et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#R%C3%B6ser--2020)). Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) illustrate a diversity of approaches: direct mitigation targets, strategies, plans and actions for low-GHG emission development, or the pursuit of mitigation co-benefits resulting from economic diversification plans and/or adaptation actions ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC%20Secretariat--2021)). The NDCs vary in their scope, content and time frame, reflecting different national circumstances, and are widely heterogeneous in both stringency and coverage of mitigation efforts ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC%20Secretariat--2016), 2021; [Pauw et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pauw--2018); [Campagnolo and Davide 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Campagnolo--2019); [Pauw et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pauw--2019)). The mitigation targets in the new or updated NDCs range from economy-wide absolute emission reduction targets to strategies, plans and actions for low-emission development, with specific time frames or implementation periods specified. Less than 10% of parties’ NDCs specify when their emissions are expected to peak and some of these parties express their target as a carbon budget ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2021](https://www

. Less than 10% of parties’ NDCs specify when their emissions are expected to peak and some of these parties express their target as a carbon budget ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC%20Secretariat--2021)). Many long-term strategies submitted by Parties to the UNFCCC refer to net zero emissions or climate neutrality, carbon neutrality, or GHG neutrality with reference to 2050, 2060 or mid-century targets ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC%20Secretariat--2021)). The growing prevalence and coverage of emission targets is documented in[Figure 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/ch13.html#_idTextAnchor048).

Almost all Parties outlined domestic mitigation measures as key instruments for achieving mitigation targets in specific priority areas such as energy supply (89%), transport (80%), buildings (72%), industry (39%), agriculture (67%), LULUCF (75%) and waste (68%). Renewable energy generation was the most frequently indicated mitigation option (84%), followed by improving energy efficiency of buildings (63%) and multi-sector energy efficiency improvement (48%); afforestation, reforestation and revegetation (48%); and improving energy efficiency of transport (45%) ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC%20Secretariat--2021)). Parties often communicated mitigation options related to the circular economy, including reducing waste (29%) and recycling waste (30%) and promoting circular economy (25%)

. Parties often communicated mitigation options related to the circular economy, including reducing waste (29%) and recycling waste (30%) and promoting circular economy (25%). Many Parties highlighted policy coherence and synergies between their mitigation measures and development priorities, which included long-term low-emission development strategy(LT-LEDS), the sustainable development goals (SDGs) and, for some, green recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Some countries approach NDCs as an opportunity to integrate mitigation objectives and broader economic shifts or sectoral transformations (medium evidence, medium agreement ). For example, Brazil’s 2016 NDC focussed on emissions from land-use change, including agricultural intensification, to align mitigation with a national development strategy of halting deforestation in the Amazon, and increasing livestock production ([De Oliveira Silva et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#De%20Oliveira%20Silva--2018)). While the forest sector accounts for the bulk of Madagascar’s mitigation potential, its NDC promotes GHG mitigation in both AFOLU and energy sectors to maximise co-benefits, and achieve a higher number of sustainable development goals (SDGs) ([Nogueira et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nogueira--2020)).
##  Box 13. 1 | EU Climate Policy Portfolio and the European Green Deal![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The European Union (EU)[1](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/ch13.html#footnote-000) has developed an encompassing climate governance framework ([Kulovesi and Oberthür 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kulovesi--2020)), having ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2002. In 2003 the EU adopted an Emissions Trading System for sectors with large GHG emitters, which started in 2005. From 2007 to 2009, the EU revised its climate policies, including for vehicle emissions, renewable energy and energy efficiency, and adopted targets for 2020 for GHG emissions reductions, renewable energy shares and energy efficiency improvements. It also adopted in 2009 an Effort Sharing Decision for Member States’ emissions reductions for the period 2013–2020 in sectors not covered by the ETS ([Boasson and Wettestad 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2013); [Bertoldi 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2013); [Bertoldi 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bertoldi--2018)). The ETS has been improved multiple times, including through a 2015 Market Stability Reserve to reduce the surplus of emission allowances ([Chaton et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chaton--2018); [Wettestad and Jevnaker 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wettestad--2019)). In 2010, the European Commission created a directorate-general (equal to a ministry at the domestic level) for Climate Action. Between 2014 and 2018, the EU agreed on emission reduction targets for 2030 of 30% GHG emission reductions compared to 1990, and again revised its climate policy portfolio including new targets for renewable energies and energy efficiency and a new Effort Sharing Regulation ([Fitch-Roy et al. 2019a](https://www.ipcc
. 2019a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fitch-Roy--2019a); [Oberthür 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Oberth%C3%BCr--2019)).

From 2018, climate planning and reporting has been regulated by the EU Governance Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2018/1999), requiring member states to develop detailed and strategic National Energy and Climate Plans ([Knodt et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Knodt--2020)). In 2019, the European Commission, backed by the European Council (heads of states and government in the EU) and the European Parliament, launched a new broad climate and environment initiative; the ‘European Green Deal’, implying the revision of many EU polices and introducing the Climate Pact (European Commission 2019a). This roadmap develops a ‘new growth strategy for the EU’ aimed at reaching climate neutrality by 2050 and spans multiple sectors

. This roadmap develops a ‘new growth strategy for the EU’ aimed at reaching climate neutrality by 2050 and spans multiple sectors. In 2020, the European Commission introduced a new climate law establishing the framework for achieving the climate neutrality by 2050 principle, and upgraded its 2030 GHG emission reduction target to at least net 55% reduction, which was adopted in June 2021 (European Commission 2020a)

. In June 2021, the new policy package ‘Fit for 55’ was adopted by the Commission; the packages included a proposal for the revision of the ETS, including its extension to shipping and a separate emission trading system for road transport and buildings, a revision of the effort sharing regulation, an amendment of the regulation setting CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, a revision of the energy tax directive, a new carbon border adjustment mechanism, a revision of renewable energy and energy efficiency targets and directives, and a new social fund to make the transition to climate neutrality fair.
