##  13.2.3Approaches to National Institutions and Governance ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
###  13.2.3.1The Forms of Climate Institutions ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

###  13.2.3.1The Forms of Climate Institutions ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Universal ‘best-practice’ formulations of organisations may not be applicable across country contexts, but institutions that are suited to national context can be ratcheted up over time in their scope and effectiveness (medium evidence, medium agreement ). National climate institutions take diverse forms because they emerge out of country-specific interactions between national climate politics and existing institutional structures. Certain institutional forms tend to be common across countries, such as expert climate change commissions; a review finds eleven such institutions in existence as of mid-2020. Although this institutional form may be common, these commissions vary in terms of expertise, independence and focus ([Abraham-Dukuma et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Abraham-Dukuma--2020)), reinforcing the important shaping role of national context.

A review of institutions in eight countries suggests three broad processes through which institutions emerge: ‘purpose-built’ dedicated institutions focused explicitly on mitigation; ‘layering’ of mitigation objectives on existing institutions; and ‘latent’ institutions created for other purposes that nonetheless have implications for mitigation outcomes ([Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)). In relatively few countries do new, purpose-built, legally-mandated bodies created specifically for climate mitigation exist although this number is growing; examples include the UK ([Averchenkova et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2018)), China ([Teng and Wang 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Teng--2021)), Australia ([Keenan et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Keenan--2012)) and New Zealand ([Timperley 2020](https://www.ipcc

. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Keenan--2012)) and New Zealand ([Timperley 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Timperley--2020)). These cases indicate that dedicated and lasting institutions with a strategic long-term focus on mitigation emerge only under conditions of broad national political agreement around climate mitigation as a national priority ([Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)). However, the specific forms of those institutions differ, as illustrated by the case of the UK’s Climate Change Committee established as an independent agency (Box 13.2) and China, which is built around a top-down planning structure (Box 13.3).

Where economy-wide institutions do not exist, new institutions may still address sub-sets of the challenge. In Australia, while political conditions resulted in the repeal of an overarching Clean Energy Act in 2014, although a Climate Change Authority continued, other institutions primarily focused on the energy sector such as the Clean Energy Regulator, the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, and the Australia Renewable Agency continued to shape energy outcomes ([MacNeil 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#MacNeil--2021)).

Where new dedicated organisations have not emerged, countries may layer climate responsibilities on existing institutions; the addition of mitigation to the responsibilities of the US Environmental Protection Agency is an example ([Mildenberger 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2021)). Layering is also a common approach when climate change is embedded within consideration of multiple objectives of policy. In these cases, climate institutions tend to be layered on sectoral institutions for the pursuit of co-benefits or broader development concerns. Examples include India, where energy security was an important objective of renewable energy promotion policy (Pillai and [Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)), Brazil’s mitigation approach focused on sectoral forest policy ([Hochstetler 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)), Brazil’s mitigation approach focused on sectoral forest policy ([Hochstetler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2021)) and South Africa’s emphasis on job creation as a necessary factor in mitigation policy ([Chandrashekeran et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chandrashekeran--2017); [Rennkamp 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rennkamp--2019)). Prior to this process of layering, sectoral institutions, such as in forest and energy sectors, may play an important latent role in shaping climate outcomes, before climate considerations are part of their formal mandate.

New rules and organisations are not only created, they are also dismantled or allowed to wither away. Cases of institutional dismantling or neglect include the Australian Clean Energy Act ([Crowley 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Crowley--2017); [MacNeil 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#MacNeil--2021)), the Indian Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change, which, while formally functional, effectively does not meet (Pillai and [Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)), and the weakening of climate units inside sectoral ministries in Brazil ([Hochstetler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2021))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2021)). While there is limited literature on the robustness of climate institutions, case studies suggest institutions are more likely to emerge, persist and be effective when institutions map to a framing of climate change that has broad political support (medium evidence, medium agreement ). Thus while mitigation focused framings and institutions may win political support in some countries, in other cases sectorally focused or multiple objectives oriented institutions may be most useful and resilient ([Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)).

###  13.2.3.2Addressing Climate Governance Challenges ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Climate governance challenges include ensuring coordination, building consensus by mediating conflict, and setting strategy (medium evidence,  high agreement ). Coordination is important because climate change is an all-of-economy and society problem that requires cross-sectoral and cross-scale action; building consensus is needed because large-scale transformations can unsettle established interests; and strategy setting is required due to the transformative and time-bound nature of climate mitigation ([Dubash et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)). Yet, climate institutions have a mixed record in addressing these challenges.

Institutions that provide coordination, integration across policy areas and mainstreaming are particularly important given the scope and scale of climate change ([Candel and Biesbroek 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Candel--2016); [Tosun and Lang 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tosun--2017)) ([Section 13.7](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.7)). Ministries of environment are often appointed as de facto agents of coordination, but have been hampered by their limited regulative authority and ability to engage in intra-governmental bargaining with ministries with larger budgets and political heft ([Aamodt 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aamodt--2018)).

Creation of a high-level coordinating body to coordinate across departments and mainstream climate into sectoral actions is another common approach ([Oulu 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Oulu--2015)). For example, Kenya has created a National Climate Change Council, which operates through a climate change directorate in the environment ministry to mainstream climate change at the county level ([Guey and Bilich 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Guey--2019)). [Zhou and Mori (2011)](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhou--2011) suggest that well-functioning inter-agency coordination mechanisms require support from heads of government, involvement by industry and environment agencies; and engagement by multiple sectoral agencies

. However, coordination mechanisms without a clear authority and basis for setting directions run the risk of ‘negative coordination’, a process through which ministries comment on each other’s proposals, removing any ideas that run counter to the interests of their own ministry, leading to even weaker decisions ([Flachsland and Levi 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Flachsland--2021)). Countries with dedicated, new climate institutions tend to have a more explicit and authorised body for climate coordination, such as China’s National Leading Group (Box 13.3).

Without explicit coordination with finance ministries, there is a risk of parallel and non-complementary approaches. For example, the South African Treasury pursued a carbon tax without clear indication of how it interfaced with a quantitative sectoral budget approach espoused by the environment ministry (Tyler and [Hochstetler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2021)). [Skovgaard (2012)](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skovgaard--2012) suggests that there is an important distinction between finance ministries that bring a limiting ‘budget frame’ to climate action, versus a ‘market failure frame’ that encourages broader engagement by relevant ministries.

Coordination within federal systems poses additional complexities, such as overlapping authority across jurisdictions, multiple norms in place, and approaches to coordination across scales ([Brown 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Brown--2012)). Multi-level governance systems such as the EU can influence the design and functioning of climate policies and institutions in member states, such as Germany ([Skjærseth 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skj%C3%A6rseth--2017); [Jänicke and Wurzel 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#J%C3%A4nicke--2019); [Flachsland and Levi 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Flachsland--2021)) and the UK ([Lockwood 2021a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lockwood--2021a)). In some cases, this can result in distinct European modes of governance as has been suggested occurred in the case of wind energy ([Fitch-Roy 2016](https://www.ipcc

. In some cases, this can result in distinct European modes of governance as has been suggested occurred in the case of wind energy ([Fitch-Roy 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fitch-Roy--2016)).

Within countries, institutional platforms allow federal and sub-national governments to negotiate and agree on policy trajectories ([Gordon 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gordon--2015)). Because transition to a low-carbon future is likely to create winners and losers over different time scales; institutions are needed to mediate these interests and build consensus on future pathways ([Kuzemko et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kuzemko--2016); [Lockwood et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lockwood--2017); [Finnegan 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Finnegan--2019); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020)). Institutions that provide credible knowledge can help support ambition. For example, analysis by the UK Climate Change committee has been harnessed, including by non-state actors, to prevent backsliding on decisions ([Lockwood 2021a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lockwood--2021a))

For example, a renewable energy policy community emerged in China through key agenda setting meetings ([Shen 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2017)), and in India, a National Solar Mission provided a platform for the renewable energy industry (Pillai and [Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)). Conversely, institutions can also exert a drag on change through ‘regulatory inertia’, as in the case of the UK energy regulator Ofgem, which has exercised veto powers in ways that may limit a low-carbon transition ([Lockwood et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lockwood--2017)).

Institutions can also create spaces to accommodate concerns of other actors ([Upadhyaya et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Upadhyaya--2021)). Deliberative bodies, such as Germany’s Enquete Commission ([Weidner and Mez 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Weidner--2008); [Flachsland and Levi 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Flachsland--2021)) or the Brazilian Forum on Climate Change (Tyler and [Hochstetler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2021)) provide a space for reconciling competing visions and approaches to climate change. Many countries are creating deliberative bodies to forge ‘Just Transition’ strategies ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9))

. Many countries are creating deliberative bodies to forge ‘Just Transition’ strategies ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)). a recent innovation is the creation of Citizens’ Assemblies that bring together representative samples of citizens to deliberate on policy questions with the intent of informing them ([Devaney et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Devaney--2020); [Sandover et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sandover--2021)). The ability of institutions to forge agreement also rests on attention to procedural justice (Box 13.4).

Since addressing climate change requires transformative intent and shifting development pathways (Sections 1.6, 3.6, 4.3, 4.4, 13.9, 17.3.2, and Cross-Chapter Box 5 in Chapter 4), institutions that can devise strategies and set trajectories are useful enablers of transformation. Strategy setting often requires an overarching framework such as through framework laws that set targets ([Averchenkova et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2017)), or identify key sectors and opportunities for low-carbon transition ([Hochstetler and Kostka 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2015)) and innovation ([UNEP 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNEP--2018)). Few countries have built deliberate and lasting institutions that provide strategic intent, and those that have, have pursued different approaches. The UK’s approach rests on five-yearly targets (Box 13

The UK’s approach rests on five-yearly targets (Box 13.2); Germany requires sectoral budgets enforced through the Bundestag ([Flachsland and Levi 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Flachsland--2021)); and China uses an apex decision-body to set targets ([Teng and Wang 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Teng--2021)) (Box 13.3).

##  Box 13.2 | Climate Change Institutions in the UK![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

##  Box 13.2 | Climate Change Institutions in the UK![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
The central institutional arrangements of climate governance in the UK were established by the 2008 Climate Change Act (CCA): statutory five-year carbon budgets; an independent advisory body, the Committee on Climate Change (CCC); mandatory progress monitoring and reporting to Parliament; and continuous adaptive planning following a five-yearly cycle. The CCC is noteworthy as an innovative institution that has also been emulated by other countries.

The design of the CCC was influenced by the concept of independent central banking ([Helm et al. 2003](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Helm--2003)). It has established a reputation for independent high quality analysis and information dissemination, is frequently referred to in Parliament and widely used by other actors in policy debates, all of which suggest a high degree of legitimacy ([Averchenkova et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Averchenkova--2018)). However, since the CCC only recommends rather than sets budgets ([McGregor et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McGregor--2012)), accountability for meeting the carbon budgets works primarily through reputational and political effects rather than legal enforcement.
##  Box 13.3 | China’s Climate Change Institutions![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Climate governance in China features a combination of top-down planning and vertical accountability ([Sims Gallagher and Xuan 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sims%20Gallagher--2019); [Teng and Wang 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Teng--2021)). An overarching coordination role is performed by the Leading Group on Carbon Peaking and Carbon Neutrality, appointed by and reporting to the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, and the National Leading Group on Climate Change Response, Energy Conservation, and Emissions Reduction (NLGCCR), headed by the Premier and consisting of more than 30 ministers ([Wang et al. 2018a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wang--2018a)). The Department of Climate Change (DCC) under the Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE) is the primary agency in charge of climate issues, with a corresponding local Bureau of Ecology and Environment in each province or city

. While MEE is the leading agency for climate policy, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) is the leading agency for setting overall and industry-specific targets in five-year plans, and thus has a key role in coordinating carbon emissions targets with energy and industrial development targets ([Wang et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wang--2019); [Yu 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Yu--2021)). Involvements of ministries related to foreign affairs, public finance, science and technology, as well as sector ministries such as transportation, construction, and manufacturing industries are also needed to push forward sector-specific climate initiatives. At subsidiary levels of government carbon intensity targets are enforced through a ‘targets and responsibilities’ system that is directly linked to the evaluation of governments’ performances ([Lin 2012a](https://www.ipcc
.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lin--2012a); [Li et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Li--2016)).
##  Box 13.4 | Procedural Justice![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Decision-making consistent with energy and climate justice requires attention to procedural justice ([McCauley and Heffron 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCauley--2018)), which includes how decisions are made, and who is involved and has influence on decisions ([Sovacool and Dworkin 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sovacool--2015)). Procedural justice emphasises the importance of equitable access to decision-making processes and non-discriminatory engagement with all stakeholders ([Jenkins et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jenkins--2016)), attention to the capability, particularly of marginalised groups, to shape decisions ([Holland 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Holland--2017)) and recognition of their specific vulnerabilities in collective political processes ([Schlosberg 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schlosberg--2012))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schlosberg--2012)). Consensus-building institutions should avoid reducing normative questions to technical ones, recognising that values, interests and behaviours are all shaped by ongoing climate governance ([Ryder 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ryder--2018); [Schwanen 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schwanen--2021)). Additionally, communities affected by low-carbon transition may face challenges in articulating their understandings and experiences, which needs to be addressed in the design of climate institutions ([Ryder 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ryder--2018); [Schwanen 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schwanen--2021)).

Spatially localised alternative discourses of justice are often more recognised socially than national and universal framings of climate justice ([Bailey 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bailey--2017)). Participatory forms of governance such as climate assemblies and citizen juries ([Ney and Verweij 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ney--2015)) can help enhance the legitimacy of institutional decisions, even while empirical assessments suggest that these approaches continue to face practical challenges ([Devaney et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Devaney--2020); [Sandover et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sandover--2021); [Creasy et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Creasy--2021)).
##  Box 13.5 | South Africa’s Monitoring and Evaluation System![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

South Africa’s national monitoring and evaluation system provides high-level guidance on information requirements and assessment methodologies ([DEA 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#DEA--2015)). The country is developing a comprehensive, integrated National Climate Change Information System, to enable tracking, analysis and enhancement of South Africa’s progress towards the country’s transition to a low-carbon economy and climate-resilient society ([DFFE Republic of South Africa 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#DFFE%20Republic%20of%20South%20Africa--2021)). It includes information on GHG emission reductions achieved, observed and projected climate change, impacts and vulnerabilities, the impact of adaptation and mitigation actions, financial flows and technology transfer activities. ##  13.2.4Institution Building at the Sub-national Level ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Jurisdiction over significant mitigation-related arenas like planning, housing and community development reside at the sub-national level. To address linkages between mitigation and local concerns, sub-national actors engage in institution building within a broader socio-economic and political context, with actors and institutions at a multitude of scales shaping the effectiveness of sub-national-scale interventions ([Romero-Lankao et al. 2018a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2018a)). Mitigation policies may demand coordination between sectoral and jurisdictional units that historically have not collaborated; they may require sub-national actors to confront politically sensitive issues such as carbon taxes or increases in utility rates; and they may demand a redistribution of resources to protect endangered ecosystems or vulnerable populations ([Hughes and Romero-Lankao 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2014)).

Sub-national actors have built climate institutions by creating new visions and narratives, by setting new entities or committing existing offices, providing them with funds, staff and legal authority, or by experimenting with innovative solutions that could be transferred to other local governments or scaled nationally ([Hoffmann 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hoffmann--2011); [Hoornweg et al. 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hoornweg--2011); [Aylett 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aylett--2015); [Hughes and Romero-Lankao 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2014); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2015); [Hughes 2019b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2019b))

. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2015); [Hughes 2019b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2019b)). These actors have also created task forces, referendums, coordination of financial and human resources, technical assistance, awareness campaigns and funding ([Castán Broto 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cast%C3%A1n%20Broto--2017); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2018a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2018a); [Hughes 2019b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2019b)). ###  13.2.4.1 Significance of Sub-national Networks ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
