.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kammerer--2018); [Rashidi and Patt 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rashidi--2018); [Westman and Castan Broto 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Westman--2018); [Lee and Jung 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2018); [Lee 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2019); [Schwartz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schwartz--2019)).

Transnational networks have opened opportunities for sub-national actors to play a crucial mitigation role in political stalemates ([Jones 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jones--2014); [Schwartz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schwartz--2019)). The C40, the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, and ICLEI have disseminated information on best practices and promoted knowledge sharing between sub-national governments ([Lee 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2013); [Hakelberg 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hakelberg--2014); [Heidrich et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heidrich--2016); [Kona et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kona--2016); [Di Gregorio et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2020)) ([Section 14.5.5](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kona--2016); [Di Gregorio et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2020)) ([Section 14.5.5](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-14#14.5.5)). Organisations such as the US Carbon Cycle Working Group of the United States Global Change Research Program, the Australian Climate Action Network, and the Mexican Metropolitan Environmental Commission have helped facilitate coordination and learning across multiple jurisdictions and sectors, and connected ambiguous spaces between public, private and civil society actors ([Romero-Lankao et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2015); [Horne and Moloney 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Horne--2019); [Hughes 2019b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2019b)).

Transnational networks have limited influence on climate policies where national governments exert top-down control (e.g., in the city of Rizhao, China) ([Westman et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Westman--2019)); where sub-national actors face political fragmentation, lack regulations, and financial and human resources; or where vertically-integrated governance exists, as in State of São Paulo, Santiago de Chile, and Mexico City ([Romero-Lankao et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2015); [Setzer 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2017)).

Public support for sub-national climate institutions increases when climate policies are linked to local issues such as travel congestion alleviation or air pollution control (Puppim de Oliveira 2013; [Romero-Lankao et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2013); [Simon Rosenthal et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Simon%20Rosenthal--2015); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2015); [Ryan 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ryan--2015)), or when embedded in development priorities that receive support from the national government or citizens (Jörgensen et al. 2015b; [Floater et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Floater--2016); [Dubash et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2018))

. 2015b; [Floater et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Floater--2016); [Dubash et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2018)). For example, Indian cities have engaged in international climate cooperation seeking innovative solutions to address energy, water and infrastructure problems (Beermann et al. 2016).
###  13.2.4.2Factors Influencing Institution Building at the Sub-national Level ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Availability of federal funding is a fundamental pillar of city actors’ capacity to develop mitigation policies. Administrative structures, such as the presence of a professional city manager and staff assigned specifically to climate efforts ([Simon Rosenthal et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Simon%20Rosenthal--2015)). Cooperation between administrative departments, and the creation of knowledge and data on energy use and emissions are also essential for mitigation planning ([Hughes and Romero-Lankao 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2014); [Ryan 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ryan--2015)). For example, the high technical competency of Tokyo’s bureaucracy combined with availability of historical and current data enabled the city’s unique cap-and-trade system on large building facilities ([Roppongi et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roppongi--2017)).

Visions and narratives about the future benefits or risks of climate change are often effectively advanced at the sub-national level, drawing on local governmental abilities to bring together actors involved in place-based decarbonisation across sectors ([Hodson and Marvin 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hodson--2009); [Bush et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bush--2016); [Huang et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Huang--2018); [Prendeville et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Prendeville--2018); [Levenda et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levenda--2019))

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Prendeville--2018); [Levenda et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levenda--2019)). For example, in the plans of 43 C40 Cities, climate action is framed as part of a vision for vibrant, economically prosperous, and socially just cities, that are habitable, secure, resource-efficient, socially and economically inclusive, and competitive internationally ([Romero-Lankao and Gnatz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2019)).

However, institution building is often constrained by a lack of national support, funding, human resources, coalitions, coordination across old and new organisations, and the ability to create new institutional competences ([Valenzuela 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Valenzuela--2014); [Jörgensen et al. 2015a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#J%C3%B6rgensen--2015a); [Ryan 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ryan--2015); [Dubash et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2018); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2018a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2018a); [Anderton and Setzer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Anderton--2018); [Cointe 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cointe--2019); [Di Gregorio et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2019); [Jaccard et al

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cointe--2019); [Di Gregorio et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2019); [Jaccard et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jaccard--2019); [Hughes 2019b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2019b)). Climate mitigation can also be limited by cultural norms and values of policy actors with varying levels of power, and shifting alliances ([Lachapelle et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lachapelle--2012); [Damsø et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dams%C3%B8--2016); [Giampieri et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Giampieri--2019); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2018a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2018a)).

Institution building is constrained by inequities; resources, legal remit, knowledge, and political clout vary widely within and among sub-national governments globally ([Jörgensen et al. 2015b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#J%C3%B6rgensen--2015b); [Genus and Theobald 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Genus--2016); [Joffe and Smith 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Joffe--2016); [Klinsky 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klinsky--2018); [Reckien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Reckien--2018); [Markkanen and Anger-Kraavi 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Markkanen--2019)). Dominant discourses tend to prioritise scientific and technical expertise and, thus, they focus on infrastructural and economic concerns over the concerns and needs of disadvantaged populations ([Heikkinen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc
. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heikkinen--2019); [Romero-Lankao and Gnatz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2019)).

In addition, expert driven, technical solutions such as infrastructural interventions can undermine the knowledge of lower income countries, communities or indigenous knowledge holders, yet are often used by sub-national governments ([Ford et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ford--2016); [Brattland and Mustonen 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Brattland--2018); [Nagorny-Koring 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nagorny-Koring--2019); [Whyte 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Whyte--2017), 2020). Technical solutions, such as electric vehicles or smart grids rarely address the needs and capabilities of disadvantaged communities that may not be able to afford these technologies ([Mistry 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mistry--2014); [Romero-Lankao and Nobler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2021))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mistry--2014); [Romero-Lankao and Nobler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2021)). However, mitigation strategies in sectors such as transport and buildings have often focused on technical and market outcomes, the benefits of which are limited to some, while others experience negative externalities or face health risks ([Markard 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Markard--2018); [Williams and Doyon 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Williams--2019); [Carley and Konisky 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carley--2020)). Delivering climate justice requires community-driven approaches to understanding the problem addressing structural inequities and fostering justice, while reducing carbon emissions ([Romero-Lankao et al. 2018b](https://www.ipcc

. 2018b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2018b); [Carley and Konisky 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carley--2020); [Lewis et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lewis--2020)).

To address this situation requires procedural justice that involves all communities, particularly disadvantaged, in climate mitigation decisions and policies (Box 13.4). Also essential is recognition justice, that addresses past inequities through tools such as subsidies, tariffs, rebates, and other policies ([Agyeman 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Agyeman--2013); [Rydin 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rydin--2013); [UN Habitat 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UN%20Habitat--2016)). Both tenets are key to ensure the fair distribution of benefits or negative impacts from mitigation policies (distributional justice) ([McCauley and Heffron 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCauley--2018); [Lewis et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lewis--2020))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCauley--2018); [Lewis et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lewis--2020)). However, the benefits of inclusive approaches are often overlooked in favour of growth oriented mitigation and planning ([Rydin 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rydin--2013); [Altenburg 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Altenburg--2011); [Smith 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smith--2019); [Lennon 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lennon--2020)). Box 13.6 discusses how the city of Durban has internalised climate change with attention to considerations of justice.

Moreover, deep mitigation requires moving beyond existing technological responses ([Mulugetta and Castán Broto 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mulugetta--2018)) to policies that correspond to the realities of developing countries ([Bouteligier 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bouteligier--2013)).However, best practice approaches tend to be fragmented due to the requirements of different contexts, and often executed as pilot projects that rarely lead to structural change ([Nagorny-Koring 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nagorny-Koring--2019)). Instead, context-specific approaches that include consideration of values, cultures and governance better enable successful translation of best practices ([Affolderbach and Schulz 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Affolderbach--2016); [Urpelainen 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Urpelainen--2018)).

##  Box 13.6 | Institutionalising Climate Change Within Durban’s Local Government ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Durban has effectively linked climate change agendas with ongoing sustainability actions and goals. To do so, adaptation has been broadened to include a just transition to a low-carbon future to address development, energy security and GHG reduction ([Roberts et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roberts--2016)).
Durban has mainstreamed climate and justice concerns within local government through strong local leadership by key individuals and departments; included climate concerns within various municipal short-term and long-term planning processes; mobilised civil society; enhanced local and international networking; explored funding opportunities; and restructured institutions ([Roberts et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roberts--2016)).

Durban shows that embedding responses to climate change within local government activities requires that climate change is made relevant locally and framed within a broader environmental justice framework ([Roberts 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roberts--2010)). Civil society has been key in balancing the influence of the private sector on Durban’s dynamic political process ([Aylett 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aylett--2013)).
#  13.3 Structural Factors that Shape Climate Governance ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section

A growing literature suggests that ambitious climate policy emerges out of strong domestic political support (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Aklin and ](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aklin--2020)[Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020) ; [Lamb and Minx 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lamb--2020); [Colgan et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Colgan--2021)). Such support is the outcome of political interest constellations and struggles that vary from country to country. Structural factors (such as economic wealth and natural resources, the character of the national political system, and the dominant ideas, values and beliefs) shape how climate change is governed (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Hochstetler 2020](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Hochstetler 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2020)). This section assesses the ways these structural factors affect political dynamics and decision-making, and ultimately constrain, sustain or enable development of domestic climate governance.

While these structural factors are crucial, they do not determine the outlook of given countries’ climate governance, as civic, corporate and/or political groups or individuals can be mobilised and seek to counteract these structural effects, as indicated in the following [Section 13.4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.4) that examines the role of various actors and agencies in shaping governance processes. Taken together, Sections 13.3 and 13.4 show that domestic climate governance is not fully constrained by structural factors, but rather that diverse actors can and do achieve substantial changes. 
##  13.3.1Material Endowments ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Material endowments are natural and economic resources, such as fossil fuels and renewable energy, forests and land, and economic or financial resources, which tend to shape developments of domestic climate governance (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Friedrichs and Inderwildi 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Friedrichs--2013); [Lachapelle and Paterson 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lachapelle--2013); [Bang et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bang--2015); [Lamb and Minx 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lamb--2020)). Most countries’ social and economic systems are largely developed on the basis of their material endowment, and thus they contribute to shape the distribution of political power in that country ([Hall and Soskice 2001](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hall--2001))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hall--2001)). Material endowments are by no means the only influencing factor, and actors may succeed to either circumvent or exploit material endowments to impact climate governance (limited evidence, medium agreement ) ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Green and Hale 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Green--2017); [Aklin and ](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aklin--2020)[Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020) ).

Since countries are not bound by their material endowment, countries with similar material endowments may differ in climate governance, whereas those with notable differences in material endowments may have similar policies. For instance, countries with rich fossil fuel endowments are found either adopting rather ambitious emission reduction targets and measures, or remaining weak in developing domestic climate policies ([Eckersley 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eckersley--2013); [Farstad 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Farstad--2019)). Further, countries with radically different electricity systems and energy resource potentials are found developing rather similar renewables support schemes such as feed-in-tariff subsidies and competitive tendering programmes ([Dobrotkova et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dobrotkova--2018); [Vanegas Cantarero 2020](https://www.ipcc

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dobrotkova--2018); [Vanegas Cantarero 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Vanegas%20Cantarero--2020); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). Some policy instruments are widely applied in both developed and developing countries with similar or different material endowment. For example, renewable energy auctions have been experimented by over 100 countries by the end of 2018 ([IRENA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IRENA--2019)).

Rich carbon-intensive resources and well developed infrastructure can make low-carbon activities relatively less economically profitable, and negatively influence some perceptions of climate mitigation potential ([Bertram et al. 2015a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bertram--2015a); Erickson et al. 2015). If effective climate policies are introduced despite this, they can alter the importance of country’s material endowments in a way that underpin more forceful climate governance over time. For instance, policy interventions to limit fossil fuel exploitation or support renewable energy deployment may change the value of these energy resources over time ([Schmitz et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmitz--2015); [Ürge-Vorsatz et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%C3%9Crge-Vorsatz--2018); [Chailleux 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chailleux--2020); [Colgan et al

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%C3%9Crge-Vorsatz--2018); [Chailleux 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chailleux--2020); [Colgan et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Colgan--2021)).

Developing countries face additional material constraints in climate governance due to challenges associated with underdevelopment and scarce economic or natural resources (medium evidence,  high agreement ). Hence, many developing countries design domestic climate mitigation policies in combination with policy goals that address various developmental challenges ([von Stechow et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#von%20Stechow--2016); [Deng et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Deng--2017); [Thornton and Comberti 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Thornton--2017); [Campagnolo and Davide 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Campagnolo--2019)), such as air quality, urban transportation, energy access, and poverty alleviation ([Klausbruckner et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klausbruckner--2016); [Li et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klausbruckner--2016); [Li et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Li--2016); [Melamed et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Melamed--2016); [Slovic et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Slovic--2016); [Khreis et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Khreis--2017); [Geall et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Geall--2018); [Xie et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Xie--2018)). Combining climate and developmental policies for beneficial synergies should not overlook potential trade-offs and challenges ([Dagnachew et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dagnachew--2018); [Ellis and Tschakert 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ellis--2019); [Peñasco et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dagnachew--2018); [Ellis and Tschakert 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ellis--2019); [Peñasco et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pe%C3%B1asco--2021)) ([Section 13.7.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.7.2) for wider discussion).
##  13.3.2Political Systems ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The effectiveness of domestic climate governance will significantly rely on how well it fits with the features of the countries’ specific political systems (limited evidence,  high agreement ) ([Schmitz 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmitz--2017); [Lamb and Minx 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lamb--2020)). Political systems have developed over generations and constitute a set of formal institutions, such as laws and regulations, bureaucratic structures, political executives, legislative assemblies and political parties ([Egeberg 1999](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Egeberg--1999); [Pierson 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pierson--2004))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Egeberg--1999); [Pierson 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pierson--2004)). Different political systems create differing conditions for climate governance to emerge and evolve, but because political systems are so politically and historically entrenched they are not likely to change quickly even though this could facilitate domestic climate mitigation efforts (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Duit and Galaz 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duit--2008); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). In addition, variations in governance capacities also affect climate policy making and implementation ([Meckling and Nahm 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Meckling--2018)).

Broader public participation and more open contestation spaces tend to nurture more encompassing climate policies, facilitate stronger commitments to international agreements ([Bättig and Bernauer 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A4ttig--2009); [Böhmelt et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%B6hmelt--2016)), achieve more success in decoupling economic growth from CO2 emissions ([Lægreid and Povitkina 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#L%C3%A6greid--2018)), reduce more CO2 emissions ([Clulow 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Clulow--2019); [von Stein 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#von%20Stein--2020)), and maintain lower deforestation rates (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Buitenzorgy and Mol 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Buitenzorgy--2011))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Buitenzorgy--2011)). States with less public participation and contestation space can also develop ambitious climate emission reduction targets and institutions ([Zimmer et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zimmer--2015); [Eckersley 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eckersley--2016); [Han 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Han--2017); [Engels 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Engels--2018)), but the drivers and effects of climate policies within less open and liberal political contexts has not yet been sufficiently investigated.

Election systems based on proportional representation tend to have lower emissions, higher energy efficiency, higher renewable energy deployment, and more climate friendly investment than systems where leadership candidates have to secure a majority of the votes to be elected (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Fredriksson and Millimet 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fredriksson--2004); [Lachapelle and Paterson 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lachapelle--2013); [Finnegan 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Finnegan--2019)). Such systems better enable voters supporting ambitious climate positions to influence policymaking ([Harrison and Sundstrom 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Harrison--2010); [Willis 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Harrison--2010); [Willis 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Willis--2018)), place less political risks on legislators from additional costs incurred from climate actions on voters ([Finnegan 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Finnegan--2018), 2019), and strengthen credible commitments to climate policy ([Lockwood 2021b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lockwood--2021b)). Similarly, rules that govern the relationship between governments and civic societies in decision-making have also been shown to matter in climate governance

. Similarly, rules that govern the relationship between governments and civic societies in decision-making have also been shown to matter in climate governance. Corporatist societies, where economic groups are formally involved in public policy making, have better climate-related outcomes (lower CO2 emissions and higher low-carbon investments) than liberal-pluralist countries, where a larger array of non-governmental organisations compete for informal influence, often through lobbying (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Liefferink et al. 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Liefferink--2009); [Jahn 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jahn--2016); [Finnegan 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Finnegan--2018)).

Political parties with similar ideological roots in different countries (for instance social democratic or conservative parties) may have different positions on climate governance across countries ([Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). Nevertheless, on average, a higher share of green parties in a parliament is associated with lower greenhouse gas emissions ([Neumayer 2003](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Neumayer--2003); [Jensen and Spoon 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jensen--2011); [Mourao 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mourao--2019)), and left-wing parties tend to adopt more pro-climate policy positions (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Carter 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carter--2013); [Tobin 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tobin--2017); [Farstad 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carter--2013); [Tobin 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tobin--2017); [Farstad 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Farstad--2018); [Ladrech and Little 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ladrech--2019)). There is also evidence, however, that conservative parties in some countries support climate measures ([Båtstrand 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A5tstrand--2015)) and consensus can be achieved on climate actions across the political spectrum ([Thonig et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Thonig--2021))

. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Thonig--2021)). At the same time, it seems harder to get support for new climate governance initiatives in systems where many political groups can block decision due to many veto points, for instance in systems with bicameralism (the legislature is divided into two separate assemblies) and/or in federalist governments (where regions have national political representation, e.g. USA and Brazil) (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Madden 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Madden--2014); [von Stein 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#von%20Stein--2020)) although federal systems hold out the possibility of sub-national action when federal agreement is limited ([Section 13.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)). There remains a limited literature on the role of green parties and veto points in developing countries ([Haynes 1999](https://www.ipcc

.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.2)). There remains a limited literature on the role of green parties and veto points in developing countries ([Haynes 1999](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Haynes--1999); [Kernecker and Wagner 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kernecker--2019)).

In any political system, climate policy adoption and implementation may be obstructed by corrupt practices ([Rafaty 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rafaty--2018); [Fredriksson and Neumayer 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fredriksson--2016)) that entail an abuse of entrusted power for private gain (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Treisman 2000](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Treisman--2000)). Evidence shows that CO2 emissions levels can be affected by corruption, either through the direct negative effect of corruption on law enforcement, including in the forestry sector ([Sundström 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sundstr%C3%B6m--2016)), or through the negative effect of corruption on countries’ income ([Welsch 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Welsch--2004))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Welsch--2004)).These early findings are reinforced by studies of a global sample of countries ([Cole 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cole--2007)) and from across the developing world (Sahli and Rejeb 2015; [Bae et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bae--2017); [Wang et al. 2018b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wang--2018b); [Ridzuan et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ridzuan--2019); [Habib et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Habib--2020)). Corruption also disrupts public support of climate policies by affecting the levels of trust (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Harring 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Harring--2013); [Fairbrother et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fairbrother--2019); [Davidovic and Harring 2020](https://www.ipcc

. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fairbrother--2019); [Davidovic and Harring 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Davidovic--2020)), which then impact on the compliance of climate policies. More research is required to further understand the causal mechanisms between corrupt practices and emissions.
##  13.3.3Ideas, Values and Belief Systems ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Ideas, values and beliefs affect climate governance by shaping people’s perceptions, attitude, and preferences on specific policy and governance issues (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [McCright et al. 2016b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCright--2016b); [Schifeling and Hoffman 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schifeling--2019); [Leipold et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Leipold--2019); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). While these are often entrenched, they can also change, for instance when facing growing exposures to climate risks, stronger scientific evidence, and dominant public or political discourse ([Mayer et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayer--2017); [Diehl et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayer--2017); [Diehl et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Diehl--2021)). While change tend to be incremental, the pace of change may vary substantially across countries and specific climate issue areas.

However, new norms sometimes only influence political discussion and not actual governance. For instance, more ambitious climate emission reduction targets may not lead to more effective mitigation actions or policy instruments. Put another way, words do not replace actions ([Geden 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Geden--2016)).

Different sets of beliefs can shape climate-related policies, targets, and instruments ([Boasson and Wettestad 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2013); [Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). First, beliefs link climate governance with social justice concerns; policies, targets and instruments may therefore reflect justice issues ([Fuller and McCauley 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fuller--2016); [Reckien et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Reckien--2017); [McCauley and Heffron 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCauley--2018); [Routledge et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Routledge--2018); [Bäckstrand and Lövbrand 2006](https://www.ipcc

.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCauley--2018); [Routledge et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Routledge--2018); [Bäckstrand and Lövbrand 2006](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A4ckstrand--2006), 2019). Second, climate mitigation may be seen as primarily a market correction issue and mitigation compatible with economic growth, as exemplified by ecological modernisation ([Mol et al. 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mol--2009); [Bäckstrand and Lövbrand 2006](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A4ckstrand--2006), 2019), climate capitalism ([Newell and Paterson 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Newell--2010)), market logics ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Newell--2010)), market logics ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)) or a global commons approach ([Bernstein and Hoffmann 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bernstein--2019)). Third, climate governance may be understood relative to policies on technological innovation and progress, often conceptualised as social-technical transformations ([Geels et al. 2017a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Geels--2017a)).

Significant variation in ideas, values and beliefs related to climate governance are detected across and within regions, countries, societies, organisations, and individuals (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Shwom et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shwom--2015); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021); [Knox-Hayes 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Knox-Hayes--2016); [Wettestad and Gulbrandsen 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wettestad--2018)). These factors provide the context for climate policymaking and include differences in countries’ histories ([Aamodt 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aamodt--2018); [Aamodt and Boasson 2020](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aamodt--2018); [Aamodt and Boasson 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aamodt--2020)); the political culture and regulatory traditions in governing environmental and energy issues ([Tosun 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tosun--2018); [Aamodt 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aamodt--2018); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)); and even bureaucrats’ educational background ([Rickards et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rickards--2014)). Structural factors in a country, such as deeply held value systems, are not changed rapidly, just as political systems or natural endowments, are not changed rapidly. Consequently, climate policy and governance is more effective if it takes into account these deep-rooted values and beliefs.

Differences in dominant individual preferences may also be important. The factors that shape individual ideas, values and beliefs about climate governance include trust in politicians, the state and other people in general ([Drews and van den Bergh 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Drews--2016); [Harring et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Harring--2019); [Huber et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Huber--2020)), fairness beliefs, variation in political orientation (left leaning more concerned), and class (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Schmitz et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmitz--2018); [Inglehart and Norris 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Inglehart--2017)).

Levels of climate change concern on the individual level have increased in most countries ([Shwom et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shwom--2015)), and vary with gender (females are more concerned), and place of residence (urban residents are more concerned) ([Shwom et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shwom--2015); [McCright et al. 2016a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCright--2016a); [Ziegler 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ziegler--2017)). The higher educated in developing countries tend to be more concerned ([Lee et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2015)) while individuals working in polluting industries tend to oppose forceful climate governance ([Bechtel et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bechtel--2019); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc
. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bechtel--2019); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020)).

Shifts in mainstream ideas, values and beliefs can underpin changes in climate policy choices and policy outcomes (limited evidence, medium agreement ) ([Schleich et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schleich--2018); [Mildenberger and Tingley 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2019)). For example, emission trading schemes are welcomed as a new regulatory instrument in China in the context of its market-oriented reforms and ideological shift in the past decades ([Lo 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lo--2013)). Based on the study of 167 nation-states and 95 sub-national jurisdictions with carbon pricing, researchers find that that high public belief in climate science underpin adoption of systems that produce a rather high carbon price ([Levi et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levi--2020))

. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levi--2020)). These public opinions need to be identified and leveraged in supporting specific policy choices or changes ([Mildenberger and Tingley 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2019)). Policy support tends to be greater if people believe effective measures are being taken by other actors, including other households ([Bostrom et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bostrom--2018); [Marlon et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marlon--2019)), and other countries and at the international level ([Schleich et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schleich--2018)).

On the other hand, anti-climate ideas or beliefs may arise due to the introduction of more constraining or ambitious climate policies, for example protests in reaction to toll roads in Norway, which increase the cost of driving, or protests in France against increasing carbon taxes ([Grossman 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grossman--2019); [Wanvik and Haarstad 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wanvik--2021)). The policy implication is that vulnerable or effected groups should be considered when introducing policy change, and that participation, transparency, and good communication all helps to reduce climate-related discontent.

Survey-based studies of public perceptions on hypothetical policy instruments or activities, such as carbon taxes or energy infrastructure, suggest that linking climate policy to other economic and social reforms can increase public support for climate governance ([Carattini et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carattini--2019); [Bergquist et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bergquist--2020)). People and politicians tend to underestimate other peoples’ and politicians’ willingness to support mitigation policies ([Hurlstone et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hurlstone--2014); [Mildenberger and Tingley 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2019)), but if actors are informed about other actors actual perceptions and behaviours this may reduce the tendency to underestimate climate governance support ([Mildenberger and Tingley 2019](https://www.ipcc
.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2019)).
#  13.4Actors Shaping Climate Governance ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section

While [Section 13.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.3) shows that structural factors condition climate governance, their ultimate importance also depends on whether and how various actors are mobilised ([Hochstetler 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hochstetler--2020); [Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015)). a wide range of regional and local governments as well as non-governmental actors have become increasingly engaged in climate governance, for instance through public-private partnerships and transnational networks ([Jordan et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jordan--2015); [Dorsch and Flachsland 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dorsch--2017); [Jordan et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jordan--2018)) and through the media and litigation, as discussed here.

Climate governance processes result from both slow-moving incremental changes to policy and more rapid bursts of change due to, for example, responses to dramatic weather events, general elections or global climate summits (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Aamodt and Stensdal 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aamodt--2017); [Jordan and Moore 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jordan--2020); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). While [Section 13.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.3) assessed how entrenched structural factors conditions climate governance developments, this section examines how actors are able to alter climate governance by engaging the climate policy process, undertaking litigation and interacting with media.
##  13.4.1Actors and Agency in the Public Process ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

A broad array of actors are engaged in shaping mitigation policy processes, including politicians and political parties, corporate actors, citizen groups, indigenous peoples organisations, labour unions and international organisations. Actors aiming to influence the climate-related policymaking process are studied together to understand climate policy dynamics and outcomes ([Bulkeley 2000](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2000); [Fisher 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2004); [Jost and Jacob 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jost--2004); [Jasny et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jasny--2015); [Fisher and Leifeld 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019); Jasny and [](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019)[Fisher 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019); Jasny and [](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019)[Fisher 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019) ) and collaboration and influence within climate policy networks ([Ingold and Fischer 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ingold--2014); [McAllister et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McAllister--2014); [Wagner and Ylä-Anttila 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wagner--2018); [Kammerer et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kammerer--2021)). Most research, however, focuses on one particular type of actor.

Political actors are decision-makers, and also influence whether climate governance is perceived as urgent and appropriate ([Okereke et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Okereke--2019); [Ferrante and Fearnside 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ferrante--2019); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). They include political parties, legislative assemblies and committees, governmental executives and the political leaders of governmental ministries ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015)). They are more likely to pay attention to climate issues when polling indicates high political salience with the public ([Carter 2006](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carter--2006), 2014), or when it becomes a contested issue among differing political parties ([Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carter--2006), 2014), or when it becomes a contested issue among differing political parties ([Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)). Fluctuations in the public’s interest and attention may underpin a disjointed approach in politicians’ engagement ([Willis 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Willis--2017), 2018). Policy implementation can be hampered if political actors propose frequent policy changes ([Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)).

Corporate actors often influence policies and their adoption ([Pulver and Benney 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pulver--2013); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020); [Goldberg et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Goldberg--2020)). Corporate actors acting individually or through industry associations, have worked to sway climate policy in different countries ([Falkner 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Falkner--2008); [Bernhagen 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bernhagen--2008); [Newell and Paterson 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Newell--2010); [Meckling 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Meckling--2011); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Meckling--2011); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020)). Their ability varies by country and issue (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Skjærseth and Skodvin 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skj%C3%A6rseth--2010); [Boasson and Wettestad 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2013); [Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)) and depends on material endowments ([Moe Singh 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Moe%20Singh--2012)), access to the political system ([Dillon et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dillon--2018); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dillon--2018); [Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020)), and the ability to shape ideas, values and belief systems ([Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015)). Corporate actors tend to change their climate policy preferences over time, as indicated by longitudinal studies of some European countries ([Boasson and Wettestad 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2013); [Boasson 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2015); [Boasson et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2021)).

Corporate actors are crucial to policy implementation because they are prominent emitters of the greenhouse gases and owners of carbon-intensive technologies and potential providers of solutions as developers, owners and adopters of low emission practices and technologies ([Falkner 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Falkner--2008); [Perrow and Pulver 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Perrow--2015)). Many climate policies and measures rely on businesses’ willingness to exploit newly created economic opportunities, such as support schemes for renewable energy and energy efficiency sector or carbon pricing ([Olsen 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Olsen--2007); [Newell and Paterson 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Newell--2010); [Shen 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2015); [World Bank 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Newell--2010); [Shen 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2015); [World Bank 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#World%20Bank--2019)). Some corporate actors provide climate solutions, such as renewable energy deployment, and have successfully influenced climate policy development related to feed-in tariffs, taxations, quotas, or emission trading schemes, in the EU ([Boasson 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2019)), Germany ([Leiren and Reimer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Leiren--2018)), the USA ([Stokes and Breetz 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stokes--2018)), the Nordic countries ([Kooij et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kooij--2018)), China ([Shen 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2017)) and Japan ([Li et al

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kooij--2018)), China ([Shen 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2017)) and Japan ([Li et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Li--2019)).

Fossil fuel industries have been important agenda-setters in many countries, including the USA ([Dunlap and McCright 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dunlap--2015); [Supran and Oreskes 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Supran--2017); [Downie 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Downie--2018)), the EU ([Skjærseth and Skodvin 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skj%C3%A6rseth--2010); [Boasson and Wettestad 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boasson--2013)), Australia ([Ayling 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ayling--2017)), China ([Shen and Xie 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2018); [Tan et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tan--2021)), India ([Schmitz 2017](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shen--2018); [Tan et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tan--2021)), India ([Schmitz 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmitz--2017); [Blondeel and Van de Graaf 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Blondeel--2018)), and Mexico ([Pulver 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pulver--2007)), with differing positions and impacts across countries ([Kim et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kim--2016); [Nasiritousi 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nasiritousi--2017)). In the US, the oil industry has underpinned emergence of climate scepticism ([Dunlap and McCright 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dunlap--2015); [Farrell 2016a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Farrell--2016a); [Supran and Oreskes 2017](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dunlap--2015); [Farrell 2016a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Farrell--2016a); [Supran and Oreskes 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Supran--2017)), and its spread abroad ([Dunlap and Jacques 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dunlap--2013); [Engels et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Engels--2013); [Painter and Gavin 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Painter--2016)). Corporate opposition to climate policies is often facilitated by a broad coalition of firms ([Cory et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cory--2021)).

Conservative foundations, sometimes financed by business revenues, have funded a diversity of types of groups, including think-tanks, philanthropic foundations, or activist networks to oppose climate policy ([Brulle 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Brulle--2014), 2019). However, there is limited knowledge about the conditions under which actors opposed to climate action succeed in shaping climate governance ([Kinniburgh 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kinniburgh--2019); [Martin and Islar 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Martin--2021)).

Some labour unions have developed positions and programmes on climate change ([Snell and Fairbrother 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Snell--2010); [Stevins 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stevins--2013); [Räthzel et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#R%C3%A4thzel--2018)), formed alliances with other actors in the field of climate policy ([Stevis 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stevis--2018)) and participated in domestic policy networks on climate change ([Jost and Jacob 2004](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jost--2004)), but we know little about their relative importance or success

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jost--2004)), but we know little about their relative importance or success. In countries with significant fossil fuel resources such as Australia, Norway, and the United States, labour unions, particularly industrial unions, tend to contribute to reducing the ambition of domestic climate policies mainly due to the concern of job losses ([Mildenberger 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mildenberger--2020)). Other studies find that the role of labour unions varies across countries ([Glynn et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Glynn--2017)).

Civil society actors can involve citizens working collectively to change individual behaviours that have climate implications. For example, environmental movements that involve various forms of collective efforts encourage their members to make personal lifestyle changes that reduce their individual carbon footprints ([Ergas 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ergas--2010); [Middlemiss 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Middlemiss--2011); [Haenfler et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Haenfler--2012); [Cronin et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cronin--2014); [Saunders et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Saunders--2014); [Büchs et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%BCchs--2015); [Wynes et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wynes--2018))

. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%BCchs--2015); [Wynes et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wynes--2018)). These efforts seek to change individual members’ consumer behaviours by reducing car-use and flying, shifting to non-fossil fuel sources for individual sources of electricity, and eating less dairy or meat ([Cherry 2006](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cherry--2006); [Ergas 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ergas--2010); [Middlemiss 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Middlemiss--2011); [Haenfler et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Haenfler--2012); [Stuart et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stuart--2013); [Cronin et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cronin--2014); [Saunders et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stuart--2013); [Cronin et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cronin--2014); [Saunders et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Saunders--2014); [Büchs et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%BCchs--2015); [Wynes and Nicholas 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wynes--2017); [Wynes et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wynes--2018); [Thøgersen et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Th%C3%B8gersen--2021)). Consumer/citizen engagement is sometimes encouraged through governmental directives, such as the ‘renewable energy communities’ granted by the EU renewable energy directive 2018/2001 ([The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#The%20European%20Parliament%20and%20the%20Council%20of%20the%20European%20Union--2018)). To date, there are only a limited number of case studies that measure the direct effect of participation in these types of movements as it relates to climate outcomes ([Saunders et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Saunders--2014); [Vestergren et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Vestergren--2018), 2019).

Citizens with less access to resources and power also participate by challenging nodes of power – policymakers, regulators, and businesses – to change their behaviours and/or accelerate their efforts. Tactics include lobbying, legal challenges, shareholder activism, coop board stewardship, and voting ([Gillan and Starks 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gillan--2007); [Schlozman et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schlozman--2012); [Viardot 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Viardot--2013); [Bratton and McCahery 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bratton--2015); [Yildiz et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Yildiz--2015); [Olzak et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Olzak--2016))

. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Yildiz--2015); [Olzak et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Olzak--2016)). Citizens provide the labour and political will needed to pressure political and economic actors to enact emission-reducing policies, as well as providing resistance to them ([Fox and Brown 1998](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fox--1998); [Boli and Thomas 1999](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boli--1999); [Oreskes and Conway 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Oreskes--2012); [McAdam 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McAdam--2017)).

Other citizen engagement involves a range of more confrontational tactics, such as boycotting, striking, protesting, and direct action targeting politicians, policymakers, and businesses ([Fisher et al. 2005](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2005); [Tarrow 2005](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tarrow--2005); [Fisher 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2010); [Saunders et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Saunders--2012); [Walgrave et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Walgrave--2012); [Wahlström et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wahlstr%C3%B6m--2013); [Eilstrup-Sangiovanni and Bondaroff 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eilstrup-Sangiovanni--2014); [Hadden 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hadden--2014), 2015; [O’Brien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eilstrup-Sangiovanni--2014); [Hadden 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hadden--2014), 2015; [O’Brien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#O%E2%80%99Brien--2018); [Chamorel 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chamorel--2019); [Cock 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cock--2019); 2019b; [Hadden and Jasny 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hadden--2019); [Swim et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Swim--2019)). Climate strikes and other more confrontational forms of climate activism have become increasingly common ([O’Brien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#O%E2%80%99Brien--2018); [Evensen 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Evensen--2019); D.A. Citizen engagement has also become common among indigenous groups who tend to have limited structural power but often aim to shape the formation and effects of projects that have implications to climate change. These include opposing extraction and transportation of fossil fuels on their traditional lands (especially in the Americas) ([Bebbington and Bury 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bebbington--2013); [Hindery 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hindery--2013); [Coryat 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Coryat--2015); [Claeys and Delgado Pugley 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Claeys--2017); [Wood and Rossiter 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wood--2017)); large-scale climate mitigation projects that may affect traditional rights ([Brannstrom et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Brannstrom--2017); [Moreira et al
