Yet for these climate aid initiatives to work effectively requires improved institutional architecture, better appreciation of local contexts, and more inclusive and transparent governance, based on evidence from many multilateral mechanisms like REDD+, CDM, GEF and GCF ([Gomez 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gomez--2013); [Arndt and Tarp 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Arndt--2017)), and bilateral programmes on energy, agriculture and land-use sectors ([Arndt and Tarp 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Arndt--2017); [Rogner and Leung 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogner--2018); [Moss and Bazilian 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Moss--2018)).

##  Box 13.7 | Civic Engagement: The School Strike Movement ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
On Friday 20 August 2018, Greta Thunberg participated in the first climate school strike. Since then, Fridays for Future – the name of the group coordinating this tactic of skipping school on Fridays to protest inaction on climate change – has spread around the world.

In March 2019, the first global climate strike took place, turning out more than one million people around the world ([Carrington 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carrington--2019)). Six months later in September 2019, young people and adults responded to a call to participate in climate strikes as part of the ‘Global Week for Future’ surrounding the UN Climate Action Summit ([Thunberg 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Thunberg--2019)), and the number of participants globally jumped to an estimated six million people ([Taylor et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Taylor--2019)). Although a handful of studies have reported on who was involved in these strikes, how they were connected, and their messaging ([Marris 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marris--2019); [Wahlström et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marris--2019); [Wahlström et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wahlstr%C3%B6m--2019); [Evensen 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Evensen--2019); D. [](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019)[Fisher 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2019) ; Boulianne et al. 2020; [Bevan et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bevan--2020); [Han and Ahn 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Han--2020); [Holmberg and Alvinius 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Holmberg--2020); [Jung et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jung--2020); [Martiskainen et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Martiskainen--2020); Thackeray et al. 2020; [Trihartono et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc

. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Martiskainen--2020); Thackeray et al. 2020; [Trihartono et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Trihartono--2020); [de Moor et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#de%20Moor--2021); [Fisher and Nasrin 2021b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2021b)), its consequences in terms of political outcomes and emissions reductions have yet to be fully understood ([Fisher and Nasrin 2021b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2021b)).

Although digital activism makes it easier to connect globally, it is unclear how digital technology will affect the youth climate movement, and its effects on carbon emissions. Research suggests that online activism is likely to involve a more limited range of participants and perspectives ([Bennett 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bennett--2013); [Elliott and Earl 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Elliott--2018)). Digital tactics could also mean that groups are less embedded in communities and less successful at creating durable social ties, factors that have been found to lead to longer term engagement ([Tufekci 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tufekci--2017); [Rohlinger and Bunnage 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rohlinger--2018); [Shirky 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shirky--2010)).
##  13.4.2 Shaping Climate Governance Through Litigation ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Outside the formal climate policy processes, climate litigation is another important arena for various actors to confront and interact over how climate change should be governed (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Wilensky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wilensky--2015); [Peel and Osofsky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2015), 2018; [Bouwer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bouwer--2018); [Setzer and Byrnes 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019); [Calzadilla 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Calzadilla--2019); [Setzer and Vanhala 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019); [Paiement 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Paiement--2020); [Wegener 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wegener--2020))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Paiement--2020); [Wegener 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wegener--2020)). Climate litigation is an attempt to control, order or influence the behaviour of others in relation to climate governance, and it has been used by a wide variety of litigants (governments, private actors, civil society and individuals) at multiple scales (local, regional, national and international) ([Osofsky 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Osofsky--2007); [Lin 2012b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lin--2012b); [Keele 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Keele--2017); [McCormick et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCormick--2018); [Peel and Osofsky 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2018); [Setzer and Vanhala 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2018); [Setzer and Vanhala 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019)). Climate litigation has become increasingly common (UNEP2020b), but its prevalence varies across countries (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Peel and Osofsky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2015); [Wilensky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wilensky--2015); [Bouwer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bouwer--2018); [Lin and Kysar 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lin--2020); [Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)). This is not surprising, given that courts play differing roles across varying political systems and law traditions ([La Porta et al. 1998](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#La%20Porta--1998)).

This sub-section focuses on relevant climate litigation for policies and institutions. Climate litigation is further discussed in Sections 14.5.1.2 (linkages between mitigation and human rights) and [Section 14.5.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-14#14.5.3) (cross-country implications and international courts/tribunals).

The vast majority of climate cases have emerged in United States, Australia and Europe, and more recently in developing countries ([Humby 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Humby--2018); [Kotze and du Plessis 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kotze--2019); [Peel and Lin 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2019); [Setzer and Benjamin 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019); [Zhao et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhao--2019); [Rodríguez-Garavito 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rodr%C3%ADguez-Garavito--2020)). As of 31 May 2021, 1841 cases of climate change litigation from around the world had been identified

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rodr%C3%ADguez-Garavito--2020)). As of 31 May 2021, 1841 cases of climate change litigation from around the world had been identified. Of these, 1387 were filed before courts in the United States, while the remaining 454 were filed in 39 other countries and 13 international or regional courts and tribunals (including the courts of the European Union). Outside the US, Australia (115), the UK (73) and the EU (58) remain the jurisdictions with the highest volume of cases. The majority of cases, 1006, have been filed since 2015 ([Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)). The number of climate litigation cases in developing countries is also growing. There are at least 58 cases in 18 Global South jurisdictions (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Humby 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Humby--2018); [Kotze and du Plessis 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Humby--2018); [Kotze and du Plessis 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kotze--2019); [Peel and Lin 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2019); [Setzer and Benjamin 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019); [Zhao et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhao--2019); [Rodríguez-Garavito 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rodr%C3%ADguez-Garavito--2020); [Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)).

Overall, courts have also played a more active role for climate governance in democratic political systems ([Peel and Osofsky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2015); [Eskander et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eskander--2021)). Whether and to what extent differing law traditions and political systems influence the role and importance of climate litigation has, however, not been examined enough scientifically ([Setzer and Vanhala 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019); [Peel and Osofsky 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2020)).

The majority of climate change litigation cases are brought against governments, by civic and non-governmental organisations and corporations ([Eisenstat 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eisenstat--2011); [Markell and Ruhl 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Markell--2012); [Wilensky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wilensky--2015); [Fisher et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fisher--2017); [Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)). Many, although not all of these cases, seek to ensure that governmental action on climate change is more ambitious, and better aligned with the need to avert or respond to climate impacts identified and predicted by the scientific community ([Markell and Ruhl 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Markell--2012); [Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Markell--2012); [Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)). Climate aligned cases against governments can be divided into two distinct categories: claims challenging the overall effort of a State or its organs to mitigate or adapt to climate change (sometimes referred to as ‘systemic climate litigation’) ([Jackson 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jackson--2020)) and claims regarding authorisation of third-party activity ([Bouwer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bouwer--2018); [Gerrard 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gerrard--2021); [Ghaleigh 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ghaleigh--2021)).

Systemic climate litigation that seeks an increase in a country’s ambition to tackle climate change has been a growing trend since the first court victories in the Urgenda case in the Netherlands (see Box 13.8 below) and the Leghari case in Pakistan in 2015. These cases motivated a wave of similar climate change litigation across the world ([Roy and Woerdman 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roy--2016); [Ferreira 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ferreira--2016); [Peeters 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peeters--2016); [Mayer 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayer--2019); [Paiement 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Paiement--2020); [Barritt 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barritt--2020); [Sindico et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sindico--2021))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barritt--2020); [Sindico et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sindico--2021)). Between 2015 and 2021, individuals and communities initiated at least 37 cases (including Urgenda and Leghari) against states ([Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)), challenging the effectiveness of legislation and policy goals ([Jackson 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jackson--2020); [Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)). Some cases also seek to shape new legal concepts such as ‘rights of nature’ recognised in the Future Generations case in Colombia ([Savaresi and Auz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Savaresi--2019); [Rodríguez-Garavito 2020](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Savaresi--2019); [Rodríguez-Garavito 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rodr%C3%ADguez-Garavito--2020)) and ‘ecological damage’ in the case of Notre Affaire à Tous and others vs France ([Torre-Schaub 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torre-Schaub--2021)).

Moreover, there are a number of regulatory challenges to state authorisation of high-emitting projects, which differs from systemic casesagainst states ([Bouwer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bouwer--2018); [Hughes 2019a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2019a)). For instance, the High Court in Pretoria, South Africa, concluded that climate change is a relevant consideration for approving coal-fired power plants ([Humby 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Humby--2018)). Similarly, the Federal Court of Australia concluded that the Minister for the Environment owed a duty of care to Australian children in respect to climate impacts when exercising a statutory power to decide whether to authorise a major extension to an existing coal mine ([Peel and Markey-Towler 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2021)).

Climate change litigation has also been brought against corporations by regional or local governments and non-governmental organisations ([Wilensky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wilensky--2015); [Ganguly et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ganguly--2018); [Foerster 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Foerster--2019)). One type of private climate change litigation alleges climate change-related damage and seeks compensation from major carbon polluters ([Ganguly et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ganguly--2018); [Wewerinke-Singh and Salili 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wewerinke-Singh--2020)). The litigators claim that major oil producers are historically responsible for a significant portion of global greenhouse gas emissions ([Heede 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heede--2014); [Frumhoff et al

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heede--2014); [Frumhoff et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Frumhoff--2015); [Ekwurzel et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ekwurzel--2017); [Stuart-Smith et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stuart-Smith--2021)). These cases rely on advancements in climate science, specifically climate attribution ([Marjanac et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marjanac--2017); [Marjanac and Patton 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marjanac--2018); [McCormick et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCormick--2018); [Minnerop and Otto 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Minnerop--2020); [Burger et al. 2020b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burger--2020b); [Stuart-Smith et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Minnerop--2020); [Burger et al. 2020b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burger--2020b); [Stuart-Smith et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stuart-Smith--2021)). It is alleged that major carbon emitters had knowledge and awareness of climate change and yet took actions to confound or mislead the public about climate science ([Supran and Oreskes 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Supran--2017)). Strategic climate change litigation has also been used to hold corporations to specific human rights responsibilities ([Savaresi and Auz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Savaresi--2019); [Savaresi and Setzer 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Savaresi--2021)) (Box 13.8).

In addition to direct cases targeting high emitters, litigation is also now being used to argue against financial investments in the fossil fuel industry ([Franta 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Franta--2017); [Colombo 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Colombo--2021)). In May 2021, the Hague District Court of the Netherlands issued a ground-breaking judgment holding energy company Royal Dutch Shell (RDS) legally responsible for greenhouse gas emissions from its entire value chain (Macchi and Zeben 2021). Claims have also been brought against banks, pension funds and investment funds for failing to incorporate climate risk into their decision-making, and to disclose climate risk to their beneficiaries ([Wasim 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wasim--2019); [Solana 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solana--2020); [Bowman and Wiseman 2020](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wasim--2019); [Solana 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solana--2020); [Bowman and Wiseman 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bowman--2020)). These litigation cases also impact on the financial market without directly involving specific financial institutions into the case ([Solana 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solana--2020)) but somehow aim to change their risk perceptions and attitude on high carbon activities ([Griffin 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Griffin--2020)).

The outcomes of climate litigation can affect the stringency and ambitiousness of climate governance ([McCormick et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCormick--2018); [Eskander et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eskander--2021)). In the United States, pro-regulation litigants more commonly win in relation to renewable energy and energy efficiency cases, and more frequently lose in relations to coal-fired power plant cases ([McCormick et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCormick--2018)). Outside the US, more than half (58%) of litigation have outcomes that are aligned with climate action ([Setzer and Higham 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2021)). But these cases can also have impacts outside of the legal proceedings before, during and after the case has been brought and decided ([Setzer and Vanhala 2019](https://www.ipcc

. But these cases can also have impacts outside of the legal proceedings before, during and after the case has been brought and decided ([Setzer and Vanhala 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Setzer--2019)). These impacts include changes in the behaviour of the parties ([Peel and Osofsky 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peel--2015); [Pals 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pals--2021)), public opinion ([Hilson 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hilson--2019); [Burgers 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burgers--2020)), financial and reputational consequences for involved actors ([Solana 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solana--2020)), and impact on further litigation ([Barritt 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barritt--2020))

Individual cases have also attracted considerable media attention, which in turn can influence how climate policy is perceived ([Nosek 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nosek--2018); [Barritt and Sediti 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barritt--2019); [Hilson 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hilson--2019); [Paiement 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Paiement--2020)). While there is evidence to show the influence of some key cases on climate agenda-setting ([Wonneberger and Vliegenthart 2021](https://www.ipcc

##  Box 13.8 | An Example of Systemic Climate Litigation: Urgenda vs State of the Netherlands![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The judgement in Urgenda vs State of the Netherlands established the linkage between a state’s international duty, domestic actions, and human rights commitments as to the recommendations of IPCC’s AR5 ([Burgers and Staal 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burgers--2019); [Antonopoulos 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Antonopoulos--2020)). It was the first to impose a specific emissions reduction target on a state ([de Graaf and Jans 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#de%20Graaf--2015);[ Cox 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%20Cox--2016); [Loth 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Loth--2016)). The District Court of The Hague ordered the Dutch Government to reduce emissions by at least 25% by the end of 2020

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Loth--2016)). The District Court of The Hague ordered the Dutch Government to reduce emissions by at least 25% by the end of 2020. Following the decision of the district court of The Hague in 2015 the Dutch government announced that it would adopt additional measures to achieve the 25% emissions reduction target by 2020 ([Mayer 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayer--2019)). The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal in 2018 and the Supreme Court in 2019. Since the first judgment in 2015 significant changes in the climate policy environment have been reported, the results of which have included the introduction of a Climate Act and the decision to close all remaining coal fired power plants by 2030 ([Verschuuren 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Verschuuren--2019); [Wonneberger and Vliegenthart 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wonneberger--2021)).
##  13.4.3Media as Communicative Platforms for Shaping Climate Governance ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Media is another platform for various actors to present, interpret and shape debates around climate change and its governance ([Tindall et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tindall--2018)). The media coverage of climate change has grown steadily since 1980s ([O’Neill et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#O%E2%80%99Neill--2015); [Boykoff et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2019)), but the level and type of coverage differs over time and from country to country (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Boykoff 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2011); [Schmidt et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmidt--2013); [Schäfer and Schlichting 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sch%C3%A4fer--2014))

. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmidt--2013); [Schäfer and Schlichting 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sch%C3%A4fer--2014)). Media can be a useful conduit to build public support to accelerate mitigation action, but may also be utilised to impede decarbonisation endeavours ([Boykoff 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2011); [O’Neill et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#O%E2%80%99Neill--2015); [Farrell 2016b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Farrell--2016b); [Carmichael et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carmichael--2017); [Carmichael and Brulle 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carmichael--2018)). Different media systems in different regions and countries and with unique cultural and political traditions also affect how climate change is communicated ([Eskjær 2013](https://www

. Different media systems in different regions and countries and with unique cultural and political traditions also affect how climate change is communicated ([Eskjær 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eskj%C3%A6r--2013)).

A broad variety of media platforms cover climate change issues, including traditional news media, such as newspapers and broadcasting, digital social media ([Walter et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Walter--2018)), creative narratives such as climate fiction and films ([Svoboda 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Svoboda--2016)); humour and entertainment media ([Brewer and McKnight 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Brewer--2015); [Skurka et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skurka--2018); [Boykoff and Osnes 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2019)); and strategic communications campaigns ([Hansen and Machin 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hansen--2008); [Hoewe and Ahern 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hoewe--2017))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hansen--2008); [Hoewe and Ahern 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hoewe--2017)). Media coverage can have far-reaching consequences on policy processes, but we know less about its relative importance compared to other policy shaping factors (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Liu et al. 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Liu--2011); [Boykoff 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2011); [Hmielowski et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hmielowski--2014)).

Popular culture images, science fictions and films of ecological catastrophe can dramatically and emotively convey the dangers of climate change ([Bulfin 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulfin--2017)). The overall accuracy of the media coverage on climate change has improved from 2005 to 2019 in the United Kingdom (UK), Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and the USA ([McAllister et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McAllister--2021)). Moreover, coverage of climate science is increasing. One study (MeCCO) has tracked media coverage of climate change from over 127 sources from 59 countries in North and Latin America, Europe, Middle East, Africa, Asia and Oceania ([Boykoff et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2021))

However, increasing media coverage does not always lead to more accurate coverage of climate change mitigation, as it can also spur diffusion of misinformation ([Boykoff and Yulsman 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Boykoff--2013); [van der Linden et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#van%20der%20Linden--2015); [Whitmarsh and Corner 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Whitmarsh--2017); [Fahy 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fahy--2018); [Painter 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Painter--2019))

#  13.5 Sub-national Actors, Networks, and Partnerships ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section

In many countries, sub-national actors and networks are a crucial component of climate mitigation as they have remit over land-use planning, waste management, infrastructure, housing and community development, and their jurisdictions are often where the impacts of climate change are felt (robust evidence,  high agreement ). Depending on the legal framework and other institutional constraints, sub-national actors play crucial roles in developing, delivering and contesting decarbonisation visions and pathways ([Schroeder et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schroeder--2013); [Ryan 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ryan--2015); [Abbott et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Abbott--2016); [Bäckstrand et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A4ckstrand--2017); [Amundsen et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Amundsen--2018); [Fuhr et al

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A4ckstrand--2017); [Amundsen et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Amundsen--2018); [Fuhr et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fuhr--2018)) ([Section 13.3.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.3.3)).

Sub-national actors include organisations, jurisdictions, and networks (e.g., a coalition of cities or state authorities). These are either formal or informal, profit or non-profit and public or private ([Avelino and Wittmayer 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Avelino--2016)). For example, corporations are formal, private, and for-profit, the state and labour organisations are formal, public, and non-profit, and communities are private, informal, and non-profit. An intermediary sector, crossing the boundaries between private and public, for profit and non-profit, includes energy cooperatives, not-for-profit energy enterprises, and the scientific community ([Avelino and Wittmayer 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Avelino--2016)).

To address the challenge of climate mitigation, a range of actors across sectors and jurisdictions have created coalitions for climate governance, operating as actor-networks. For example, mitigation policies are particularly effective when they are integrated with co-benefits such as health, biodiversity, and poverty reduction ([Romero-Lankao et al. 2018a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2018a)). Transnational business and public-private partnerships and initiatives, as well as international cooperation at the sub-national and city levels are discussed in Chapter 14.
##  13.5.1Actor-networks and Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The decision adopting the Paris Agreement welcomed contributions of sub-national actors to mobilising and scaling up ambitious climate action (see also Chapter 14). They engage in climate relevant mechanisms, such as the Sustainable Development Goals and the New Urban Agenda. Sub-national actors fill a gap in national policies, participate in transnational and sub-national climate governance networks and facilitate learning and exchange among governmental, community, and private organisations at multiple levels, gathering knowledge and best practices such as emission inventories and risk management tools that can be applied in multiple contexts ([Kona et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kona--2016); [Sharifi and Yamagata 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sharifi--2016); [Michaelowa and Michaelowa 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Michaelowa--2017); [Warbroek and Hoppe 2017](https://www.ipcc

.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%C3%9Crge-Vorsatz--2018); [Amundsen et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Amundsen--2018); [Heikkinen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heikkinen--2019); [Hultman et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hultman--2020)).

Sub-national climate change policies exist in more than 142 countries and exemplify the increasing significance of mitigation policy at the sub-national level ([Hsu et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2018)). However, estimations of the number of sub-national actors pledging voluntary climate action are challenging and underreporting is a concern ([Hsu et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2018); [Chan and Morrow 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chan--2019)). As can be seen in[Figure 13.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/) more than 10,500 cities and nearly 250 regions representing more than 2 billion people, factoring for overlaps in population between these jurisdictions, have pledged climate action as of December 2020 ([Hsu et al. 2020a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2020a))

. 2020a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2020a)). More jurisdictions in Europe and North America have pledged action, but in terms of population almost all regions are substantially engaged in sub-national action.

Many of these efforts are organised around transnational or regional networks. For example, a coalition of 130 sub-national (in other words, state, and regional) governments, representing 21% of the global economy and 672 million people, has pledged about 9% emissions reduction compared to a base year (CDP 2020). More than 10,000 cities, representing more than 10% of the global population, participate in the Global Covenant of Mayors, C40 Cities ([Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Global%20Covenant%20of%20Mayors%20for%20Climate%20and%20Energy--2018)), and ICLEI’s – Local Governments for Sustainability carbon registry ([Hsu et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2018)). In Europe alone, more than 6000 cities have adopted their own climate action plans ([Palermo et al. 2020a](https://www.ipcc

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2018)). In Europe alone, more than 6000 cities have adopted their own climate action plans ([Palermo et al. 2020a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Palermo--2020a)) and nearly 300 US sub-national actors – cities and states – were committed to maintaining momentum for climate action as part of the ‘We Are Still In’ coalition ([We Are Still In coalition 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#We%20Are%20Still%20In%20coalition--2020)) in the absence of national US climate legislation. Further, as of October 2020, more than 826 cities and 103 regional governments had made specific pledges to decarbonise, whether in a specific sector (e.g., buildings, electricity, or transport) or through their entire economies, pledging to reduce their overall emissions by at least 80% (NewClimate Institute and Data Driven EnviroLab 2020)

.g., buildings, electricity, or transport) or through their entire economies, pledging to reduce their overall emissions by at least 80% (NewClimate Institute and Data Driven EnviroLab 2020). Cities such as Barcelona, Spain and Seattle, Washington have adopted net zero goals for 2050 in policy legislation, while many more cities throughout the world, including the Global South such as Addis Ababa in Ethiopia, have net zero targets under consideration ([ECIU 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#ECIU--2019), 2021).
Sub-national mitigation policies are highlighted below, based on the taxonomy of policies in [Section 13.6.1](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6.1):

a)  Economic instruments: as of 2020, there were carbon pricing initiatives (ETS, carbon tax or both) in 24 sub-national jurisdictions ([World Bank 2021a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#World%20Bank--2021a)). Examples include emission trading systems within North America, such as the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) and Western Climate Initiative (which also includes two Canadian provinces); tax rebates for the purchase of EVs; a carbon tax in British Columbia;and a cap-and-trade scheme in Metropolitan Tokyo ([Houle et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Houle--2015); [Murray and Rivers 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Murray--2015); [Hibbard et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hibbard--2018); [Bernard and Kichian 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bernard--2019); [Raymond 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hibbard--2018); [Bernard and Kichian 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bernard--2019); [Raymond 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Raymond--2019); [Xiang and Lawley 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Xiang--2019); [Chan and Morrow 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chan--2019)).

b)  Regulatory instruments: policies such as land use and transportation planning, performance standards for buildings, utilities, transport electrification, and energy use by public utilities, buildings and fleets are widely prevalent ([Bulkeley 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Jones 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jones--2013); [C40 and ARUP 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#C40%20and%20ARUP--2015); [Martinez et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Martinez--2015); [Hewitt and Coakley 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hewitt--2019); [Palermo et al. 2020b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Palermo--2020b))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hewitt--2019); [Palermo et al. 2020b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Palermo--2020b)). Policies such as regulatory restrictions, low emission zones, parking controls, delivery planning and freight routes, focus on traffic management and reduction of local air pollution but also have a mitigation impact ([Slovic et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Slovic--2016); [Khreis et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Khreis--2017); [Letnik et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Letnik--2018)). For instance, in coordination with national governments, sub-national actors in China, Europe and USA have introduced access to priority lanes, free parking and other strategies fostering the roll-out of EVs ([Creutzig 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Creutzig--2016); [Zhang and Bai 2017](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Creutzig--2016); [Zhang and Bai 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhang--2017); [Teske et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Teske--2018); [Zhang and Qin 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhang--2018); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2021)).

c)  Land-use planning addresses building form, density, energy, and transport, which are relevant for decarbonisation ([Creutzig et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Creutzig--2015); [Torabi Moghadam et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torabi%20Moghadam--2017); [Teske et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Teske--2018)). Its effectiveness is limited by absent or fragmented jurisdiction, financial resources and powers, competition between authorities and policy domains, and national policies that restrict local governments’ ability to enact more ambitious policies ([Fudge et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fudge--2016); [Gouldson et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gouldson--2016); [Petersen 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Petersen--2016))

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gouldson--2016); [Petersen 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Petersen--2016)). Most rapidly growing smaller cities in Latin America, Asia and Africa lack capacity for urban planning and enforcement ([Romero-Lankao et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2015); [Creutzig 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Creutzig--2016)).

d)  Other policies: these include information and capacity building, such as carbon labelling aimed at providing carbon footprint information to consumers ([Liu et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Liu--2016)); disclosure and benchmarking policies in buildings to increase awareness of energy issues and track mitigation progress ([Hsu et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2017); [Papadopoulos et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Papadopoulos--2018)); and procurement guidelines developed by associations ([Sustainable Purchasing Leadership Council 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sustainable%20Purchasing%20Leadership%20Council--2021)). For instance, a building retrofit programme was initiated in New York and Melbourne to foster energy efficiency improvements through knowledge provision, training, and consultation ([Trencher et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Trencher--2016); [Trencher and van der Heijden 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Trencher--2019)). Also significant is government provision of public good, services, and infrastructure ([Romero Lankao et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero%20Lankao--2019)), which includes provision of electric buses or buses on renewable fuels for public transportation ([Kamiya and Teter 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kamiya--2019)) and zero emission urban freight transport ([Quak et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Quak--2019)), sustainable food procurement for public organisations in cities ([Smith et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smith--2016)), decentralised energy resources ([Marquardt 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marquardt--2014); [Hirt et al

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smith--2016)), decentralised energy resources ([Marquardt 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marquardt--2014); [Hirt et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hirt--2021); [Kahsar 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kahsar--2021)), and green electricity purchase via community choice aggregation programmes and franchise agreements ([Armstrong 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Armstrong--2019)).
##  13.5.2Partnerships and Experiments ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Partnerships, such as those among private and public, or transnational and sub-national entities, have been found to enable better mitigation results in areas outside direct government control such as residential energy use, emissions from local businesses, or private vehicles ([Fenwick et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fenwick--2012); Castán Broto and [Bulkeley 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Aylett 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aylett--2014); [Hamilton et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hamilton--2014); [Bulkeley et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2016); [Wakabayashi and Arimura 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wakabayashi--2016); [Grandin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grandin--2018))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wakabayashi--2016); [Grandin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grandin--2018)). Partnerships take advantage of investments that match available grants or enable a local energy project, or enhance the scope or impact of mitigation ([Burch et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burch--2013)).

Sub-national actors have also been associated with experiments and laboratories, which promise to achieve the deep change required to address the climate mitigation gap ([Smeds and Acuto 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smeds--2018); [Marvin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marvin--2018)). Experiments span smart technologies, for example, in Malmö, Sweden (Parks 2019), Eco-Art, Transformation-Labs and other approaches that question the cultural basis of current energy regimes and seek reimagined or reinvented futures (Castán Broto and [Bulkeley 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Guy et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Guy--2015); [Voytenko et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Voytenko--2016); [Hodson et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hodson--2018); [Peng and Bai 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Voytenko--2016); [Hodson et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hodson--2018); [Peng and Bai 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peng--2018); [Smeds and Acuto 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smeds--2018); [Culwick et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Culwick--2019); [Pereira et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pereira--2019); [Sengers et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sengers--2019)). They may include governance experiments, from formally defined policy experiments to informal initiatives that mobilise new governance concepts ([Kivimaa et al. 2017a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kivimaa--2017a); [Turnheim et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc

. 2017a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kivimaa--2017a); [Turnheim et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Turnheim--2018)), and co-design initiatives and grassroots innovations ([Martiskainen 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Martiskainen--2017); [Sheikh and Bhaduri 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sheikh--2021)). These initiatives often expand the scope for citizen participation. For example, Urban Living Labs foster innovation, coproducing responses to existing problems of energy use, energy poverty and mobility that integrate scientific and expert knowledge with local knowledge and common values ([Voytenko et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Voytenko--2016); [Marvin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marvin--2018))

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Voytenko--2016); [Marvin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Marvin--2018)). The European Network of Living Labs – with a global outreach – has established a model of open and citizen-centric innovation for policy making. The proliferation of Climate Assemblies at the national and sub-national level further emphasises the increasing role that citizens can play in both innovating and planning for carbon mitigation ([Sandover et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sandover--2021)).

State and local authorities are often central to initiating and implementing experiments and use an incremental, ‘learning by doing’ governing approach ([Bai et al. 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bai--2010); [Nevens et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nevens--2013); Castán Broto and [Bulkeley 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Mcguirk et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mcguirk--2015); [Nagorny-Koring and Nochta 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nagorny-Koring--2018); [Hodson et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hodson--2018); [Peng and Bai 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peng--2018); [Smeds and Acuto 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smeds--2018); [Culwick et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peng--2018); [Smeds and Acuto 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Smeds--2018); [Culwick et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Culwick--2019); [Sengers et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sengers--2019)). Experiments relate to technological learning and changes in policies, practices, services, user behaviour, business models, institutions, and governance (Castán Broto and [Bulkeley 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Wieczorek et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wieczorek--2015); [Kivimaa et al. 2017a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kivimaa--2017a); [Laurent and Pontille 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Laurent--2018); [Torrens et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Torrens--2019)).

Experimentation has contributed to learning, changes in outcomes when implemented, and shifts in the political landscape ([Turnheim et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Turnheim--2018)). Experiments, however, are often isolated and do not always result in longer-term, more widespread changes. The transformative potential (understood as changes in the fundamental attributes of natural and human systems, see Annex I: Glossary) of experiments is constrained by uncertainty about locally relevant climate change solutions and effects; a lack of comprehensive, and sectorally inclusive national policy frameworks for decarbonisation; budgetary and staffing limitations; and a lack of institutional and political capacity to deliver integrated and planned approaches ([Evans and Karvonen 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Evans--2014); [Mcguirk et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Evans--2014); [Mcguirk et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mcguirk--2015); [Bulkeley et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2016); [Voytenko et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Voytenko--2016); [Wittmayer et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wittmayer--2016); [Webb et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Webb--2017); [Grandin et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grandin--2018); [Hölscher et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#H%C3%B6lscher--2018); [Nagorny-Koring 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nagorny-Koring--2019); [Sengers et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sengers--2019)).
##  13.5.3Performance and Global Mitigation Impact ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The performance of sub-national actors’ mitigation policies have been measured using criteria such as existence of mitigation targets, incentives for mitigation, definition of a baseline, and existence of a monitoring, reporting, and verification procedure ([Hsu et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2019)). Existing evaluations range from small-scale studies assessing the mitigation potential of commitments by sub-national regions, cities and companies in the USA or in 10 high-emitting economies ([Roelfsema 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roelfsema--2017); [Hsu et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2019)), to larger studies finding that over 9149 cities worldwide could mitigate 1400 MtCO2-eq in 2030 ([Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Global%20Covenant%20of%20Mayors%20for%20Climate%20and%20Energy--2018); [Hsu et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2018), 2019). These sub-national mitigation potential estimates vary since a range of approaches exists for accounting for overlaps between sub-national governments and their nested jurisdictions (e.g., states, provinces, and national governments) ([Roelfsema et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roelfsema--2018); [Hsu et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2019)). One analysis found that the cities of New York, Berlin, London, Greater Toronto, Boston, and Seattle have achieved on average a 0.27 tCO2-eq per capita per year reduction ([Kennedy et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kennedy--2012)). [Hsu et al. (2020c)](https://www.ipcc

.27 tCO2-eq per capita per year reduction ([Kennedy et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kennedy--2012)). [Hsu et al. (2020c)](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2020c) found that 60% of more than 1000 European cities, representing 6% of the EU’s total emissions, are on track to achieving their targets, reducing more than 51 MtCO2-eq. While evidence is limited, there are concerns that implementation challenges persist with city level plans, particularly tied to management of initiatives and engagement of the population ([Messori et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Messori--2020)).

Whether participation in transnational climate initiatives impacts sub-national governments’ achievement on climate mitigation goals is uncertain. Some find that higher ambition in climate mitigation commitments did not translate into greater mitigation ([Kona et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kona--2016); [Hsu et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hsu--2019)). Other studies associate participation in networks with increased solar photovoltaic systems (PV) investment ([Khan and Sovacool 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Khan--2016); [Steffen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Steffen--2019)), and with potential to achieve carbon emissions reductions per capita in line with a global 2°C scenario ([Kona et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kona--2016)).

Reporting networks may attract high-performing actors, suggesting an artificially high level of cities interested in taking climate action or piloting solutions (self-selection bias) that may not be effective elsewhere (van der Heijden 2018). Many studies present a conservative view of potential mitigation impact because they draw upon publicly reported mitigation actions and exclude sub-national actions that are not reported ([Kuramochi et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kuramochi--2020)).

In addition to direct mitigation contributions, climate action partnerships may deliver indirect effects that, while difficult to quantify, ensure long-term change ([Chan et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chan--2015)). Experimentation and policy innovation helps to establish best practices ([Hoffmann 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hoffmann--2011)); set new norms for ambitious climate action that help build coalitions ([Chan et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chan--2015); [Bernstein and Hoffmann 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bernstein--2018)); and translate into knowledge sharing or capacity building ([Lee and Koski 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2012); [Hakelberg 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hakelberg--2014); [Purdon 2015](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2012); [Hakelberg 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hakelberg--2014); [Purdon 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Purdon--2015); [Acuto and Rayner 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Acuto--2016)). Emergent researchexplores whether, in addition to realising outcomes, mitigation initiatives also provide the resources, skills and networks that governments and other stakeholders currently use to target other development goals ([Shaw et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shaw--2014); [Wolfram 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wolfram--2016); [Wiedenhofer et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wiedenhofer--2018); [Amundsen et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Amundsen--2018); [Heikkinen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wiedenhofer--2018); [Amundsen et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Amundsen--2018); [Heikkinen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heikkinen--2019)).

#  13.6Policy Instruments and Evaluation ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section
Institutions and governance processes described in previous section result in specific policies, that governments then implement and that shape actions of many stakeholders. This section assesses the empirical experience with the range of policy instruments available to governments with which to shape mitigation outcomes. [Section 13.7](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.7) that follows deals with how these instruments are combined into packages, and [Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9) addresses economy-wide measures and issues.

Many different policy instruments for GHG reduction are in use. They fall into a few major categories that share key characteristics. This section provides one possible taxonomy of these major types of policy instruments, presents a set of criteria for policy evaluation, and synthesises the literature on the most common mitigation policies. The emphasis is on recent empirical evidence on the performance of different policy instruments and lessons that can be drawn from these experiences. This builds on and enhances the AR5 Chapter 15, which provided a more theoretical treatment of policy instruments for mitigation.
##  13.6.1Taxonomy and Overview of Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
###  13.6.1.1Taxonomy of Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

##  13.6.1Taxonomy and Overview of Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
###  13.6.1.1Taxonomy of Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
A large number of policies and policy instruments can affect GHG emissions and/or sequestration, whether their primary purpose is climate change mitigation or not. Consequently, consistent with the approach in this chapter, this section adopts a broad interpretation to what is considered mitigation policy. Also, the section recognises the multiplicity of policies that overlap and interact.

Environmental policy instruments, including for climate change mitigation, have long been grouped into three main categories – (i) economic instruments, (ii) regulatory instruments, and (iii) other instruments – although the specific terms differ across disciplines and additional categories are common ([Kneese and Schultze 1975](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kneese--1975); [Jaffe and Stavins 1995](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jaffe--1995); [Nordhaus 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nordhaus--2013); [Wurzel et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wurzel--2013)). Examples of common policies in each category are shown in Table 13.1, but this is not a comprehensive list. Principles of and empirical experience with the various instruments are synthesised in Sections 13.6.3 to 13.6.5, international interactions are covered in [Section 13.6.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13
.6.3 to 13.6.5, international interactions are covered in [Section 13.6.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6.6).

Table 13.1 | Classification of mitigation policies.   
| Category  | Examples of common types of mitigation policy instruments  |  
| --- | --- |  
| Economic instruments  | Carbon taxes, GHG emissions trading, fossil fuel taxes, tax credits, grants, renewable energy subsidies, fossil fuel subsidy reductions, offsets, R&D subsidies, loan guarantees  |  
| Regulatory instruments  | Energy efficiency standards, renewable portfolio standards, vehicle emission standards, ban on SF6 uses, biofuel content mandates, emission performance standards, methane regulations, land-use controls  |  
| Other instruments  | Information programmes, voluntary agreements, infrastructure, government technology procurement policies, corporate carbon reporting  |  
###  13.6.1.2Coverage of Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

###  13.6.1.2Coverage of Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
An increasing share of global emissions sources is subject to mitigation policies, though coverage is still incomplete ([Eskander and Fankhauser 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eskander--2020); [Nascimento et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nascimento--2021)).

While consistent information on global prevalence of policies is not available, in G20 countries the use of various policy instruments has increased steadily over the past two decades ([Nascimento et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nascimento--2021)). The share of countries that had mitigation policy instruments in place rose across all sectoral categories, albeit to different extents in different sectors and for different policy instruments (Figure 13.4). Among G20 countries the electricity and heat generation has the greatest number of policies in place, and the agriculture and forestry sector the fewest ([Nascimento et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nascimento--2021)).

![](https://ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/figures/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Figure_13_4.png)
