. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Labeaga--2021)). Some subsidies, like tiered electricity rates, benefit low-income groups. Reductions of broad subsidies lead to price increases for fuels, electricity, transport, food and other goods and services that adversely affect the most economically vulnerable ([Coady et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Coady--2015); [Zeng and Chen 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zeng--2016); [Rentschler and Bazilian 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rentschler--2017)). Distributing some of the revenue saved can mitigate the adverse economic impacts on low-income groups ([Dennis 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dennis--2016); [Zeng and Chen 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zeng--2016); [Labeaga et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dennis--2016); [Zeng and Chen 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zeng--2016); [Labeaga et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Labeaga--2021); [Schaffitzel et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schaffitzel--2020)).

The emissions reduction that could be achieved from fossil fuel subsidy removal depends on the specific context such as magnitude and nature of subsidies, energy prices and demand elasticities, and how the fiscal savings from reduced subsidies are used. Modelling studies of global fossil fuel subsidy removal result in projected emission reductions of between 1% and 10% by 2030 ([Delpiazzo et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Delpiazzo--2015); [IEA 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IEA--2015); [Jewell et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jewell--2018); [IISD 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IISD--2019)) and between 6.4% and 8.2% by 2050 ([Schwanitz et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schwanitz--2014); [Burniaux and Chateau 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burniaux--2014)).

An extensive literature documents the difficulties of phasing out fossil fuel subsidies ([Schmidt et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schmidt--2017); [Gass and Echeverria 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gass--2017); [Skovgaard and van Asselt 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skovgaard--2018); [Kyle 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kyle--2018); [Perry 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Perry--2020); [Gençsü et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gen%C3%A7s%C3%BC--2020)). Fossil fuel industries lobby to maintain producer subsidies and consumers protest if they are adversely affected by subsidy reductions ([Fouquet 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fouquet--2016); [Coxhead and Grainger 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Coxhead--2018))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fouquet--2016); [Coxhead and Grainger 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Coxhead--2018)). Yemen (2005 and 2014), Cameroon (2008), Bolivia (2010), Nigeria (2012), Ecuador (2019) all abandoned subsidy reform attempts following public protests ([Rentschler and Bazilian 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rentschler--2017); [Mahdavi et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mahdavi--2020)). Indonesia is an example where fossil fuel subsidy removal was successful, helped by social assistance programmes and a communication effort about the benefits of reform ([Chelminski 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chelminski--2018); [Burke and Kurniawati 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burke--2018))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chelminski--2018); [Burke and Kurniawati 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burke--2018)). To-date instances of fossil fuel subsidy reform or removal have been driven largely by national fiscal and economic considerations ([Skovgaard and van Asselt 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skovgaard--2019)).

##  13.6.4Regulatory Instruments ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Regulatory instruments are applied by governments to cause the adoption of desired processes, technologies, products (including energy products) or outcomes (including emission levels). Failure to comply incurs financial penalties and/or legal sanctions. Regulatory instruments range from performance standards, which prescribe compliance outcomes – and in some cases allow flexibility to achieve compliance, including the trading of credits – to more prescriptive technology-specific standards, also known as command-and-control regulation. Regulatory instruments play an important role to achieve specific mitigation outcomes in sectoral applications (robust evidence,  high agreement ). Mitigation by regulation often enjoys greater political support but tends to be more economically costly than mitigation by pricing instruments (robust evidence, medium agreement ).

###  13.6.4.1Performance Standards , Including Tradable Credits ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Performance standards grant regulated entities freedom to choose the technologies and methods to reach a general objective, such as a minimum market share of zero-emission vehicles or of renewable electricity, or a maximum emissions intensity of electricity generated. Tradable performance standards allow regulated entities to trade compliance achievement credits; under-performers can buy surplus credits from over-performers thereby reducing the aggregate cost of compliance ([Fischer 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fischer--2008)).

Tradable performance standards have been applied to numerous sectors including electricity generation, personal vehicles, building energy efficiency, appliances, and large industry. An important application is Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) for electricity supply, which require that a minimum percentage of electricity is generated from specified renewable sources sometimes including nuclear and fossil fuels with CCS when referred to as a clean electricity standard ([Young and Bistline 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Young--2018)) (Chapter 6). This creates a price incentive to invest in renewable generation capacity. Such incentives can equivalently be created through feed-in tariffs, a form of subsidy ([Section 13.6.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6.3)) and some jurisdictions have had both instruments ([Matsumoto et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Matsumoto--2017))

.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6.3)) and some jurisdictions have had both instruments ([Matsumoto et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Matsumoto--2017)). RPS can differ in features and stringency, and are in operation in many countries and sub-national jurisdictions, including a majority of US states ([Carley et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carley--2018)).

Vehicle emissions standards are a common form of performance standard with flexibility (Chapter 9). a corporate fuel efficiency standard specifies an average energy use and/or GHG emissions per kilometre travelled for vehicles sold by a manufacturer. Another version of this policy, the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) standard, requires vehicle sellers to achieve minimum requirements for sales of zero-emission vehicles ([Bhardwaj et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bhardwaj--2020)). Both instruments allow manufacturers to use tradable credits to achieve compliance.

Low-carbon fuel standards (LCFS), which set an average life-cycle carbon intensity for energy that declines over time, are another example. LCFS are in place in many different jurisdictions (Chapter 9) and have been applied to petroleum products, natural gas, hydrogen and electricity ([Yeh et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Yeh--2016)). An LCFS allows regulated entities to trade credits creating the potential for high carbon intensity fuel suppliers to cross-subsidise low-carbon intensity transport energy providers including low-carbon biofuels, hydrogen and electricity ([Axsen et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Axsen--2020)).

Trading and other flexibility mechanisms improve the economic efficiency of standards by harmonising the marginal abatement costs among companies or installations subject to the standard. Nevertheless tradable performance standards are less economically efficient in achieving emissions reductions than carbon pricing, sometimes by a significant amount ([Giraudet and Quirion 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Giraudet--2008); [Chen et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Chen--2014); [Holland et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Holland--2015); [Fox et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fox--2017); [Zhang et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhang--2018)).
###  13.6.4.2Technology Standards ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Technology standards take a more prescriptive approach by requiring a specific technology, process or product. They typically take one of three forms: requirements for specific pollution abatement technologies; requirements for specific production methods; or requirements for specific goods such as energy efficient appliances. They can also take the form of phase-out mandates, as applied for example to planned bans of internal combustion engines for road transport ([Bhagavathy and McCulloch 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bhagavathy--2020)), coal use; for example, Germany’s decisions to phase out coal ([Oei et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Oei--2020)), and some industry processes and products, for example, hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and use of sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) in some products (see Box 13.10 on non-CO2 gases)
.10 on non-CO2 gases). Technology standards are also referred to as command-and-control standards, prescriptive standards, or design standards.

Technology standards are a common climate policy particularly at the sector level (Chapters 6–11). Technology standards tend to score lower in terms of economic efficiency than carbon pricing and performance standards ([Besanko 1987](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Besanko--1987)). But they may be the best instrument for situations where decisions are not very responsive to price signals such as consumer choices related to energy efficiency and recycling and decisions relating to urban land use and infrastructure choices.

By mandating specific compliance pathways, technology standards risk locking-in a high-cost pathway when lower cost options are available or may emerge through market incentives and innovation ([Raff and Walter 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Raff--2020)). Furthermore, standards may require high-cost GHG reductions in one sector while missing low-cost options in another sector. Technology standards can also stifle innovation by blocking alternative technologies from entering the market ([Sachs 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sachs--2012)). Benefits of technology standards include their potential to achieve emission reductions in a relatively short time frame and that their effectiveness can be estimated with some confidence ([Montgomery et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Montgomery--2019)).
###  13.6.4.3Performance of Regulatory Instruments ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

###  13.6.4.3Performance of Regulatory Instruments ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Regulatory policy instruments tend to be more economically costly than pricing instruments, as explained above. However, regulatory policies may be preferred for other reasons.

In some cases, regulatory policy can elicit greater political support than pricing policy ([Tobler et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tobler--2012); [Lam 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lam--2015); [Drews and van den Bergh 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Drews--2016)). For example, USA citizens have expressed more support for flexible regulation like the RPS than for carbon taxes ([Rabe 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rabe--2018)). And a survey in British Columbia a few years after the simultaneous implementation of a carbon tax and two regulations – the LCFS and a clean electricity standard – found much less strong opposition to the regulations, even after being informed that they were costlier to consumers ([Rhodes et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rhodes--2017))

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rhodes--2017)). The degree of public support for regulations depends, however, on the type of regulation, as outright technology prohibitions can be unpopular ([Attari et al. 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Attari--2009); [Cherry et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cherry--2012)).

In comparison to economic instruments, regulatory policies tend to cause greater cost of living increases in percentage terms for lower income consumers – called policy regressivity ([Levinson 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Levinson--2019); [Davis and Knittel 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Davis--2019)). And unlike carbon taxes, regulations do not generate revenues that can be used to compensate lower income groups.

A renewable energy procurement obligation in South Africa successfully required local hiring with perceived positive results ([Walwyn and Brent 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Walwyn--2015); [Pahle et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pahle--2016)), a clean energy regulation in Korea was perceived to provide greater employment opportunities ([Lee 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lee--2017)), and a UK obligation on energy companies to provide energy retrofits to low-income households improved energy affordability according to participants ([Elsharkawy and Rutherford 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Elsharkawy--2018)).

From an energy system transformation perspective, technology standards, including phase-out mandates, have particular promise to achieve profound change in specific sectors and technologies ([Tvinnereim and Mehling 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tvinnereim--2018)). As such policies change the technologies available in the market, then economic instruments can also have a greater effect ([Pahle et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pahle--2018)).
##  Box 13.10 | Policies to Limit Emissions of Non-CO2Gases![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Non-CO2 gases weighted by their 100-year GWPs represent approximately 25% of global GHG emissions, of which methane (CH4) accounts for 18%, nitrous oxide (N2O) 4%, and fluorinated gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3) 2% (Minx et al. 2021). Only a small share of these emissions are subject to mitigation policies.

Methane (CH4). Anthropogenic sources include agriculture, mainly livestock and rice paddies, fossil fuel extraction and processing, fuel combustion, some industrial processes, landfills, and wastewater treatment ([EPA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EPA--2019)). Atmospheric measurements indicate that methane emissions from fossil fuel production are larger than shown in emissions inventories ([Schwietzke et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schwietzke--2016)). Only a small fraction of global CH4 emissions is regulated. Mitigation policies focus on landfills, coal mines, and oil and gas operations.

Regulations and incentives to capture and utilise methane from coal seams came into effect in China in 2010 ([Tan 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tan--2018); [Tao et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tao--2019)). Inventory data suggest that emissions peaked and began a slow decline after 2010 ([Gao et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gao--2020)) though satellite data indicate that China’s methane emissions, largely attributable to coal mining, continued to rise in line with pre-2010 trends ([Miller et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Miller--2019)). Methane emissions from sources including agriculture, waste and industry are included in some offset credit schemes, including the CDM and at national level in Australia’s Emissions Reductions Fund ([Australian Climate Change Authority 2017](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Australian%20Climate%20Change%20Authority--2017)) and the Chinese Certified Emission Reduction (CCER) scheme ([Lo and Cong 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lo--2017)).

Nitrous oxide (N2O). N2O emissions are produced by agricultural soil management, livestock waste management, fossil fuel combustion, and adipic acid and nitric acid production ([EPA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EPA--2019)). Most N2O emissions are not regulated and global emissions have been increasing. N2O emissions by adipic and nitric acid plants in the EU are covered by the ETS ([Winiwarter et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Winiwarter--2018)). N2O emissions are included in some offset schemes. China, the United States, Singapore, Egypt, and Russia produce 86% of industrial N2O emissions offering the potential for targeted mitigation action ([EPA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EPA--2019)).

Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). Most HFCs are used as substitutes for ozone depleting substances. The Kigali Amendment (KA) to the Montreal Protocol will reduce HFC use by 85% by 2047 ([UN Environment 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UN%20Environment--2018)). To help meet their KA commitments developed country parties have been implementing regulations to limit imports, production and exports of HFCs and to limit specific uses of HFCs.

The EU, for example, issues tradable quota for imports, production and exports of HFCs. Prices of HFCs have increased as expected ([Kleinschmidt 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kleinschmidt--2020)) which has led to smuggling of HFCs into the EU (European Commission 2019b). HFC use has been slightly (1–6%) below the limit each year from 2015 through 2018 ([EEA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EEA--2019)). China and India released national cooling action plans in 2019, laying out detailed, cross-sectoral plans to provide sustainable, climate friendly, safe and affordable cooling ([Dean et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dean--2020)).

Perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3). With the exception of SF6, these gases are emitted by industrial activities located in the European Economic Area (EEA) and a limited number (fewer than 30) of other countries. Regulations in Europe, Japan and the USA focus on leak reduction as well as collection and reuse of SF6 from electrical equipment. Other uses of SF6 are banned in Europe ([European Union 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#European%20Union--2014)).
PFCs are generated during the aluminium smelting process if the alumina level in the electrolytic bath falls below critical levels ([EPA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EPA--2019)). In Europe these emissions are covered by the EU ETS. The industry is eliminating the emissions through improved process control and a shift to different production processes.

The semiconductor industry uses HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3 for etching and deposition chamber cleaning ([EPA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EPA--2019)) and has a voluntary target of reducing GHG emissions 30% from 2010 by 2020 ([World Semiconductor Council 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#World%20Semiconductor%20Council--2017)). Europe regulates production, import, export, destruction and feedstock use of PFCs and SF6, but not NF3 ([EEA 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EEA--2019)). In addition, fluorinated gases are taxed in Denmark, Norway, Slovenia and Spain.
In some jurisdictions, the analysis of regulatory instruments is subject to an assessment on the basis of a shadow cost of carbon, which can influence the choice and design of regulations that affect GHG emissions (Box 13.11).
##  Box 13.11 | Shadow Cost of Carbon in Regulatory Analysis![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

##  Box 13.11 | Shadow Cost of Carbon in Regulatory Analysis![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
In some jurisdictions, public administrations are required to apply a shadow cost of carbon to regulatory analysis.

Traditionally, for example in widespread application in the United States, the shadow cost of carbon is calibrated to an estimate of the social cost of carbon as an approximation of expected future cumulative economic damage from a unit of greenhouse gas emissions ([Metcalf and Stock 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Metcalf--2017)). Social cost of carbon is usually estimated using integrated assessment models and is subject to fundamental uncertainties ([Pezzey 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pezzey--2019)). An alternative approach, used for example in regulatory analysis in the United Kingdom since 2009, is to define a carbon price that is thought to be consistent with a particular targeted emissions outcome. This approach also requires a number of assumptions, including about future marginal costs of mitigation ([Aldy et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aldy--2021)).

##  13.6.5Other Policy Instruments ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
A range of other mitigation policy instruments are in use, often playing a complementary role to pricing and standards.
###  13.6.5.1Transition Support Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Effective climate change mitigation can cause economic and social disruption where there is transformative change, such as changes in energy systems away from fossil fuels ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)). Transitional assistance policies can be aimed to ameliorate effects on consumers, workers, communities, corporations or countries ([Green and Gambhir 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Green--2020)) in order to create broad coalitions of supporters or to limit opposition ([Vogt-Schilb and Hallegatte 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Vogt-Schilb--2017)).

###  13.6.5.2Information Programmes ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Information programmes, including energy efficiency labels, energy audits, certification, carbon labelling and information disclosure, are in wide use in particular for energy consumption. They can reduce GHG emissions by promoting voluntary technology choices and behavioural changes by firms and households.
Energy efficiency labelling is in widespread use, including for buildings, and for end users products including cars and appliances. Carbon labelling is used for example for food ([Camilleri et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Camilleri--2019)) and tourism ([Gössling and Buckley 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#G%C3%B6ssling--2016)). Information measures also include specific information systems such as smart electricity meters (Zangheri et al. 2019). Chapters 5 and 9 provide detail.

Information programmes can correct for a range of market failures related to imperfect information and consumer perceptions ([Allcott 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Allcott--2016)). Alongside mandatory standards (13.6.4), information programmes can nudge firms and consumers to focus on often overlooked operating cost reductions ([Carroll et al. 2022](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carroll--2022)). For example, consumers who are shown energy efficiency labels on average buy more energy efficient appliances than those who are not ([Stadelmann and Schubert 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stadelmann--2018)). Information policies can also support the changing of social norms about consumption choices, which have been shown to raise public support for pricing and regulatory policy instruments ([Gössling et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#G%C3%B6ssling--2020)).

Energy audits provide tailored information about potential energy savings and benchmarking of best practices through a network of peers. Typical examples include the United States Better Buildings Challenge that has provided energy audits to support USA commercial and industrial building owners, energy savings have been estimated at 18% to 30% ([Asensio and Delmas 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Asensio--2017)); and Germany’s energy audit scheme for SMEs achieving reductions in energy consumption of 5–70% ([Kluczek and Olszewski 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kluczek--2017)).

Consumption-oriented policy instruments seek to reduce GHG emissions by changing consumer behaviour directly, via retailers or via the supply chain. Aspects that hold promise are technology lists, supply chain procurement by leading retailers or business associations, a carbon-intensive materials charge and selected infrastructure improvements ([Grubb et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grubb--2020)).

The information provided to consumers in labelling programmes is often not detailed enough to yield best possible results ([Davis and Metcalf 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Davis--2016)). Providing information about running costs tends to be more effective than providing data on energy use ([Damigos et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Damigos--2020)). Sound implementation of labelling programmes requires appropriate calculation methodology and tools, training and public awareness ([Liang Wong and Krüger 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Liang%20Wong--2017)). In systems where manufacturers self-report performance of their products, there tends to be misreporting and skewed energy efficiency labelling ([Goeschl 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Goeschl--2019)).

A new form of information programmes are financial accounting standards as frameworks to encourage or require companies to disclose how the transition risks from shifting to a low-carbon economy and physical climate change impacts may affect their business or asset values (Chapter 15). The most prominent such standard was issued in 2017 by the Financial Stability Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. It has found rapid uptake among regulators and investors ([O’Dwyer and Unerman 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#O%E2%80%99Dwyer--2020)).

Traditionally, corporate reporting has treated climate risks in a highly varied and often minimal way ([Foerster et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Foerster--2017)). Disclosure of climate-related risks creates incentives for companies to improve their carbon and climate change exposure, and ultimately regulatory standards for climate risk ([Eccles and Krzus 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Eccles--2018)). Disclosure can also reinforce calls for divestment in fossil fuel assets predominantly promoted by civil society organisations ([Ayling and Gunningham 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ayling--2017)), raising moral principles and arguments about the financial risks inherent in fossil fuel investments ([Green 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Green--2018); [Blondeel et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Blondeel--2019)).

###  13.6.5.3Public Procurement and Investment ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
National, sub-national and local governments determine many aspects of infrastructure planning, fund investment in areas such as energy, transport and the built environment, and purchase goods and services, including for government administration and military provisioning.

Public procurement rules usually mandate cost effectiveness but only in some cases allow or mandate climate change consideration in public purchasing, for example in EU public purchasing guidelines ([Martinez Romera and Caranta 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Martinez%20Romera--2017)). Green procurement for buildings has been undertaken in Malaysia ([Bohari et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bohari--2017)). a paper cites Taiwan (province of China) green public procurement law, which has contributed to reduced emissions intensity ([Tsai 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Tsai--2017)). In practice, awareness and knowledge of ‘green’ public procurement techniques and procedures is decisive for climate-friendly procurement ([Testa et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Testa--2016))

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Testa--2016)). Experiences in low-carbon infrastructure procurement point to procedures being tailored to concerns about competition, transaction costs and innovation ([Kadefors et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kadefors--2020)).

Infrastructure investment decisions lock-in high or low emissions trajectories over long periods. Low-emissions infrastructure can enable or increase productivity of private low-carbon investments ([Jaumotte et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jaumotte--2021)) and is typically only a little more expensive over its lifetime, but faces additional barriers including higher upfront costs, lack of pricing of externalities, or lack of information or aversion to novel products ([Granoff et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Granoff--2016)). In low-income developing countries, where infrastructure has historically lagged developed countries, some of these hurdles can be exacerbated by overall more difficult conditions for public investment ([Gurara et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gurara--2018)).

Governments can also promote low-emissions investments through public-private partnerships and government owned ‘green banks’ that provide loans on commercial or concessional basis for environmentally friendly private sector investments ([David and Venkatachalam 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#David--2019); [Ziolo et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ziolo--2019)). Public funding or financial guarantees such as contracts-for-difference can alleviate financial risk in the early stages of technology deployment, creating pathways to commercial viability ([Bataille 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bataille--2020)).

Government provision can also play an important role in economic stimulus programs, including as implemented in response to the pandemic of 2020–2021. Such programmes can support low-emissions infrastructure and equipment, and industrial or business development ([Elkerbout et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Elkerbout--2020); [Hainsch et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hainsch--2020); [Barbier 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Barbier--2020); [Hepburn et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hepburn--2020)).
###  13.6.5.4Voluntary Agreements ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

###  13.6.5.4Voluntary Agreements ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Voluntary Agreements result from negotiations between governments and industrial sectors that commit to achieve agreed goals ([Mundaca and Markandya 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mundaca--2016)). When used as part of a broader policy framework, they can enhance the cost effectiveness of individual firms in attaining emission reductions while pricing or regulations drive participation in the agreement ([Dawson and Segerson 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dawson--2008)).

Public voluntary programmes, where a government regulator develops programs to which industries and firms may choose to participate on a voluntary basis, have been implemented in numerous countries. For example, the United States Environmental Protection Agency introduced numerous voluntary programmes with industry to offer technical support in promoting energy efficiency and emissions reductions, among other initiatives ([EPA 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#EPA--2017)). a European example is the EU Ecolabel Award programme (European Commission 2020b). Agreements for industrial energy efficiency in Europe ([Cornelis 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cornelis--2019)) and Japan ([Wakabayashi and Arimura 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wakabayashi--2016)) have been particularly effective in addressing information barriers and for smaller companies

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wakabayashi--2016)) have been particularly effective in addressing information barriers and for smaller companies. The International Civil Aviation Organization’s CORSIA scheme ([Prussi et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Prussi--2021)) is an example of an international industry-based public voluntary programme.

Voluntary agreements are often implemented in conjunction with economic or regulatory instruments, and sometimes are used to gain insights ahead of implementation of regulatory standards, as in the case of energy efficiency PVPs in South Korea ([Seok et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Seok--2021)). In some cases, industries use voluntary agreements as partial fulfilment of a regulation ([Rezessy and Bertoldi 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rezessy--2011); [Langpap 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Langpap--2015)). For example, the Netherlands have permitted participating industries to be exempt from certain energy taxes and emissions regulations ([Veum 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Veum--2018)).
##  Box 13.12 | Technology and Research and Development Policy![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

##  Box 13.12 | Technology and Research and Development Policy![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Private businesses tend to under-invest in research and development because of market failures ([Geroski 1995](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Geroski--1995)), hence there is a case for governments to support research and technology development. a range of different policy instruments are used, including government funding, preferential tax treatment, intellectual property rules, and policies to support the deployment and diffusion of new technologies. [Chapter 16](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-16) treats innovation policy in-depth.
##  Box 13.13 | Possible Sources of Leakage![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Competitiveness: Mitigation policy raises the costs and product prices of regulated sources which causes production to shift to unregulated sources, increasing their emissions.

Competitiveness: Mitigation policy raises the costs and product prices of regulated sources which causes production to shift to unregulated sources, increasing their emissions.
Fossil fuel channel: Regulated sources reduce their fossil fuel use, which lowers fossil fuel prices and increases consumption and associated emissions by unregulated sources.
Land-use channel: Mitigation policies that change land use lead to land use and emissions changes in other jurisdictions ([Bastos Lima et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bastos%20Lima--2019)).
Terms of trade effect: Price increases for the products of regulated sources shift consumption to other goods, which raises emissions due to the higher output of those goods.

Terms of trade effect: Price increases for the products of regulated sources shift consumption to other goods, which raises emissions due to the higher output of those goods.
Technology channel: Mitigation policy induces low-carbon innovation, which reduces emissions by sources that adopt the innovations that may include unregulated sources ([Gerlagh and Kuik 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gerlagh--2007)).
Abatement resource effect: Regulated sources increase use of clean inputs, which reduces inputs available to unregulated sources and so limits their output and emissions ([Baylis et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Baylis--2014)).
Scale channel: Changes to the output of regulated and unregulated sources affect their emissions intensities so emissions changes are not proportional to output changes ([Antweiler et al. 2001](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Antweiler--2001)).

Intertemporal channel: Capital stocks of all sources are fixed initially but change over time affecting the costs, prices, output and emissions of regulated and unregulated products.

##  13.6.6International Interactions of National Mitigation Policies ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
One country’s mitigation policy can impact other countries in various ways including changes in their GHG emissions (leakage), creation of markets for emission reduction credits, technology development and diffusion (spillovers), and reduction in the value of their fossil fuel resources.
###  13.6.6.1Leakage Effects ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

###  13.6.6.1Leakage Effects ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Compliance with a mitigation policy can affect the emissions of foreign sources via several channels over different time scales ([Zhang and Zhang 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhang--2017)) (Box 13.13 ). The effects may interact and yield a net increase or decrease in emissions. The leakage channel that is of most concern to policymakers is adverse international competitiveness impacts from domestic climate policies.
In principle, implementation of a mitigation policy in one country creates an incentive to shift production of tradable goods whose costs are increased by the policy to other countries with less costly emissions limitation policies ([Section 12.6.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-12#12.6.3)). Such ‘leakage’ could to some extent negate emissions reductions in the first country, depending on the relative emissions intensity of production in both countries.

Ex ante modelling studies typically estimate significant leakage for unilateral policies to reduce emissions due to production of emissions intensive products such as steel, aluminium, and cement ([Carbone and Rivers 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carbone--2017)). However, the results are highly dependent on assumptions and typically do not reflect policy designs specifically aimed at minimising or preventing leakage ([Fowlie and Reguant 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fowlie--2018)).

Numerous ex post  analyses, mainly for the EU ETS, find no evidence of any or significant adverse competitiveness impacts and conclude that there was consequently no or insignificant leakage (medium evidence, medium agreement ) ([Branger et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Branger--2016); [Haites et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Haites--2018); [Koch and Basse Mama 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Koch--2019); [FSR Climate 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#FSR%20Climate--2019); [aus dem Moore et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#aus%20dem%20Moore--2019); [Venmans et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Venmans--2020); [Kuusi et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kuusi--2020); [Verde 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Verde--2020); [Borghesi et al

. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kuusi--2020); [Verde 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Verde--2020); [Borghesi et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Borghesi--2020)). This is attributed to large allocations of free allowances to emissions-intensive, trade-exposed sources, relatively low allowance prices, the ability of firms in some sectors to pass costs on to consumers, energy’s relatively low share of production costs, and small but statistically significant effects on innovation ([Joltreau and Sommerfeld 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Joltreau--2019)). Few carbon taxes apply to emissions-intensive, trade-exposed sources ([Timilsina 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Timilsina--2018)), so competitiveness impacts usually are not a particular concern.

Policies intended to address leakage include a border carbon adjustment ([Ward et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ward--2019); [Ismer et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ismer--2020)). a border carbon adjustment (BCA) imposes costs – a tax or allowance purchase obligation – on imports of carbon-intensive goods equivalent to those borne by domestic products possibly mirrored by rebates for exports ([Böhringer et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%B6hringer--2012); [Fischer and Fox 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fischer--2012); [Zhang 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhang--2012); [Böhringer et al. 2017c](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%B6hringer--2017c)) (Chapter 14). A BCA faces the practical challenge of determining the carbon content of imports ([Böhringer et al. 2017a](https://www.ipcc

.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%B6hringer--2017c)) (Chapter 14). A BCA faces the practical challenge of determining the carbon content of imports ([Böhringer et al. 2017a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%B6hringer--2017a)) and the design needs to be consistent with WTO rules and other international agreements ([Cosbey et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cosbey--2019); [Mehling et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mehling--2019)). Model estimates indicate that a BCA reduces but does not eliminate leakage ([Branger and Quirion 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Branger--2014)). No BCA has yet been implemented for international trade although such a measure is currently under consideration by some governments.

###  13.6.6.2Market for Emission Reduction Credits ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
A mitigation policy may allow the use of credits issued for emission reductions in other countries for compliance purposes (see also [Section 13.6.3.4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6.3.4) on offset credits and [Chapter 14](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-14) on international credit mechanisms). Creation of international markets for emission reduction credits tends to benefit other countries through financial flows in return for emissions credit sales (medium evidence, high agreement ).

The EU, New Zealand and Switzerland allowed participants in their emissions trading systems to use credits issued under the Kyoto Protocol mechanisms, including the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), for compliance. From 2008 through 2014, participants used 3.76 million imported credits for compliance of which 80% were CDM credits ([Haites 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Haites--2016)). [3](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/ch13.html#footnote-002) Use of imported credits has fallen to very low levels since 2014 ([World Bank 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#World%20Bank--2014); [Shishlov et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shishlov--2016)). [4](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/ch13.html#footnote-001)

The Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) is the world’s largest offset programme (Chapter 14). From 2001 to 2019 over 7500 projects with projected emission reductions in excess of 8000 MtCO2-eq were implemented in 114 developing countries using some 140 different emissions reduction methodologies ([UNFCCC 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC--2012); [UNEP DTU Partnership 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNEP%20DTU%20Partnership--2020)). Credits reflecting over 2000 MtCO2-eq of emission reductions by 3260 projects have been issued. To address additionality and other concerns the CDM Executive Board frequently updated its approved project methodologies.
###  13.6.6.3Technology Spillovers ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

###  13.6.6.3Technology Spillovers ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Mitigation policies stimulate low-carbon R&D by entities subject to those policies and by other domestic and foreign entities ([FSR Climate 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#FSR%20Climate--2019)). Policies to support technology development and diffusion tend to have positive spillover effects between countries (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Section 16.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-16#16.3)).

Innovation activity in response to a mitigation policy varies by policy type ([Jaffe et al. 2002](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jaffe--2002)) and stringency ([Johnstone et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Johnstone--2012)). In addition, many governments have policies to stimulate R&D, further increasing low-carbon R&D activity by domestic researchers. Emitters in other countries may adopt some of the new low-carbon technologies thus reducing emissions elsewhere. Technology development and diffusion is reviewed in Chapter 16.
###  13.6.6.4Value of Fossil Fuel Resources ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Fossil fuel resources are a significant source of exports, employment and government revenues for many countries. The value of these resources depends on demand for the fuel and competing supplies in the relevant international markets. Discoveries and new production technologies reduce the value of established resources. Mitigation policies that reduce the use of fossil fuels also reduce the value of these resources. A single policy in one country is unlikely to have a noticeable effect on the international price, but similar policies in multiple countries could adversely affect the value of the resources. For fossil fuel exporting countries, mitigation policies consistent with the Paris Agreement goals could result in greater costs from changes in fossil fuel prices due to lower international demand than domestic policy costs (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Liu et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Liu--2020)).

The impact on the value of established resources will be mitigated, to some extent, by the reduced incentive to explore for and develop new fossil fuel supplies. Nevertheless, efforts to lower global emissions will mean substantially less demand for fossil fuels, with the majority of current coal reserves and large shares of known gas and oil reserves needing to remain unused, with great diversity in impacts between different countries ([McGlade and Ekins 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McGlade--2015)) (Chapters 3, 6, 15).

Estimates of the potential future loss in value differ greatly. There is uncertainty about remaining future fossil fuel use under different mitigation scenarios, as well as future fossil fuel prices depending on extraction costs, market structures and policies. Estimates of total cumulative fossil fuel revenue lost range between 5–67 trillion USD ([Bauer et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bauer--2015)) with an estimate of the net present value of lost profit of around 10 trillion USD ([Bauer et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bauer--2016)). Policies that constrain supply of fossil fuels in the context of mitigation objectives could limit financial losses to fossil fuel producers (Chapter 14).
#  13.7Integrated Policy Packages for Mitigation and Multiple Objectives ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section

Since AR5, the literature on climate policies and policymaking has expanded in two significant directions. First, there is growing recognition that mitigation policy occurs in the context of multiple climate and development objectives (Chapter 4). Different aspects of these linkages are discussed across the AR6 WGIII report, including concepts and framings ([Section 1.6.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-1#1.6.2)), shifting sustainable development pathways ([Section 4.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-4#4.3) and Cross-Chapter Box 5 in Chapter 4), cross-sectoral interactions (Sections 12.6.1 and 12.6.2), evidence of co-impacts ([Section 17.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-17#17.3)), links with adaptation ([Section 4.4.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-4#4.4.2)) and accelerating the transition (Sections 13.9, 17.1.1, 17.4.5 and 17.4.6)

.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-17#17.3)), links with adaptation ([Section 4.4.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-4#4.4.2)) and accelerating the transition (Sections 13.9, 17.1.1, 17.4.5 and 17.4.6). While the concept of development pathways is salient in all countries, it may particularly resonate with policymakers in developing countries focused on providing basic needs and addressing poverty and inequality, including energy poverty ([Ahmad 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ahmad--2009); [Fuso Nerini et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fuso%20Nerini--2019); [Bel and Teixidó 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bel--2020); [Caetano et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Caetano--2020); [Röser et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#R%C3%B6ser--2020))

. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Caetano--2020); [Röser et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#R%C3%B6ser--2020)). Consequently, some countries may frame policies predominantly in terms of accelerating mitigation, while in others a multiple objectives approach linked to development pathways may dominate, depending on their specific socio-economic contexts and priorities, governance capacities ([McMeekin et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McMeekin--2019)) and perceptions of historical responsibility ([Winkler and Rajamani 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Winkler--2014); [Friman and Hjerpe 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Friman--2015); [Winkler et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Winkler--2015); [Pan et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pan--2017)).

Second, since AR5 there is growing attention to enabling transitions over time. Literature on socio-technical transitions, rooted in innovation studies, highlights the need for different policy focus at different stages of a transition ([Geels et al. 2017b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Geels--2017b),a; [Köhler et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#K%C3%B6hler--2019)) ([Section 1.7.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-1#1.7.3)). Other literature examines how broad patterns of development drive both social and mitigation outcomes through shifts in policies and a re-alignment of enabling conditions (Chapter 4). Explicit efforts to shift development pathways, for example by shifting patterns of energy demand and urbanisation, therefore offer broader mitigation opportunities (Cross-Chapter Box 5 in Chapter 4)
. Common to both approaches is an emphasis beyond the short term, and attention to enabling longer-term structural shifts in economies and societies.

Taking these trends into account, Figure 13.6 outlines the climate policy landscape, and how it maps to different parts of this Working Group III report. One axis of variation captures alternative framings of desired outcomes in national policymaking – mitigation versus multiple objectives, while the second captures the shift in policymaking from an initial focus on shifting incentives through largely individual policy instruments, to explicit consideration of how policies and economy-wide measures, including those that shift incentives, can combine to enable transitions. As a result, Figure 13.6 represents interconnected policy ideas, but backed by distinct strands of literature. Notably, each of these categories is salient to climate policymaking, although the balance may differ depending on country context.

This section particularly focuses on climate policymaking for transition – both socio-technical transitions and shifts in development pathways, while direct climate policies and co-benefits are addressed in other parts of the report, as indicated in Figure 13.6. This section focuses in particular on lessons for designing policy packages for transitions, and is complemented by discussion in [Section 13.8](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.8) on integration between adaptation and mitigation, and [Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9) on economy-wide measures and the broader enabling conditions necessary to accelerate mitigation.
##  13.7.1Policy Packages for Low-carbon Sustainable Transitions ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Since AR5 an emergent multidisciplinary literature on policy packages, or policy mixes, has emerged that examine how policies may be combined for sustainable low-carbon transitions ([Rogge and Reichardt 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2016); [Kern et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kern--2019)). This literature covers various sectors including: energy ([Rogge et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2017)); transport ([Givoni et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Givoni--2013)); industry ([Scordato et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scordato--2018)); agri-food ([Kalfagianni and Kuik 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kalfagianni--2017)); and forestry ([Scullion et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scullion--2016)).

A central theme in the literature is that transitions require policy interventions to address system level changes, thereby going beyond addressing market failures in two ways. First, structural system changes are needed for low-carbon transitions, including building low-carbon infrastructure (or example aligning electricity grids and storage with the requirements of new low-carbon technology), and adjusting existing institutions to low-carbon solutions (for example by reforming electricity market design) ([Bak et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bak--2017); [Patt and Lilliestam 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Patt--2018))

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bak--2017); [Patt and Lilliestam 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Patt--2018)). Second, explicit transformational system changes are necessary, including efforts at directing transformations, such as clear direction setting through the elaboration of shared visions, and coordination across diverse actors across different policy fields, such as climate and industrial policy, and across governance levels ([Uyarra et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Uyarra--2016); [Nemet et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nemet--2017)).

There are some specific suggestions for policy packages: Van den Bergh et al. (2021) suggest that innovation support and information provision combined with a carbon tax or market, or adoption subsidy leads to both effective and efficient outcomes. Others question the viability of universally applicable policy packages, and suggest packages need to be tailored to local objectives ([del Río 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#del%20R%C3%ADo--2014)) Consequently, much of the literature focuses on broad principles for design of policy packages and mixes, as discussed below.

Comprehensiveness, balance and consistency are important criteria for policy packages or mixes (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Rogge and Reichardt 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2016); [Scobie 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scobie--2016); [Carter et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Carter--2018); [Santos-lacueva and González 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Santos-lacueva--2018)). Comprehensiveness assesses the extensiveness of policy packages, including the breadth of system and market failures it addresses ([Rogge and Reichardt 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2016))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2016)). For example, instrument mixes that include only moderate carbon pricing, but are complemented by policies supporting new low-carbon technologies and a moratorium on coal-fired power plants may not only be politically more feasible than stringent carbon pricing alone, but may also limit efficiency losses and lower distributional impacts ([Bertram et al. 2015b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bertram--2015b)). Balance captures whether policy instruments are deployed in complementary ways given their different purposes, combining for example technology-push approaches such as public R&D with demand-pull approaches such as an energy tax. A combination of technology-push and demand-pull approaches has been shown to support innovation in energy efficient technologies in OECD countries ([Costantini et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Costantini--2017))

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Costantini--2017)). Consistency addresses the alignment of policy instruments among each other and with the policy strategy, which may have multiple and not always consistent objectives ([Rogge 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2019)). Consistency of policy mixes has been identified as an important driver of low-carbon transformation, particularly for renewable energy ([Lieu et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lieu--2018); [Rogge and Schleich 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rogge--2018)). Box 13.14 summarises the economics literature on how policies interact, to inform design of packages.
##  Box 13.14 | Policy Interactions of Carbon Pricing and Ot her Instruments![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The economics literature provides insights on policy interactions among the multiple overlapping policies that directly or indirectly affect GHG emissions, including when different levels of government are involved. Multiple mitigation policies can be theoretically justified if there are multiple objectives or market failures or to achieve distributional objectives and increase policy effectiveness ([Stiglitz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stiglitz--2019)). Examples include the coexistence of the EU ETS with vehicle emission standards and energy efficiency standards ([Rey et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rey--2013)), and the fact that 85% of the emissions covered by California’s ETS are also subject to other policies ([Bang et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bang--2017); [Mazmanian et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mazmanian--2020))

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bang--2017); [Mazmanian et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mazmanian--2020)). Policy interactions are also widespread among energy efficiency policies ([Wiese et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wiese--2018)).

Interactive effects can influence the costs of policy outcomes. With multiple overlapping and possibly non-optimal policies, the effect on total cost is not clear. A modelling study of USA mitigation policy finds the costs of using heterogeneous sub-national policies to achieve decarbonisation targets is 10% higher than national uniform policies ([Peng et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Peng--2021)). When multiple policy goals are sought, such as mitigation and R&D, a portfolio of optimal policies achieves the goals at significantly lower cost ([Fischer and Newell 2008](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fischer--2008)). In some cases, overlapping mitigation policies can raise the cost of mitigation ([Böhringer et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fischer--2008)). In some cases, overlapping mitigation policies can raise the cost of mitigation ([Böhringer et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%B6hringer--2016)) while lowering the cost of achieving other goals, such as energy efficiency improvements and expansion of renewable energy ([Rosenow et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rosenow--2016); [Lecuyer and Quirion 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lecuyer--2019)). It is possible that one or more of the policies is made redundant ([Aune and Golombek 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Aune--2021)).

While overlapping policies may raise the cost of mitigation, they increase the likelihood of achieving an emission reduction goal. Policy overlap will lead to different optimal carbon prices across jurisdictions ([Bataille et al. 2018b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bataille--2018b)). The existence of overlapping policies will usually increase administrative and compliance costs. However, ex post  analysis shows that transaction costs of mitigation policies are low and are not a decisive factor in policy choice ([Joas and Flachsland 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Joas--2016)).

The effectiveness, as well as economic and distributional effects, of a given mitigation policy will depend on the interactions among all the policies that affect the targeted emissions. Because a market instrument interacts with every other policy that affects the targeted emissions, interactions tend to be more complex for market instruments than for regulations that mandate specific emission reduction actions by targeted sources independent of other policies.

An ETS scheme implemented with existing mitigation policies may be subject to the ‘waterbed effect’ – emission reductions undertaken by some emitters may be offset by higher emissions by other ETS participants due to overlapping mitigation policies ([Schatzki and Stavins 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schatzki--2012)). This reduces the impact of the ETS and lowers carbon trading prices ([Perino 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Perino--2018)). However ex post  assessments find net emissions reductions. ETS design features such as a price floor and ‘market stability reserve’ can limit the waterbed effect ([Edenhofer et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Edenhofer--2017); [Kollenberg and Taschini 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kollenberg--2019); [Narassimhan et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kollenberg--2019); [Narassimhan et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Narassimhan--2018); [FSR Climate 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#FSR%20Climate--2019)).

A carbon tax, unlike the allowance price, does not change in response to the effect of overlapping policies but those policies may reduce emissions by sources subject to the tax and so lower the emission reductions achieved by the tax ([Goulder and Stavins 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Goulder--2011)).
