Policy interactions often occur with the introduction of new mitigation policy instruments. For example, in China several sub-national ETSs exist alongside policies to reduce emission intensity, increase energy efficiency and expand renewable energy supplies ([Zhang 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhang--2015)). These quantity-based ETSs interact with many other policies ([Duan et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duan--2017)), for example price-based provincial carbon intensity targets ([Qian et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Qian--2017)). They also interact with the level of market regulation; for example, full effectiveness of emissions pricing would require electricity market reform in China ([Teng et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Teng--2017)).

Policy packages aimed at low-carbon transitions are more effective when they include elements to enhance the phase out of carbon-intensive technologies and practices – often called exnovation – in addition to supporting low-carbon niches ([Kivimaa and Kern 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kivimaa--2016); [David 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#David--2017)). Such policies include stringent carbon pricing; changes in regime rules such as design of electricity markets; reduced support for dominant regime technologies such as removing tax deductions for private motor transport based on internal combustion engines; and changes in the balance of representation of incumbents versus new entrants in deliberation and advisory bodies

. For example, CGE modelling for China’s fossil fuel subsidy reform found that integrating both creation and destabilisation policies is able to reduce rebound effects and make the policy mix more effective ([Li et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Li--2017)). Sweden’s pulp and paper industry shows that destabilisation policies including deregulation of the electricity market and a carbon tax were an important complement to support policies ([Scordato et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Scordato--2018)), and other studies show complementary results for Finland’s building sector ([Kivimaa et al. 2017b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kivimaa--2017b)) and Norway’s transport and energy sector ([Ćetković and Skjærseth 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%C4%86etkovi%C4%87--2019)).

Policy packages for low-carbon transitions are more successful if they take into account the potential for political contestation and resistance from incumbents who benefit from high-carbon systems (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Geels 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Geels--2014); [Roberts et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roberts--2018); [Kern and Rogge 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kern--2018); [Rosenbloom 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rosenbloom--2018)). To do so, policies can be sequenced so as to address political obstacles, for example, by initially starting with policies to facilitate the entry of new firms engaged in low-carbon technologies ([Pahle et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pahle--2018))

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pahle--2018)). Such policies can generate positive feedbacks by creating constituencies for continuation of those policies, but need to be designed to do so from the outset ([Edmondson et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Edmondson--2019), 2020). For example, supporting renewable energies through feed-in tariffs can buttress coalitions for more ambitious climate policy, such as through carbon pricing ([Meckling et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Meckling--2015)). However, negative policy feedback may also arise from ineffective policy instruments that lose public support, or create concentrated losses that arouse oppositional coalitions ([Edmondson et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Edmondson--2019))

. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Edmondson--2019)). Feedback loops can operate through changes in resources available to actors; changes in expectations; and changes in government capacities ([Edmondson et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Edmondson--2019)).

Another promising strategy is to design short-term policies which might help to provide later entry points for more ambitious climate policy ([Kriegler et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kriegler--2018)) and supportive institutions. The sequencing of policies can build coalitions for climate policy, starting with green industrial policy (e.g. supporting renewable energies through feed-in tariffs) and introducing or making carbon pricing more stringent when supportive coalitions of stringent climate policy have been formed ([Meckling et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Meckling--2015)). Similarly, investing in supportive institutions, with competencies compatible with low-carbon futures, are a necessary supportive element of transitions ([Pahle et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pahle--2018); [Rosenbloom et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Pahle--2018); [Rosenbloom et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rosenbloom--2019); [Domorenok et al. 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Domorenok--2021)).

##  13.7.2Policy Integration for Multiple Objectives and Shifting Development Pathways ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
This sub-section assesses policy integration and packages required to enable shifts in development pathways, with a particular focus on sectoral scale transitions. However, because shifting development pathways requires broad transformative change, it complements discussion on broader shifts in policymaking such as fiscal, educational, and infrastructure policies (Cross-Chapter Box 5 in Chapter 4) and to the alignment of a wide range of enabling conditions required for system transitions ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)).

In many countries, and particularly when climate policy occurs in the context of sustainable development, policymakers seek to address climate mitigation in the context of multiple economic and social policy objectives (medium evidence, robust agreement ) ([Halsnæs et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Halsn%C3%A6s--2014); [Campagnolo and Davide 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Campagnolo--2019); [Cohen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cohen--2019)). Studies suggest that co-benefits of climate policies are substantial, especially in relation to air quality, and can yield better mitigation and overall welfare, yet these are commonly overlooked in policymaking (robust evidence, robust agreement ) ([Nemet et al. 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nemet--2010); [Ürge-Vorsatz et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc

. 2010](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nemet--2010); [Ürge-Vorsatz et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%C3%9Crge-Vorsatz--2014); [von Stechow et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#von%20Stechow--2015); [Mayrhofer and Gupta 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayrhofer--2016); [Roy et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roy--2018); [Bhardwaj et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bhardwaj--2019); [Karlsson et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Karlsson--2020)). Other studies have shown the existence of strong complementarities between the SDGs and realisation of NDC pledges by countries ([McCollum et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCollum--2018))

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCollum--2018)). An explicit attention to development pathways can enhance the scope for mitigation, by paying explicit attention to development choices that lock-in or lock-out opportunities for mitigation, such as around land use and infrastructure choices (Cross-Chapter Box 5 in Chapter 4). While the pay-offs are considerable to an approach to mitigation that takes into account linkages to multiple objectives and the opportunity to shift development pathways, there are also associated challenges with implementing this approach to policymaking.

First, spanning policy arenas and addressing multiple objectives places considerable requirements of coordination on the policymaking process (Howlett and del Rio 2015; [Obersteiner et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Obersteiner--2016)). Climate policy integration suggests several steps should precede actual policy formulation, beginning with a clear articulation of the policy frame or problem statement ([Adelle and Russel 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Adelle--2013); [Candel and Biesbroek 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Candel--2016)). For example, a greenhouse gas limitation framework versus a co-benefits framing would likely yield different policy approaches

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Candel--2016)). For example, a greenhouse gas limitation framework versus a co-benefits framing would likely yield different policy approaches. It is then useful to identify the range of actors and institutions involved in climate governance – the policy subsystem, the goals articulated, the level at which goals are articulated and the links with other related policy goals such as energy security or energy access ([Candel and Biesbroek 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Candel--2016)). The adoption of specific packages of policy instruments should ideally follow these prior steps that define the scope of the problem, actors and goals.

In practice, integration has to occur in the context of an already existing policy structure, which suggests the need for finding windows of opportunity to bring about integration, which can be created by international events, alignments with domestic institutional procedures, and openings created by policy entrepreneurs ([Garcia Hernandez and Bolwig 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Garcia%20Hernandez--2020)). Integration also has to occur in the context of existing organisational routines and cultures, which can pose a barrier to integration ([Uittenbroek 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Uittenbroek--2016)). Experience from the EU suggests that disagreements at the level of policy instruments are amenable to resolution by deliberation, while normative disagreements at the level of objectives require a hierarchical decision structure ([Skovgaard 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skovgaard--2018))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Skovgaard--2018)). As this discussion suggests, the challenge of integration operates in two dimensions: horizontal – between sectoral authorities such as ministries or policy domains such as forestry – or vertical – either between constitutional levels of power or within the internal mandates and interactions of a sector ([Howlett and del Rio 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Howlett--2015); [Di Gregorio et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2017)). There are also important temporal dimensions to policy goals, as policy and benchmarks have to address not just immediate success but also indications of future transformation ([Dupont and Oberthür 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dupont--2012); [Dupont 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dupont--2015)).

Second policymaking for shifting development pathways has to account for inherent uncertainties in future development paths ([Moallemi and Malekpour 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Moallemi--2018); [Castrejon-Campos et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Castrejon-Campos--2020)). These uncertainties may be greater in developing countries that are growing rapidly and where structural features of the economy including infrastructure and urbanisation patterns are fluid. For example, reviews of modelling studies of Chinese ([Grubb et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grubb--2015)) and Indian emissions futures (Spencer and [Dubash 2021](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)) find that differences in projections can substantially be accounted for by alternative assumptions about future economic structural shifts

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dubash--2021)) find that differences in projections can substantially be accounted for by alternative assumptions about future economic structural shifts. Consequently, an important design consideration is that policy packages should be robust, that is, perform satisfactorily for all key objectives under a broad range of plausible futures ([Kwakkel et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kwakkel--2016); [Maier et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Maier--2016); [Castrejon-Campos et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Castrejon-Campos--2020)). Such an approach to decision-making can be contrasted with one that tries to design an optimal policy package for the ‘best guess’ future scenario ([Maier et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Maier--2016))

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Maier--2016)). Moreover, policy packages can usefully be adapted dynamically to changing circumstances as part of the policy process ([Haasnoot et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Haasnoot--2013); [Hamarat et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hamarat--2014); [Maier et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Maier--2016)) including by using exploratory modelling techniques that allow comparison of trade-offs across alternative future scenarios ([Hamarat et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hamarat--2014)). Another approach is to link quantitative models with a participatory process that enables decision-makers to test the implications of alternative interventions ([Moallemi and Malekpour 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Moallemi--2018)). [Rosenbloom et al. (2019)](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Moallemi--2018)). [Rosenbloom et al. (2019)](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rosenbloom--2019) suggest that because policy mixes should adapt to changing circumstances, instead of stability of a particular mix, transitions require embedding policies within a long-term orientation toward a low-carbon economy, including a transition agenda, social legitimacy for this agenda, and an appropriate ecosystem of institutions.

Third, achieving changes in development pathways requires engaging with place-specific context. It requires attention to existing policies, political interests that may gain or lose from a transition, and locally specific governance enablers and disablers. As a result, while there may be approaches that carry over from one context to another, implementation requires careful tailoring of transition approaches to specific policy and governance contexts. Cross-Chapter Box 9 in this chapter summarises case studies of sectoral transitions from other chapters in this report (Chapters 5 to 12) to illustrate this complexity. Broader macroeconomic transformative shifts are discussed in more detail in [Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9).

Common to all the sectoral cases in Cross-Chapter Box 9 is a future-oriented vision of sectoral transition often focused on multiple objectives, such as designing tram-based public transport systems in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe to simultaneously stimulate urban centers, create jobs and enable low-carbon transportation. Sectoral transitions are enabled by policy mixes that bring together different combinations of instruments – including regulations, financial incentives, convening, education and outreach, voluntary agreements, procurement and creation of new institutions – to work together in a complementary manner. The effectiveness of a policy mix depends on conditions beyond design considerations and also rests on the larger governance context within which sector transitions occur, which can include enabling and disabling elements

. Enabling factors illustrated in Cross-Chapter Box 9 include strong high level political support, for example to address deforestation in Brazil despite powerful logging and farmer interests, or policy design to win over existing private interests, for example, by harnessing distribution networks of kerosene providers to new LPG technology in Indonesia. Disabling conditions include local institutional contexts, such as the lack of tree and land tenure in Ghana, which, along with the monopoly of the state marketing board, posed obstacles to Ghana’s low-carbon cocoa transition. These examples emphasise the importance of attention to local context if policy integration and the design of policy mixes are to effectively lead to transitions guided by multiple climate and development objectives.

#  13.8Integrating Adaptation, Mitigation and Sustainable Development ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)Expand section

There is growing consensus that integration of adaptation and mitigation will advance progress towards sustainable development, and that ambitious mitigation efforts will reduce the need for adaptation in the long term (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([IPCC 2014a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2014a)). There is no level of mitigation, however, that will completely erase the need for adaptation to climate change (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Mauritsen and Pincus 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mauritsen--2017)). It is therefore urgent to design and implement a multi-objective policy framework for mitigation, adaptation, and sustainable development that considers issues of equity and long-term developmental pathways across regions (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Jordan et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jordan--2018); [Mills‐Novoa and Liverman 2019](https://www.ipcc

. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Jordan--2018); [Mills‐Novoa and Liverman 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mills%E2%80%90Novoa--2019); [Wang and Chen 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wang--2019)). This section explores the logic behind the integration of adaptation and mitigation in practice ([Section 13.8.1](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.8.1)), the approaches to this integration including climate-resilient pathways, ecosystem-based solutions, and a nexus approach ([Section 13.8.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.8.2)); examples of the adaption and mitigation relationships and linkages ([Section 13.8.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.8.3)); and enabling and disabling factors for governance of mitigation and adaption.
##  13.8.1 Synergies Between Adaptation and Mitigation ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Integrated climate-development actions require a context-specific understanding of synergies and trade-offs with other policy priorities (Figure 13.6) with the aim of implementing mitigation/adaptation policies that reduce GHG emissions while simultaneously strengthening resilience and reducing vulnerability (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Klein et al. 2005](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klein--2005); [IPCC 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2007); [Zhao et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zhao--2018); [Mills‐Novoa and Liverman 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mills%E2%80%90Novoa--2019); [Solecki et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solecki--2019))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mills%E2%80%90Novoa--2019); [Solecki et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solecki--2019)). Efficient, equitable and inclusive policies which also acknowledge and contribute directly to other pressing priorities such reducing poverty, improving health, providing access to clean water, and fostering sustainable consumption and production practices are helpful for mitigation/adaptation goals (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Landauer et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Landauer--2019); [Grafakos et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grafakos--2020)).

Adaptation and mitigation are deeply linked in practice – at the local level, for instance, asset managers address integrated low-carbon resilience to climate change impacts and urban planners do the same ([Ürge-Vorsatz et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#%C3%9Crge-Vorsatz--2018); [Grafakos et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grafakos--2020)) (Table 13.3). Similarly, ecosystem-based (or nature-based) solutions, may generate co-benefits by simultaneously sinking carbon, cooling urban areas through shading, purifying water, improving biodiversity, and offering recreational opportunities that improve public health ([Raymond et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Raymond--2017)). Accurately identifying and qualitatively or quantitatively assessing these co-benefits ([Stadelmann et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Raymond--2017)). Accurately identifying and qualitatively or quantitatively assessing these co-benefits ([Stadelmann et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Stadelmann--2014); [Leiter and Pringle 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Leiter--2018); [Leiter et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Leiter--2019)) is central to an integrated adaptation and mitigation policy evaluation.

Some studies press the need to consider the complex ways that power and interests influence how collective decisions are made, and who benefits from and pays for these decisions, of climate policy and to be aware of unintended consequences, especially for vulnerable people living under poor conditions ([Mayrhofer and Gupta 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayrhofer--2016); [De Oliveira Silva et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#De%20Oliveira%20Silva--2018)). The specific adaptation and mitigation linkages will differ by country and region, as illustrated by Box 13.15.
##  Box 13.15 | Adaptation and Mitigation Synergies in Africa![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Synergies between mitigation and adaptation actions and sustainable development that can enhance the quality and pace of development in Africa exist at both sectoral and national levels. Available data on NDCs show the top mitigation priorities in African countries include energy, forestry, transport and agriculture and waste, and adaptation priorities focus on agriculture, water, energy and forestry. The energy sector dominates in mitigation actions and the agricultural sector is the main focus of adaptation measures, with the latter sector being a slightly larger source of greenhouse gases than the former ([Mbeva et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mbeva--2015); [African Development Bank 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#African%20Development%20Bank--2019); [Nyiwul 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nyiwul--2019)).

Renewable energy development can support synergies between mitigation and adaptation by stimulating local and national economies through microenterprise development; providing off-grid affordable and accessible solutions; and contributing to poverty reduction through increased locally available resource use and employment and increased technical skills ([Nyiwul 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nyiwul--2019); [Dal Maso et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dal%20Maso--2020)). The Paris Agreement’s technology transfer and funding mechanisms could reduce renewable energy costs and providing scale economics to local economies.

Barriers to achieving these synergies include the absence of suitable macro-and micro- level policy environments for adaptation and mitigation actions; coherent climate change policy frameworks and governance structures to support adaptation; institutional and capacity deficiencies in climate and policy research such as on data integration and technical analysis; and the high financial needs associated with the cost of mitigation and adaptation ([African Development Bank 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#African%20Development%20Bank--2019); [Nyiwul 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nyiwul--2019))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#African%20Development%20Bank--2019); [Nyiwul 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nyiwul--2019)). Strengthening of national institutions and policies can support maximising synergies and co-benefits between adaptation and mitigation to reduce silos and redundant overlaps, increase knowledge exchange at the country and regional levels, and support engagement with bilateral and multilateral partners and mobilising finance through the mechanisms available ([African Development Bank 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#African%20Development%20Bank--2019)).
##  13.8.2Frameworks That Enable the Integration of Adaption and Mitigation ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

The IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report  (AR5) emphasised the importance of climate-resilient pathways – development trajectories that combine adaptation and mitigation through specific actions to achieve the sustainable development goals ([Prasad et al. 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Prasad--2009); [Lewison et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Lewison--2015); [Fankhauser and McDermott 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fankhauser--2016); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2016); [Solecki et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Solecki--2019)) – from the household to the state level, since risks and opportunities vary by location and the specific local development context (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([IPCC 2014b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2014b); [Denton et al
.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2014b); [Denton et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Denton--2015)).

Synergies between adaptation and mitigation are included in many of the NDCs submitted to the UNFCCC, as part of overall low-emissions climate-resilient development strategies ([UNFCCC Secretariat 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UNFCCC%20Secretariat--2016)). a majority of developing countries have agreed to develop National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) in which many initiatives contribute simultaneously to the SDGs ([Schipper et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Schipper--2020)) as well to mitigation efforts ([Hönle et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#H%C3%B6nle--2019); [Atteridge et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Atteridge--2020)). For example, developing countries recognise that adaptation actions in sectors such as agriculture, forestry and land-use management can reduce GHGs

. For example, developing countries recognise that adaptation actions in sectors such as agriculture, forestry and land-use management can reduce GHGs. Nevertheless, other more complex trade-offs also exist between bioenergy production or reforestation and the land needed for agricultural adaptation and food security ([African Development Bank 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#African%20Development%20Bank--2019); [Hönle et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#H%C3%B6nle--2019); [Nyiwul 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nyiwul--2019)) (Chapter 7). For some of the Small Islands Development States (SIDS), forestry and coastal management, including mangrove planting, saltmarsh and seagrass are sectors that intertwine both mitigation and adaptation ([Duarte et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duarte--2013); [Atteridge et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc

. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duarte--2013); [Atteridge et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Atteridge--2020)). Integrated efforts also occur at the city level, such as the Climate Change Action Plan of Wellington City, which includes enhancing forest sinks to increase carbon sequestration while at the same time protecting biodiversity and reducing groundwater runoff as rainfall increases ([Grafakos et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grafakos--2019)).

To fully maximise their potential co-benefits and trade-offs of integrating adaptation and mitigation, these should be explicitly sought, rather than accidentally discovered ([Spencer et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Spencer--2017); [Berry et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Berry--2015)), and policies designed to account for both (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Caetano et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Caetano--2020)). For example, the REDD+ initiative focus on mitigation by carbon sequestration was set up to provide co-benefits such as: nature protection, political inclusion, monetary income, economic opportunities

. However, some unintended trade-offs may have occurred such as physical displacement, loss of livelihoods, increased human–wildlife conflicts, property claims, food security concerns, and an unequal distribution of benefits to local population groups ([Bushley 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bushley--2014); [Duguma et al. 2014a](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duguma--2014a); [Gebara et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gebara--2014); [Kongsager and Corbera 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kongsager--2015); [Anderson et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Anderson--2016); [Di Gregorio et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2016), 2017)

. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Anderson--2016); [Di Gregorio et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2016), 2017). Ultimately, ecosystem (or nature-based) strategies, such as the use of wetlands to create accessible recreational areas that improve public health while improving biodiversity, sinking carbon and protecting neighbourhoods from extreme flooding events, may lead to more efficient and cost-effective policies ([Klein et al. 2005](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klein--2005); [Locatelli et al. 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Locatelli--2011); [Kongsager et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kongsager--2016); [Mills‐Novoa and Liverman 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mills%E2%80%90Novoa--2019)).

The ‘nexus’ approach is another widely used framework that describes the linkages between water, energy, food, health and other socio-economic factors in some integrated assessment approaches ([Rasul and Sharma 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Rasul--2016)). The Food-Energy-Water (FEW)nexus, for example, considers how water is required for energy production and supply (and thus tied to mitigation), how energy is needed to treat and transport water, and how both are critical to adaptable and resilient food production systems ([Mohtar and Daher 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mohtar--2014); [Biggs et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Biggs--2015)). Climate change impacts all these dimensions in the form of multi-hazard risk ([Froese and Schilling 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Froese--2019))

. Climate change impacts all these dimensions in the form of multi-hazard risk ([Froese and Schilling 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Froese--2019)). Although integrative, the FEW nexus faces many challenges including: limited knowledge integration; coordination between different institutions and levels of government; politics and power; cultural values; and ways of managing climate risk ([Leck and Roberts 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Leck--2015); [Romero-Lankao et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2017); [Mercure et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mercure--2019)). More empirical assessment is needed to identify potential overlaps between sectoral portfolios, as this could help to delineate resources allocation for synergies and to avoid trade-offs.
##  Box 13.16 | Latin America Region Adaptation Linking Mitigation: REDD+ Lessons ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Thirty-three countries in the Latin American region have submitted their NDCs, and 70% of their initiatives have included mitigation and adaptation options focusing on sustainable development ([Bárcena et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A1rcena--2018); [Kissinger et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kissinger--2019)). However, most of these policies are disconnected across sectors ([Loaiza et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Loaiza--2017); [Locatelli et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Locatelli--2017)). National governments have identified their relevant sectors as: energy, agriculture, forestry, land-use change, biodiversity, and water resources (see Figure 1 below). The region houses 57% of the primary forest of the planet. REDD+ aims to reduce GHG while provide ecosystems services to vulnerable communities ([Bárcena et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc

. The region houses 57% of the primary forest of the planet. REDD+ aims to reduce GHG while provide ecosystems services to vulnerable communities ([Bárcena et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#B%C3%A1rcena--2018)). Lessons from successful REDD+ programmes include the benefits of a multilevel structure from international to national down to strong community organisation, as well as secure resources funding, with most of the projects relying on external sources of funding (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([Loaiza et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Loaiza--2017); [Kissinger et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kissinger--2019))

. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Loaiza--2017); [Kissinger et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kissinger--2019)). However, there is limited evidence of effective adaptation co-benefits, which may be related to the lack of provision of forest standards; a disproportionate focus on mitigation and lack of attention to the well-being of the population in rural and agricultural areas ([Kongsager and Corbera 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kongsager--2015)).

Conflicts have emerged over political views, government priorities of resources (oil, bioenergy, hydropower), and weak governance among national and local authorities, indigenous groups and other stakeholders such as NGOs which play a critical role in the technological and financial support for the REDD+ initiative ([Reed 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Reed--2011); [Kashwan 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kashwan--2015); [Gebara et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gebara--2014); [Locatelli et al. 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Locatelli--2011), 2017). a more holistic approach which recognises these social, environmental and political drivers would appear to have benefits but assessment is needed to allow evidence-based actionable policy statements.

###  13.8.3.1Governing the Linkages Between Mitigation and Adaptation at the Local, Regional, and Global Scales ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

International policy frameworks, such as the 2015 Paris Agreement, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Disk Reduction, and the New Urban Agenda for sustainable urban systems, provide an integrated approach for both adaptation and mitigation, while promoting sustainable development and climate resilience across scales (from global, regional, to local government actions (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Duguma et al. 2014b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duguma--2014b); [Heidrich et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heidrich--2016); [Di Gregorio et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2017); [Locatelli et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Locatelli--2017); [Nachmany and Setzer 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nachmany--2018); [Mills‐Novoa and Liverman 2019](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nachmany--2018); [Mills‐Novoa and Liverman 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mills%E2%80%90Novoa--2019)). Even so, the specific ways that these linkages are governed vary widely depending on institutional and jurisdictional scale, competing policy priorities, and available capacity ([Landauer et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Landauer--2019)).

Supranational levels of action such as the EU climate change policy have influenced the development and implementation of Climate Change Action Plans (CCAPs) at the sub-national level ([Heidrich et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heidrich--2016); [Villarroel Walker et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Villarroel%20Walker--2017); [Reckien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Reckien--2018)). While adaptation is gaining prominence and is increasingly included in the NDCs of EU nations, the implementation of adaptation and mitigation by EU states are at different stages ([Fleig et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fleig--2017)). [Fleig et al. (2017)](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fleig--2017) found that all EU states, with the exception of Hungary, have adopted a framework of laws tackling mitigation and adaptation to climate change

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Fleig--2017) found that all EU states, with the exception of Hungary, have adopted a framework of laws tackling mitigation and adaptation to climate change. However, an assessment of climate legislation in Europe pointed out that there has been little coordination between mitigation and adaptation, and that implementation varies according to different national conditions ([Nachmany et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nachmany--2015)). More recently, however, integrated adaptation/mitigation plans have been prepared in Europe under the Covenant of Mayors, in which synergies and trade-offs can be better revealed and assessed ([Bertoldi et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bertoldi--2020)).

Local governments and cities are increasingly emerging as important climate change actors ([Gordon and Acuto 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gordon--2015)) ([Section 13.5](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.5)). While cities and local governments are developing Climate Change Action Plans (CCAPs), plans that explicitly integrate the design and implementation of adaptation and mitigation are a minor percentage, with few cities establishing inter-relationships between them ([Nordic Council of Ministers 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nordic%20Council%20of%20Ministers--2017); [Grafakos et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Grafakos--2018)). Compared to national climate governance, local governments are more likely to develop and advance climate policies, generating socio-economic or environmental co-benefits, and improve communities’ quality of life ([Gill et al. 2007](https://www.ipcc

. 2007](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gill--2007); [Bowen et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bowen--2014); [Duguma et al. 2014b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duguma--2014b); [Mayrhofer and Gupta 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Mayrhofer--2016); [Deng et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Deng--2017); [Hennessey et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hennessey--2017)). ##  13.8.4Integrated Governance Including Equity and Sustainable Development ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
Climate policy integration carries implications for the pursuit of the SDGs, given that it is nearly impossible to achieve the desired socio-economic gains if fundamental environmental issues, such as climate change, are not addressed ([Gomez-Echeverri 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Gomez-Echeverri--2018)). Research on climate resilient development pathways ([Roy et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Roy--2018)), for instance, argues for long-term policy planning that combines the governance of national climate and SD goals, builds institutional capacity across all sectors, jurisdictions, and actors, and enhances participation and transparency (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Chapter 4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-4) and 17).

In the Global South, climate change policies are often established in the context of sustainable development and of other pressing local priorities (e.g., air pollution, health, and food security). National climate policy in these countries tends to give prominence to adaptation based on country vulnerability, climatic risk, gender-based differences in exposur to that risk, and the importance of local/traditional and indigenous knowledge ([Beg et al. 2002](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Beg--2002); [Duguma et al. 2014b](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duguma--2014b)). Despite the evidence that integrated mitigation and adaptation policies can be effective and efficient ([Klein et al. 2005](https://www.ipcc

.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Duguma--2014b)). Despite the evidence that integrated mitigation and adaptation policies can be effective and efficient ([Klein et al. 2005](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klein--2005)) and can potentially reduce trade-offs, there is still limited evidence of how such integrated policies would specifically contribute to progress on the SDGs (robust evidence,  high agreement ) (Kongsager et al.2016; [Di Gregorio et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2017); [Antwi-Agyei et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Antwi-Agyei--2018); De Coninck et al. 2018; [Campagnolo and Davide 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Campagnolo--2019)).

Where mainstreaming of environmental concerns has been attempted through national plans, they have had success in some cases when backed by strong political commitments that support a vertical coordination structure rather than horizontal structures led by the focus ministry ([Nunan et al. 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nunan--2012)). Such political commitments are therefore crucial to success but insufficient in and of themselves ([Runhaar et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Runhaar--2018); [Wamsler et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wamsler--2020)). Integration of the budget process is particularly important, as are aligned time frames across different objectives ([Saito 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Saito--2013))

. Integration of the budget process is particularly important, as are aligned time frames across different objectives ([Saito 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Saito--2013)). Recognition of the functional interactions across policy sectors is improved by a translation of long-term policy objectives into a plan that aligns with integration goals ([Corry 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Corry--2012); [Oels 2012](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Oels--2012); [Dupont 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dupont--2019)).

There are important links between inequality, justice and climate change ([Ikeme 2003](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ikeme--2003); [Bailey 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bailey--2017)). Many of these operate through the benefits, costs and risks of climate action (distributive justice), while others focus on differential participation and recognition of sub-national actors and marginalised groups (procedural justice) ([Bulkeley and Castán Broto 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Bulkeley et al. 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bulkeley--2013); [Hughes 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2013); [Reckien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Reckien--2018); [Romero-Lankao and Gnatz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2019)).

Justice principles are rarely incorporated in climate change framing and action([Sovacool and Dworkin 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Sovacool--2015); [Genus and Theobald 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Genus--2016); [Heikkinen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Heikkinen--2019); [Romero-Lankao and Gnatz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2019)). Yet, equity is salient to mitigation debates, because climate change mitigation policies can have also negative impacts ([Brugnach et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Brugnach--2017); [Ramos-Castillo et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Ramos-Castillo--2017); [Klinsky 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klinsky--2018)), exacerbated by poverty, inequality and corruption([Reckien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Klinsky--2018)), exacerbated by poverty, inequality and corruption([Reckien et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Reckien--2018); [Markkanen and Anger-Kraavi 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Markkanen--2019)). The siting of facilities and infrastructure that advance decarbonisation (such as public transit infrastructure, renewable energy facilities and so on) may have implications for environmental justice. Integrated attention to justice in climate, environment and energy, as well as involvement of host communities in siting assessments and decision-making processes, can help to avoid such conflict ([McCord et al. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCord--2020); [Hughes and Hoffmann 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2020))

. 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#McCord--2020); [Hughes and Hoffmann 2020](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Hughes--2020)). As a result, successful policy integration goes beyond optimising public management routines, and must resolve key trade-offs between actors and objectives ([Meadowcroft 2009](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Meadowcroft--2009); [Nordbeck and Steurer 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nordbeck--2016)).

The potential for transformative climate change policy that delivers both adaptation and mitigation is also shaped by a number of enabling and disabling factors tied to governance processes (robust evidence,  high agreement ) ([Burch et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burch--2014)) ([Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9)).
##  Box 13.17 | Enabling and Disabling Factors for Integrated Governance of Mitigationand Adaptation![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

Ensuring participatory governance and social inclusion. Interlinkages in the food-energy-water nexus highlight the importance of inclusive processes ([Shaw et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Shaw--2014); [Nakano et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Nakano--2017); [Cook and Chu 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cook--2018); [Romero-Lankao and Gnatz 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Romero-Lankao--2019)). The cultivation of urban grassroots innovations and social innovation may accelerate progress ([Wolfram and Frantzeskaki 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Wolfram--2016)), as may the development of carefully-designed climate and energy dialogues that enable learning among multiple stakeholders ([Cashore et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cashore--2019)).

Considering synergies and trade-offs with broader sustainable development priorities. The explicit consideration of synergies and trade-offs will enable more integrated policy making ([Dang et al. 2003](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Dang--2003); [von Stechow et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#von%20Stechow--2015)). Policy frameworks to do so are just emerging, such as analysis of trade-offs between energy and water policies and agriculture ([Huggel et al. 2015](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Huggel--2015); [Antwi-Agyei et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Antwi-Agyei--2018)).

Employing a diverse set of tools to reach targets. Building codes, land-use plans, public education initiatives, and nature-based solutions such as green ways may impact adaptation and mitigation simultaneously ([Burch et al. 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burch--2014)). Ecological restoration provides another suite of tools, for instance the Brazilian target of restoring and reforesting 0.12 million km 2 of forests by 2030, which can enhance biodiversity and ecosystem services while also sinking carbon ([Bustamante et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Bustamante--2019)). Mandatory retrofits to improve indoor air quality can also increase energy efficiency and resilience to climate change impacts ([Friel et al. 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Friel--2011); [Houghton 2011](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Houghton--2011)).

Monitoring and evaluating key indicators, beyond only greenhouse gas emissions, such as biodiversity, water quality, and affordability: An integrated approach requires robust process for collecting data on these indicators. Challenges are related to the limited evidence-base on synergies, co-benefits, and trade-offs across sectors and jurisdictions ([Di Gregorio et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Di%20Gregorio--2016); [Kongsager et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kongsager--2016); [Locatelli et al. 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Locatelli--2017); [Zen et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Zen--2019)). Moreover, adaptation policies mostly lack measurable targets or expected outcomes increasing the challenge of designing an integrated framework ([OECD 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#OECD--2017)).

Iterative and adaptive management. Adaptive management helps to address the underlying uncertainty ([Kundzewicz et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Kundzewicz--2018)) that characterises implementation of integrated approaches to adaptation and mitigation. Policy integration needs to be considered iteratively along the process of development, implementation, and evaluation of climate policies.
Strategic partnerships that coordinate efforts.  Strategic partnerships among diverse actors, therefore, bring diverse technical skills and capacities to the endeavour ([Burch et al. 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Burch--2016); [Islam and Khan 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Islam--2017)). However, realising strategic approaches for joint adaptation and mitigation require adequate financial, technical and human resources.

Participatory and collaborative planning approaches can help overcome injustices and address power differentials. Participatory and collaborative planning approaches can provide multiple spaces of deliberation where marginalised voices can be heard ([Blue and Medlock 2014](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Blue--2014); [UN Habitat 2016](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#UN%20Habitat--2016); [Castán Broto and Westman 2017](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Cast%C3%A1n%20Broto--2017); [Waisman et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Waisman--2019)). These tools organise climate and sustainability action by addressing its democratic deficit and facilitating the recognition of multiple perspectives in environmental planning alongside material limits of development ([Agyeman 2013](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Agyeman--2013)).

##  13.9.1Introduction ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)
[Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9) assesses literature related to economy wide and cross – sector systemic change as an approach to accelerate climate mitigation.

It focuses specifically on policy and institutions, as two of the six enabling conditions for economy-wide system change and thus provides a third dimension of the role of policy and institutions to climate mitigation. Enabling conditions in general are discussed in [Chapter 4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-4) of the SR1.5 ([IPCC 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2018)), as well as [Chapter 4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-4) of this report. This section follows on from [Section 13.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.6) (single policy instruments) and 13.7 (policy packages). [Section 13.9](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9) literature follows closely on from [Section 13.7](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.7) literature on policy packages, which discusses change within one system, although there remains an overlap.

[Section 13.9.2](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9.2) provides a brief introduction to policy and institutions as two of the six dimensions of enabling conditions, and the importance of enabling conditions to systemic change and climate mitigation. [Section 13.9.3](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9.3) briefly introduces actions for transformative justice, which seek to restructure the underlying system framework that produces mitigation inequalities. [Section 13.9.4](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9.4) provides a brief overview of net zero policies and targets (often no more than aspirational), which imply economy-wide measures and system change. [Section 13.9.5](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9.5) assesses the literature arguing for a system restructuring approach to climate mitigation, based on systemic restructuring. [Section 13.9.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9

.9.5) assesses the literature arguing for a system restructuring approach to climate mitigation, based on systemic restructuring. [Section 13.9.6](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9.6) assesses the literature on stimulus packages and green new deals which aim for systemic change, sometimes with value for climate mitigation. And finally, [Section 13.9.7](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-13#13.9.7) assesses emerging literatures which argues that there are existing challenges to accelerating climate mitigation that may be overcome by systemic change and targeted actions.
##  13.9.2Enabling Acceleration ![](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/share.png)

IPCC AR6 WG3, particularly Chapter 4, following on from the IPCC WG3 SR1.5 ([IPCC 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2018)), has highlighted the importance of enabling conditions for delivering successful climate mitigation actions. The AR6 Glossary term for enabling conditions is: ‘enabling conditions include finance, technological innovation, strengthening policy instruments, institutional capacity, multi-level governance, and changes in human behaviour and lifestyles (medium evidence,  high agreement ) (see Glossary). The IPCC SR1.5 report adds to these six dimensions saying enabling conditions also includes ‘inclusive processes, attention to power asymmetries and unequal opportunities for development and reconsideration of values’ (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([IPCC 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2018))

.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2018)). Not only is the presence of enabling conditions necessary for delivering the successful implementation of single policy instruments and policy packages, but also for delivering systemic change (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([de Coninck et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#de%20Coninck--2018); [IPCC 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#IPCC--2018); [Waisman et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Waisman--2019)). The feasibility of 1.5°C compatible pathways is contingent upon enabling conditions for systemic change (medium evidence,  high agreement ) ([de Coninck et al. 2018](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#de%20Coninck--2018); [Waisman et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Waisman--2019)).

At the same time, again following on from SR1.5 report, [Section 1.8.1](https://www.ipcc.ch/chapters/chapter-1#1.8.1) explains that there are six feasibility dimensions of successful delivery of climate goals. These feasibility dimensions include geophysical; environmental and ecological; technological; economic; behaviour and lifestyles and institutional dimensions. The presence or absence of enabling conditions would affect the feasibility of mitigation as well as adaptation pathways and can reduce trade-offs while amplifying synergies between options ([Waisman et al. 2019](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-13/#Waisman--2019)). Policies and institutions, which are two of the six enabling conditions, are therefore central to accelerated mitigation and systemic change
